While fellow "The Odyssey" co-stars Zendaya and Anne Hathaway have stolen the spotlight for similar reasons throughout 2026, the "Primetime" actor has quietly appeared in quite a few high-profile roles throughout the last several months. A24's "The Drama" (also co-starring Zendaya) left quite the impression on audiences and at the box office, as did the aforementioned retelling of "The Odyssey" by Christopher Nolan. And, as if his memorable line about getting "these beggars out of here" wasn't enough, he's set to follow all that up with a turn in "Dune: Part Three" later this December.

But don't sleep on "Primetime," the other major production by "You Can See Everything" co-director Lance Oppenheim this year. Starring Pattinson as Chris Hansen, the host behind the controversial TV show in the early aughts "To Catch a Predator," the film takes an unflinching, stylish, and occasionally surrealistic approach to the real-life figure who publicly shamed and embarrassed so many troubled minds with nefarious intent. But was this done for heroic and well-intentioned reasons? Or is there more to be uncovered beneath that bleached hair, distinctive voice, and wild-eyed chase for ratings and pop-culture buzz?

Well, audiences will now get a chance to decide for themselves, as "Primetime" is being made available to watch at home. The news comes a little over a month after its release in theaters, where it's actually still playing in certain locations. But for those who may have missed it the first time around, read on for all the details about how to catch it from the comfort of your living room.

The dark and unsettling satire that is "Primetime" is officially coming home, which is certain to lend a strong sense of irony to anyone watching this A24 movie about one of the most notorious television shows ever made. Based on the real-life controversy surrounding host Chris Hansen and his "To Catch a Predator" reality series, the film comes from director Lance Oppenheim and stars Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, "Superman" breakout Skyler Gisondo, Bokeem Woodbine, Tony Revolori, Anna Faris, and even singer/songwriter Phoebe Bridgers.

But, for now, audiences can look forward to experiencing "Primetime" in all its unsettling, R-rated drama at home.

#3568. Southern Charm’s Taylor Happy to 'Have Life Back' After 'Unfaithful' Exes

Southern Charm alum Taylor Ann Green is opening up about how her life has changed after ending two relationships with allegedly unfaithful exes.

“I couldn’t be happier to have my life back,” Taylor, 32, revealed during a Sunday, November 1, Instagram Q&A with fans.

In June, Taylor confirmed on “The Viall Files” that she’d recently split from ex-boyfriend Gaston Rojas after three years together. Taylor suspected that Gaston, 34, may have cheated on her, though she said that he denied any infidelity.

Prior to her relationship with Gaston, Taylor’s tumultuous romance with Southern Charm costar Shep Rose played out on the hit Bravo show — ultimately ending when she discovered he’d been unfaithful, too. Shep, 47, confessed that he had indeed cheated on Taylor, even saying that “sometimes it was fun” to fool around behind her back.

In light of two tough breakups back-to-back, Taylor was quite candid on Sunday when a fan asked her for “the dirty deets” about her split with Gaston.

“Really nothing to it other than finding out about an ongoing affair with a girl in New York #goknicks,” she quipped via Instagram. “The only difference between one cheating ex over the other is that one of them *cough cough* was at least man enough to admit his faults and not lie to cover it up.”

She continued, “For that, I will have (and have had) respect, forgive and move forward. We are better for it.”

Southern Charm fans have speculated that Taylor and Shep may be getting back together after they were spotted filming the Bravo reality show earlier this year. (A Southern Charm season 12 trailer showed the former couple dancing together on a cast trip to Maui, much to the dismay of Shep’s friends, Craig Conover and Austen Kroll.)

Shep remained coy about where he currently stands with Taylor while speaking to Us at Bravo Fan Fest in Charleston on October 24, cryptically hinting that “everything’s great” between them.

“We talked for 45 minutes yesterday on the phone,” he told Us.

Asked whether they might get back together, Shep slyly teased with a big grin, “You’re going to have to find out, darling.”

For her part, Taylor clarified on “The Viall Files” in June that filming Southern Charm scenes with her ex didn’t necessarily mean that they were getting back together.

“I have seen the rumors that we’re getting back together or hooking up again or whatever, and that is not true,” she stressed. “Even if I wanted to hook up with Shep again or get back together, I would hope I have a little bit more respect for myself to go from one cheating ex to the other.”

Southern Charm premieres on Bravo Thursday, November 12, at 9 p.m. ET. Stream new episodes the next day on Peacock.

In a crowded market of over-ear noise-canceling headphones, it can be tricky to find a pair with a distinctive style that stands out from the rest. Enter the retro-futuristic line of statement-making Nothing headphones. One of the brand’s popular pairs, the Nothing Headphone (1), is 33% off and down to $199 (originally $299), marking a record-low price.

The Nothing Headphone (1) pairs spatial head tracking audio with adaptive ANC, providing up to 80 hours of playback with ANC off and 35 hours with ANC on. A five-minute charge delivers up to five hours of playback, though this figure will vary based on volume and feature use. If you still want to remain aware of your surroundings, you can turn on transparency mode. Still, if you don’t mind fiddling with the EQ and your priorities are a cool-looking aesthetic and plush, sizable earcups, the Nothing Headphone (1) is worth considering.

Johnny Depp is an accomplished character actor with a long and wildly successful career. Arguably one of Depp's best roles is as Captain Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which are streaming in their entirety with a Disney+ subscription. I didn't expect the 63 year-old to have jokes when talking about possibly returning to the franchise alongside Orlando Bloom's Will Turner.

While Depp will return to theaters in Ebenezer this month, some moviegoers are hoping to see him return in a future Pirates of the Caribbean movie. During a recent interview with People, the Edward Scissorhands actor was asked about possibly returning to the beloved franchise, and responded with:

Well, I think we should have a contest of who can grow the fastest non-beard. Because neither of us can grow a beard, I don’t think. I can’t, for sure, but maybe he can. I don’t know.

Shots fired. Despite having facial hair in the Pirates of the Caribbean films, it turns out that neither Johnny Depp nor Orlando Bloom can actually grow a beard. While sidestepping whether or not he'd be down to return as Jack Sparrow, the Sweeney Todd actor was sure to poke fun at both himself, and his famous co-star.

Ebenezer marks Depp's first real return to a big Hollywood movie since the verdict of his defamation trial with Amber Heard was revealed. He spent a few years living abroad and getting out of the spotlight, but he's back playing the title role of Ti West's forthcoming holiday movie. Only time will tell if the upcoming book to screen adaptation ends up being considered one of the best Christmas movies of all time, but it seems like a game changer for the actor.

There's been chatter about more Pirates movies for a few years. At one point multiple movies were in development, including one that would star Margot Robbie. Unfortunately, there hasn't been any concrete updates about one of these projects moving forward in the development process. Although with Johnny Depp returning to the big screen, I have to assume that the chatter surrounding the franchise, and his possible return as Captain Jack Sparrow, will get louder.

Depp starred as the protagonist in all five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which ran in theaters from 2003 to 2017. The same can't be said for Orlando Bloom, who was absent for On Stranger Tides. He ended up returning in Dead Men Tell No Tales, which is the most recent installment in the action/adventure property.

All five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies are streaming now on Disney+. Only time will tell if a sixth movie ends up being green lit by the powers that be at Disney, but there does seem to be a ton of chatter about that possibility online.

#3565. How To Watch Zach Cregger's Resident Evil At Home

This has been a wonderful year for video game movie fans. We've seen both big productions and even indie movies translate the world of video games to cinema with much success (check out our list of the best video game adaptations of 2026 here).

The best movie based on a video game this year is Zach Cregger's "Resident Evil," which actually ignores the exact plot of the long-running Capcom franchise. Instead of being a faithful game recreation, it actually tells an original story that understands the true appeal of the best games in the "Resident Evil" franchise. Cregger crafted a horror comedy that's all about the frustration of finding yourself in an impossible situation where absolutely nothing works in your favor, and the comedy that comes from everything going wrong at the worst possible moment.

After dominating the box office, "Resident Evil" is finally coming home, with platforms like Fandango at Home listing the film with a release date for November 3, 2026 (you can of course choose another platform like Prime Video, or Apple TV). That means you can purchase or rent "Resident Evil" to watch from the comfort or horrors of home as soon as tomorrow, for the typical VOD price of $24.99 to purchase.

We don't know if "Resident Evil" will arrive on digital platforms with any bonus features just yet. That being said, we have seen and heard plenty about the making of the movie. When /Film had the chance to speak with Weta's Kevin Smith, one of the visual effects supervisors in the movie, he talked about how ridiculously complicated the sewer zombie was — especially with all the blood and goop coming out of his guts.

"Resident Evil" does what the best video game adaptations do — makes you feel like you're in the world of the game, even if it's telling an entirely different story than the familiar source mateiral. The film often feels like one of the journal entries you find in a "Resident Evil" game, a tragic story of a poor schmuck who messes around and finds themselves turned into a zombie.

Based on some of his comments about making the film, it seems unlikely Zach Cregger will return to make a sequel, but given how successful it's been at the box office, it's only a matter of time before we return to Raccoon City again.

#3564. Heat Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at LA Gun Range

Michael Mann was rushed to the hospital Saturday, after the director of films such as Collateral, The Insider, and Ferrari accidentally shot himself at a Los Angeles gun range. According to People, the bullet from Mann's gun struck his leg while the 83-year-old artist was returning the firearm to its holster.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a spokesperson for Mann said in a statement to media.

In a separate statement that did not name Mann, the Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the incident, which TMZ reports occurred at The Range LA, a members-only shooting club on the Westside region of Los Angeles.

Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, and Michael Mann at the world premiere of Heat.

“Yesterday at around 4 p.m., officers responded to the 11000 block of Missouri Avenue for a radio call for shots fired at that location," the LAPD statement reads. "Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition. An injury report was completed.”

According to Deadline, the incident is not expected to delay work on Heat 2, which is scheduled to begin production in January, 2027. The director, who has been nominated for four Academy Awards and is the winner of two Emmys and a BAFTA, is also responsible for films including Hunter (1986) and The Last of the Mohicans (1992); he is also known for creating the acclaimed television series Miami Vice.

Michael Mann's latest film, the sequel to 1995 crime classic Heat, will explore the origins of the characters played by Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the original film. Its cast reportedly includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Adolescence creator Stephen Graham.

#3563. Thor Director Taika Waititi Slams Critics After His Jenna Ortega Sci-Fi Movie Flops

Director Taika Waititi isn't too happy with critics of his latest movie, "Klara and the Sun." The filmmaker behind "Thor: Ragnarok" and "Jojo Rabbit" recently took to social media to share his thoughts on the matter after his sci-fi movie starring Jenna Ortega flopped at the box office.

Posting on Instagram, Waititi shared a screenshot of a Screen Rant article highlighting the movie's audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, which sits at a decent 74%. The problem? It holds a lousy 24% critical approval rating. It's those critics that Waititi took issue with, writing:

"I haven't read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people. So, this Halloween, let's spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn't achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. The same people who also hated 'Jojo Rabbit.' Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin."

"Klara and the Sun" is based on the 2021 book of the same name by Kazuo Ishiguro. It centers on Klara (Ortega), an Artificial Friend who meets Josie (Mia Tharia) and begins to heal her family, bringing light into the latter's complicated world with her innocent wonder and unwavering loyalty. For most critics, though, Waititi's movie failed to live up to the potential that existed on the page in Ishiguro's novel.

However, that wasn't at all the case with 2019's "Jojo Rabbit," despite what Waititi implied in his post. On the contrary, that movie was generally well-liked and became one of the big winners at the 2020 Oscars, taking home the Best Adapted Screenplay prize (on top of being nominated for Best Picture). It was a hit in theaters, too, bringing in $90 million against a $14 million budget.

It's one thing for a filmmaker like Taika Waititi to be disappointed that a movie didn't perform well. Indeed, "Klara and the Sun" hasn't even made $2 million at the box office against a $20 million budget. It's not an expensive movie, but with a cast that includes "Wednesday" star Jenna Ortega and Oscar-nominee Amy Adams, Sony Pictures had much higher expectations.

Recall that Waititi was on top of the world after "Thor: Ragnarok" saved a "dying" Chris Hemsworth, becoming a huge hit and reviving the "Thor" franchise within the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Waititi's sequel, "Thor: Love and Thunder," was also a success, but its reception was far less warm. Sadly, it's been a downhill slide since then, with Waititi's "Next Goal Wins" becoming a box office bomb in 2023.

That said, this is far from the first time that a high-profile filmmaker has taken aim at critics. "Gods of Egypt" director Alex Proyas really hates film critics, but he hasn't had a meaningful hit in some time. Elsewhere, "Clerks" director Kevin Smith rather publicly took aim at critics in the 2010s. Smith later made peace with movie critics, but it was a much-discussed issue at the time. It happens, but it's rarely a great look for the director doing the complaining.

The issue is that critics can slightly help a movie, but they rarely move the needle all that much in terms of selling tickets. If critical opinion mattered more, a great many acclaimed films would make a lot more money. But that's not the reality we live in. Either way, Waititi has big feelings about all of this, which he's opted to air out in public.

#3561. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Where The Hero Dies

Needless to say, this article will be full of spoilers.

There are many things the "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" franchises have in common, not the least of which is hope. The former is set in a utopian future wherein human prejudice, capitalism, and war have all been dispensed with in favor of a society built on diplomacy, peace, and sharing. Similarly, all "Star Wars" stories posit that fascism is an impermanent state that's constantly being batted back down by the forces of good, no matter how often it tries to reassert itself. Heck, the first "Star Wars" movie was subtitled "A New Hope," showing the cycle at work.

But for every "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" film, there are lots of other science fiction movies that end on notes of sacrifice, death, or despair. In our darker moods, we humans often don't feel very good about the future, and that hopelessness can be reflected in our sci-fi tales. For every utopia, there is a dystopia. For every instance of humankind uniting to save their planet, there is a tale of humanity failing to stop its own self-destruction.

Indeed, the following five sci-fi movies feature protagonists who die. Some of the deaths are tragically noble. Others, however, are wasteful and harrowing, providing lessons for audiences about the dangers of various sins. All of them leave viewers in a poignant state, though, so let's look into the shadows of what is to come.

Ted Post's "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" was the first follow-up to Franklin J. Schaffner's 1968 classic "Planet of the Apes." If the original film is an on-the-nose satire of human interaction (transposing apes and humans in the planetary pecking order), then "Beneath" just pushes things into more obvious territory. The movie stars James Franciscus as Brent, a human astronaut who, as part of a rescue mission, somehow ends up on the same distant-future Earth that Taylor (Charlton Heston) did in "Planet of the Apes." Once there, Brent discovers that the apes are gearing up to take over the Forbidden Zone under the command of the gorilla Ursus (James Gregory), which Dr. Zaius (Maurice Evans) objects to.

In "Planet of the Apes," all the humans of the future appear to be mute and feral. Its sequel, on the other hand, reveals there is a subterranean enclave of surviving, ghoul-like humans who've developed psychic powers. The human psychics also worship an unexploded nuclear bomb, admiring its power. Taylor and Brent eventually meet up, but Taylor is naturally terrified when he sees the bomb's Alpha Omega markings, knowing that this particular bomb is capable of, just by itself, ending all life on the planet.

As it so happens, this is Chekhov's doomsday bomb. Once the bomb is introduced, we know that "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" can't possibly end well. Sure enough, when Taylor is mortally wounded at the end of the film, he curses and collapses on the bomb's detonation switch. In this case, the hero dies, along with everyone else on Earth. It's one of the bleakest endings in sci-fi history.

Douglas Trumbull's 1972 film "Silent Running" is so good that it made /Film's Jeremy Smith a lifelong sci-fi fan. More specifically, it's something of a dystopian movie and shows what happens when an idealist with principles butts heads with an uncaring, commercialized future that doesn't care about the calm, complexity, and beauty of the natural world. Everyone ought to watch this one, especially if you liked "Project Hail Mary" (and I know you did).

In the dystopian future of "Silent Running," humans have ruined Earth to the point of killing all its forests. Specimens of many planet species have been kept alive on spacebound repositories, which exist in giant greenhouse-like geodesic domes. Bruce Dern plays Freeman Lowell, a botanist who has been tasked with looking after the samples on a ship called the Valley Forge. The Valley Forge is owned by American Airlines.

When the ship is ordered to jettison its plants and head back to Earth (as it's needed for commercial purposes), Freeman turns on his corporate bosses and proves that he's willing to kill his human crew mates to protect the forest domes. Shockingly, he actually manages to escape with one of the domes, although he loses others in the process. By the end of the movie, Freeman even makes the ultimate sacrifice to keep the forest protected.

Of course, "Silent Running" is a commentary on modern-day environmentalism and how horrible commercialism always seems to outweigh the needs of our planet. Is "Silent Running" preachy? Yes. Is it tragic and great? Also yes.

John Carpenter's 1988 film "They Live" stands as a vital criticism of the United States under Ronald Reagan. In the film, the nameless protagonist, "Nada" (Roddy Piper), finds a pair of alien-constructed sunglasses that allow him to see through all the secret alien disguises on Earth. Certain citizens are revealed to be creepy aliens in disguise, but more so, billboards, magazines, and advertisements are shown to be masking subliminal messages that make human consumers more complacent by ordering them to "OBEY," "STAY ASLEEP," or "CONSUME."

Nada is hardly the best person to make this alien discovery. He's a blue-collar drifter without the means to handle this weird revelation, and when he tries to tell someone else about it, they end up fighting for a really, really, really long time. That's not a joke, either, as Piper and his co-star Keith David beat the hell out of each other for what feels like 20 minutes.

Luckily, Nada has connections within the local shanty town. There, he learns the aliens have been mingling with Earth's wealthy and using brain-scrambling signals to keep the impoverished docile. "They Live" then ends with a raid on the alien compound with Nada, David's Frank Armitage, and a few others trying to shut down the alien signal once and for all.

Although a sci-fi movie, it's easy to believe that "They Live" might very well be a documentary. The ultra-wealthy, we seem to inherently understand, are deliberately controlling us through media and money. It felt true in 1988, and it definitely feels true now. Nada ends up taking care of business, but not before being mortally wounded. In the film's most inspiring scene, his final act on this planet is to flip the middle finger to the aliens, spitting his last breath at them.

In 2011, Lars von Trier released the second entry in what might be considered his "Depression Trilogy," a series of movies that began with 2009's "Antichrist" and ended with 2013's "Nymphomaniac." The second film, "Melancholia," is just as much a metaphor for depression as it is a sci-fi apocalypse flick. "Melancholia" takes place in a world where a rogue planet, known as Melancholia, is going to slingshot around Earth before looping back in space and colliding with it, ending all life. The gravitational loops are a little dance of death, a preview of the apocalypse.

With this impending doom looming in the background, the movie centers on Justine (Kirsren Dunst), a newly-married woman who finds herself sliding back into the depression she has long fought off. When she learns that all life on Earth will end, Justine finds herself grimly pleased. She asserts that all life on Earth is evil, there is no other life in the universe, and that human extinction would be a blessing. Death cannot be stopped, and its coming is a release. Meanwhile, eerie things start to happen as Melancholia approaches. Electricity begins behaving weirdly. Certain characters flee, but where should they go? Justine doesn't panic. She's apathetic.

In the end, no one in the film lives. "Melancholia" is a beautiful, harrowing, and shockingly accurate portrait of a depressed mind. Justine has simply stopped caring about anything because it feels like there is no escape. Because, in the mind of Lars von Trier, there isn't.

You already know if "Melancholia" is your kind of movie. Just be sure to follow it with something more optimistic, like "Apocalypse Now."

Coralie Fargeat's 2024 horror hit "The Substance" is hardly subtle. Demi Moore stars as Elisabeth Sparkle, a celebrated actor who's recently made her living by hosting a TV workout program. Her disgusting boss (Dennis Quaid) fires her early in the film, all but saying out loud that she's too old to be a heartthrob anymore. From there, Elisabeth is put in contact with a shadowy pharmaceutical company that mails her doses of "The Substance," which promises to make her young again ... in a sense.

Sure enough, when Elisabeth injects herself with The Substance, she passes out, her back splits open like a cocoon, and a younger woman (Margaret Qualley) crawls out. These two women are the same person, but the younger one decides to take the name Sue. According to the rules of The Substance, Elisabeth and Sue have to take turns being conscious, one week each, with Sue feeding off Elisabeth's spinal fluids. Naturally, though, "Sue" doesn't want to go back to being the "old" Elisabeth she resents, and the consequences of what happens when the rules of The Substance are broken are quickly made horrifically clear.

By the end of the movie, Elisabeth has become a literal puddle of dead puffy flesh on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. "The Substance" is openly about the callowness of Hollywood and its dogged tendency to cast aside women "of a certain age" in favor of youthful ingénues. It should be recalled that Moore was nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress for "The Substance" but lost to a youthful ingénue, Mikey Madison. The message of "The Substance" played out in real life. How darkly poetic.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At this point, I've accepted that Taylor Swift operates on an entirely different creative clock than the rest of us. Of all the behind-the-scenes stories to come out of the 2026 movie schedule, I wasn't prepared for what Toy Story 5 director Andrew Stanton had to say about how quickly she wrote "I Knew It, I Knew You" after seeing the Pixar sequel. The guy has spent decades making some of animation's most beloved films, but apparently even he couldn't keep his language family-friendly when he heard what she'd done. Here’s his NOT PG reaction after Swift wrote the song in less than a day.

During a recent Q&A with Swift, Stanton recalled how the singer ended up contributing a song to the film. Swift's brother Austin had urged her to watch an early cut while she was exhausted from the Eras Tour, and she finally agreed once she'd recovered. She immediately connected with Jessie, the cowgirl at the center of the sequel, and called Stanton from the screening room that afternoon. Hours later, Disney's music team called him again, this time with news he couldn't quite believe:

You [Swift] saw it that morning with your brother, and that was at 10 o'clock. And then at noon my FaceTime rings, and it's from Tom, but it's you guys, you and Austin, and you're still in your seats and you're gushing about the movie. And you said, ‘You want to do the song?’ Like, there wasn't even a debate about this or a discussion. It was just, ‘You want to do the song?’ We're like, ‘Great, great, great.’ And we almost got off so that you couldn't change your mind.

I love that Stanton's first instinct was to end the call before the “Shake it Off” performer could reconsider. Getting her to agree to write the song was already a pretty big deal, but he had no idea just how quickly things were about to move. He continued:

And then I go home that night, and Tom calls me, the head of music, and says, ‘She wrote the song.’ I'm like, ‘What?’ And I'm like, ‘No, no, no, no. She found it or she had it already. She relabeled it.’ And he's like, ‘No, she's in the studio and she's written the song, and I'm driving right now to hear it.’ I'm like, ‘Wow, get the f out of here.’

I kind of love that his first assumption was that Swift must have quietly pulled an old song off the shelf and given it a Toy Story label. He seemed genuinely baffled that someone could watch a movie in the morning and have a song ready before dinner. Apparently Stanton wasn't the only Toy Story veteran surprised by the music icon's involvement.

Stanton's day somehow got weirder. Around 9 that evening, he got another FaceTime call, this time from Disney CEO Bob Iger, who stood beside Swift and raved about the track. Stanton recalled asking the music A-lister if she'd really written it before calling her "a beast." The director didn't hear the finished song in person until several days later, when he flew to Los Angeles. He added:

I got choked up when I heard it. And the only other time I've heard a song that just dropped from thin air and was perfect was when Randy Newman came in and played 'You've Got a Friend in Me" on a piano with six of us.

That's serious praise, especially coming from someone who helped shape Pixar's original era. Newman's "You've Got a Friend in Me" remains one of the most recognizable movie songs of all time, and Swift has said she didn't want her contribution to feel out of place. She wrote and produced "I Knew It, I Knew You" with longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff, drawing on her country roots and Jessie's complicated history of being left behind.

While the song came together ridiculously fast, Stanton offered a beautiful explanation: Swift's lifelong connection to Toy Story prepared her for it. The filmmaker said the tune really took "a lifetime" to write, starting with her watching the films as a kid. I think that's a much sweeter explanation than the one he gave on that first phone call.

Toy Story 5 is now streaming with a Disney+ subscription, with the Taylor Swift and Antonoff track playing over the end credits. And if you need a reason to revisit the flick, picture Stanton losing his mind and dropping F-bombs on FaceTime over the song.

#3559. Tomi Adeyemi Does Not Want to Talk About the Children of Blood and Bone Movie

“You are a once in a generation talent,” says Tomi Adeyemi, tears in her eyes. The author is not paying me a compliment; she is reading a line from one of her numerous fan letters.

Adeyemi is a New York Times bestselling writer, a feat she accomplished at twenty-four with her 2018 fantasy debut novel Children of Blood and Bone—the first in her Legacy of Orïsha trilogy, which marries old-fashioned American YA with West African mythology. Her new novel, The Siren—released in September—follows Emery, a freshman at Dartmouth desperate to find her place as she undertakes a series of trials to join the titular group of powerful girls on campus.

This is Adeyemi’s first time since childhood not writing fantasy; maybe her first time period, since she says the first book she ever wrote was a Parent Trap fan fiction. But it’s also an attempt to move past the widely successful young-adult fantasy with which she made her name—as well as the drama surrounding the film adaptation of Adeyemi’s debut novel, an experience she has called the worst thing she ever lived through.

In now-deleted TikToks, Adeyemi said that she’s distancing herself from the film, she won’t watch it, and that she blocked one of its leads, Amandla Stenberg, on social media. Sources indicated to VF this summer that Adeyemi got more creative control over the film than most first-time authors do, including a co-screenwriting credit; they also noted that she's switched talent agencies multiple times since striking an initial deal with ICM. “There must be something [going on] because she’s burned every bridge,” one insider who works in the book-to-film space said.

When we meet, Adeyemi says that she doesn’t want to talk about that.

Instead, she talks about how she used to exclusively write fantasy because the world wasn’t safe enough for her to write anything else. Now, though, she no longer feels like she has to hide behind magic. “I’ve become someone who can inhabit it fully,” she says. “When you allow a woman to grow her claws, I am more akin to a jungle cat than I am a house plant.” She breaks into a chorus of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” adding a Jackson 5-esque run: “Da-da-da, oh, baby, yeah-yeah.” She tells me that sometimes, when she connects with certain people—like me—she just can’t help herself from singing. “The stars, the moon!” she belts—lines from Florence + the Machine’s “Cosmic Love.”

Adeyemi’s a musical person. She saw Florence play at Lollapalooza: “Somehow, Florence wielded her magic so I was able to get to the very front row, and she’s singing to me. I’m like, Look at this wild woman, howling to the moon.” This reminds her of a scene from her new book: when Roux, the girl Emery idolizes, is introduced. Adeyemi writes Roux dancing on a table, kicking glasses, alive and wild. Emery wants to be like that; so does Adeyemi. She explains this before singing some more: “You woke up like that, you woke up like that.”

Adeyemi’s admiration for Roux is almost tangible. She smiles dreamily when she speaks about her creation, leaving you to wonder if there was a specific person this character was based on.

Though Adeyemi started working on The Siren in 2020, she says the novel’s published version was written entirely last year. She’s gotten used to trying, and trying again; while applying for fiction writing classes in college, Adeyemi says, she was rejected five semesters in a row. One professor actually told her he couldn’t teach her to write, an anecdote she’s happy to relate now: “Hello! So many bestsellers later.” She spent four and a half years writing her first, unpublished novel, which she says was rejected 63 times. Only then did she write Children of Blood and Bone.

Adeyemi says she writes to free herself—and while one can’t be sure exactly what she had to free herself from last year, the film adaptation of Blood and Bone was shot in 2025. That’s also when Adeyemi allegedly fell out with Stenberg. And while they’re spelled differently, it’s notable that Roux—The Siren’s charismatic villain—has the same name as one of Stenberg’s most popular characters, Rue in the first Hunger Games movie.

Female authors are often asked, unfairly, whether they are writing their own lives into a story. Yet it’s also impossible to ignore the parallels between Emery and Adeyemi herself. Both are Ivy-educated writers and self-proclaimed outsiders. Adeyemi also doesn’t shy from comparisons between herself and her most recent main character: she says that all authors write themselves, because doing so is a vehicle for understanding. Reading The Siren is like stepping into her consciousness.

So is interviewing her. Adeyemi has a tendency to go off on tangents about astrology, tarots, mystical energy. “Do you remember how it felt when the entire universe came alive? All these spindles, nerve endings rise,” she asks me at one point, holding out her arms. “If you could feel the stars and taste the wind?”

The novel is wrapped up in themes of belonging, identity, and loneliness—a narrative Adeyemi tells me she relates to. “I think if you don’t belong to yourself, you don’t belong anywhere,” she says—though Adeyemi also thinks that her Aquarius placements mean people like her will never fit in, because they are not designed to. Take “our most iconic Aquarius rising, Audrey Hepburn,” or SZA, who famously wears fairy wings onstage and on red carpets. “How painful must it have been when you were on land?” Adeyemi asks her fellow Aquarius rhetorically. “How painful must it have been to learn how to fly? How painful is it for the butterflies inside before they become their butterflies?”

Adeyemi herself appears on the cover of The Siren—something that “has never been done before,” she says. “But a lot of what I do has never been done before. I remember choosing the image because I saw the darkness, that power in Emery. I’ve never seen that look in anyone else’s eye.”

There was a time where having her books adapted for the screen felt like the epitome of Adeyemi’s work. The author no longer feels that way: “I am the epitome of my work,” she says. And as she said on those now-deleted TikToks, she really would rather not talk about the film adaptation of her first novel at all.

We avoid the topic during our initial conversation. When our time runs out, though, Adeyemi tells me she’d like to talk more at a later date. When I do eventually speak to Adeyemi again—and ask about the Blood and Bone film—she shuts down physically. Her smile drops; the question throws off the energy of the conversation, almost like a betrayal has occurred. I ask another question, and Adeyemi tells me that she is getting a call. She turns off her camera, and I sit in silence for seven minutes.

Eventually, Adeyemi returns and asks if I am still there. She tells me, “The Siren is number three, New York Times.” She’s feeling the hot flash version of goosebumps, she says, like she just finished a marathon.

Adeyemi says that all of this—her career, her work, her writing process—was inspired by extreme fear. She speaks about it in the second person: “An agonizing understanding that you’ve been taught to work so hard to build a better life, [but] you might not get to build that life. It could be snapped away from you like that. I live in that terror.” She’s gone through her own trials: not just the long journey to publishing Blood and Bone, but the internet’s scrutiny over the comments she made about the Blood and Bone adaptation. “I’m exceptionally proud of who I am today,” she says, though “life is terrifying.”

In our first conversation, Adeyemi had said The Siren might be her last book—that she might be finished with writing altogether. “You can depart from all these previous eras of your life with a gentle sort of ruthlessness,” she said, “and then tomorrow can actually be a new day.” Now, she seems reenergized by the idea of work, telling me that she’s met children’s literacy organizations that try to inspire kids with the work of James Baldwin, Octavia Butler, and herself. “I’m proud of writing this from a really hard time and place,” she says, “and I wanna continue Emery’s journey.”

I ask her what changed between that interview and this one. Her smile freezes; she laughs awkwardly before hesitantly replying, “I think it’s interesting talking to you in the summer and then talking to you post this tour. I don’t know how the piece will end up, since you’re getting two very distinct cross sections.”

She takes another beat. “So that quote felt more… there was more of a resonance the first time we spoke. As I’m sitting here with you now, I just have a vision of myself writing deeply.”

The time between our talks seems to have given her space for deep reflection. I remind Adeyemi what she’d told me about feeling more like a jungle cat than a houseplant, and ask if she felt she had to be a jungle cat during her journey with the Blood and Bone film. “I think all women have to be in tune with their power. I think Black women have to be in tune with their power, dark-skinned Black women especially,” she answers. “There’s a sense of gravity that wouldn’t have been there without knowing what it is to step into my power and voice. You owe it to yourself to feel safe, and if you’re the only one there to defend yourself, you have to have the claws.”

As the film’s January release inches closer, one has to wonder if Adeyemi has a desire to retract her claws—and her statements about the movie. Or at least whether everything that’s transpired has changed her relationship with her debut novel. “I think my relationship with myself has changed more than anything,” Adeyemi answers. When narrating the audiobook for The Siren, she noticed that Emery doesn’t recognize her own genius. That broke Adeyemi’s heart, because the character’s insecurities came from a personal place. The difference between her character and her own feelings also shows Adeyemi’s own growth: “You don’t feel that way anymore,” she told herself.

When asked whether she might try to make another movie someday—or adapt The Siren—she answers firmly: “I’ve already done that journey. It’s a lot of work, but it’s not work that is for myself. When you commit to doing something on screen, it’s more about everyone else on the other side of that screen. I think because I have such a directorial and cinematic approach to my writing, I do value having experienced everything.” Selling the rights to your novel means essentially giving it away to other people, she says. That was extremely difficult for her. “I don’t need anyone in this world.”

Maybe Adeyemi’s film future lies instead in front of the camera. She did film a cameo in Blood and Bone, and one in the second Devil Wears Prada film: “At the beginning of the year, I thought, Oh, I would like to try acting,” she laughs now. “By the end of the year, I had a cameo across from Viola Davis and another across from Meryl Streep.” In the future, she’d be interested in voice acting and animation. Or live-action—but maybe only if, say, Jon Chu asked her to star in a Bollywood rom-com with Dev Patel.

“SASUKE!” She yells the name of a Naruto character in a high-pitched voice, then adds in her normal voice, “I’m clearly a very animated person.”

Dexter Morgan is back on the prowl in the Season 2 premiere of Dexter: Resurrection, and I saw my favorite character again from last season! Eric Stonestreet returned once again as the Rapunzel Killer, but unfortunately, the return was short-lived.

Al Walker was tracked down by Dexter while on vacation with his family, as he was "working" while traveling to parks with his wife and kids. Dex was able to "do what he does," as Harrison puts it, and now no pony-tailed women have to worry about Rapunzel anymore. As satisfying as it was, I'm upset that Dexter: Resurrection is once again killing off fun guest stars.

Last season, Dexter: Resurrection gave us a great plot twist with the Serial Killers Club, which was quickly decimated by the Bay Harbor Butcher. There was a stacked cast of great guest stars, but by the end of the season, they were all dead except for Eric Stonestreet's character.

I had high hopes he'd be a big bad in Season 2, but that hope was squashed pretty quickly. I kind of guessed that would be the case given how many new guest stars were a part of this season, but it's disappointing the show didn't hold off and do a season dedicated to Rapunzel where Dex was on the road.

Dexter: Resurrection has two major guest stars this season, with Dan Stevens playing the Five Boroughs Killer and Brian Cox playing the New York Ripper. Both are big names tied to the Season 2 plot, and with Dexter being so concerned about legacy, it feels as though he's going to try to take out both of them.

I Have A Theory About Dexter: Resurrection And His Downfall. Why I Think Season 2 Could Address It

That's kind of the point of Dexter, to be fair. He's a serial killer who hunts other killers, so I can't sit here and act like Resurrection is going against what this series is about. I just feel as though he's felt very untouchable thus far, and maybe that these serial killers aren't as crafty as the ones from the original series?

I guess I fear that Dexter is becoming an Avengers-level type of anti-hero, and it feels like we haven't seen him face any real adversity. I know that's funny to say with him having been shot by his own son, but he and Harrison were able to put that aside really quickly. I'm just hoping we see Dex face a little more adversity in these upcoming episodes on the 2026 TV schedule, because I fear he's untouchable.

Catch new episodes of Dexter: Resurrection on Paramount+ on Fridays. I'm eager to see how the rest of this season plays out, and if Dexter and Harrison end the season in some trouble with the law.

#3557. How To Watch Sense And Sensibility (2026) At Home

There's a reason Jane Austen's 1811 novel "Sense and Sensibility" has been adapted so many times to the screen and the stage. The story of the Dashwood sisters, as they experience love and heartbreak after being forced to move away from their family estate and into the cottage of a relative, is as timeless in its coming of age story as it is timely and relatable in its themes and sharp social commentary.

There are many movies based on Jane Austen books, some retaining the period setting and others taking a more modern approach. The best Jane Austen movies are the ones that simply focus on the relatable and complex heroine and the hardships they endure. Case in point, Georgia Oakley's 2026 adaptation of "Sense and Sensibility" starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne. /Film's own Ben Pearson praised the film as one you absolutely should watch even in a crowded movie landscape, highlighting how "funny, charming, sweet, and full of suppressed yearning" this adaptation is, and even comparing it to Greta Gerwig's 2019 film adaptation of "Little Women."

After the film failed to make much of an impact in movie theaters, Focus Features is bringing "Sense and Sensibility" to digital platforms on November 3, 2026. Those wanting to actually own the movie rather than just lease it from a platform that can take it away from you at their whim, will have to wait until December 15, 2026 for Universal Pictures Home to release the film on Blu-ray.

It's been over 30 years since Ang Lee's phenomenal 1995 version of "Sense and Sensibility," but now we have a new take that offers a similarly gorgeous-looking movie adaptation. Georgia Oakley's movie  gives the relationship between the Dashwood sisters a bigger focus, especially in how they grow and learn from one another amid their respective romances.

The film also stars Caitríona Balfe, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, and Fiona Shaw — who has a standout scene. Even if "Sense and Sensibility" didn't really make a splash at the box office and doesn't make much of an impact during awards season, it is a tale worth experiencing, whether for the first time, or just for a new time.

The home video release of "Sense and Sensibility" also arrives with this bonus content at participating retailers.

#3556. Substack’s Cofounder Might Not Know How to Save the Media—But He Knows How to Outplay It

As recently as a few years ago, Substack was struggling to shed the perception that it was radioactive. “Substack Has a Nazi Problem,” read the headline of a 2023 Atlantic story that surfaced “scores of white-supremacist, neo-Confederate, and explicitly Nazi newsletters” on the platform, which was, in some instances, taking its standard 10% profit from them. Over 200 Substack writers wrote an open letter opposing the company’s hands-off approach to content moderation, and several high-profile writers and publications migrated to competitors.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Charli xcx publish there—Kylie Jenner has said she’d like to—as do new media phenomena like Feed Me and The Free Press. The platform has significant footholds in fashion, AI, politics, literature, celebrity gossip, and most everything in between. In the opening pages of his book, How to Save the Media, McKenzie recalls drinking whiskey at the Chelsea Hotel alongside former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown, who now publishes the popular Fresh Hell newsletter on Substack. The United Kingdom–born Brown, like McKenzie, came to America from abroad, only to rise to the highest rungs of its media world, and she seemed now to see him as a peer.

“You’re a New Zealander, aren’t you?” she asked McKenzie. “There’s something to being an outsider.”

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, speaking from the Toni Morrison Conference Room at Substack’s San Francisco headquarters, McKenzie appeared uncomfortable with the idea that his book, liberally sprinkled with such encounters with the cream of the Substack crop, amounted to a victory lap. He was, despite a generally mild manner and steadfast earnestness, relentlessly on message. “I’m always going to be like a broken record coming back to the importance of direct relationships,” McKenzie acknowledged. It’s the Substack theory of fixing an ailing media ecosystem: replacing the ad-based chaos sown by the internet with a more nourishing connection between writer and reader, and having consumers pay for the media they want to see in the world rather than subject themselves to the whims of an attention economy controlled by big social media companies. McKenzie admitted his book’s title was a provocation, but “for me, it’s backing up the gospel that I’m trying to preach.”

Still, we could agree that something about the controversies that dogged the platform in recent years now seems quaint—that Substack has achieved some fundamental conquest. Instead of reactively responding to the “Nazi problem,” the company chose to stick with its hands-off approach to content moderation, and the outcry dissipated: Substack remains the go-to home for your established journalists striking out on their own (Jim Acosta, Nate Silver) as well as your upstart media operations repurposing the expertise once best associated with legacy outlets (The Bulwark, The Ankler). I suggested to McKenzie that the platform today is akin to Instagram or Grindr: a tech company, yes, but also an undeniable element of the fabric of contemporary life.

From a writer’s perspective, one knock-on effect of the Substack boom has been the rising cachet around writing itself, despite the spree of recent news stories declaring the end of reading. There are so many—too many?—personal essayists and gift guide impresarios emerging seemingly out of nowhere. (“I’m not snobby about that,” McKenzie said. “I think everyone should try to write and no one should be discouraged through peer pressure from writing.”) And then there is the ever-increasing atomization across media, with political discourse splaying out across countless newsletters that are only intermittently in conversation with one another. Is this new cacophony strictly better than the ones we encountered on Facebook and Twitter? Part of the reason the open letter concerning Nazi Substack newsletters didn’t stick, perhaps, was that no one is reading the same things anyway.

McKenzie is currently chipping away at Anna Karenina. “I honestly think writing is good and reading is good,” he said, echoing the kind of unadorned aphorisms he sometimes issues on X. As far as the purported literacy emergency, he says, “I don’t see many centuries of progress on this fundamental communication form being undone overnight.” Our “cultural crisis,” McKenzie thinks, has more to do with the distribution mechanisms of writing, and “is intrinsically tied to the state of the media system.”

After departing small-town New Zealand to pursue a career in journalism, McKenzie, 44, tried his hand at tech reporting in Hong Kong and San Francisco. Later, while working at the messaging app Kik, he and the company’s chief technology officer Chris Best hatched their plan to reroute the flow of publishing profits away from social media companies and toward writers. (Best is Substack’s CEO, while McKenzie works as its “chief writing officer” and heads up the company’s partnerships and talent acquisition efforts.)

“We had more direct relationships in the traditional media system,” McKenzie said, referring to, for example, a subscription to a print newspaper. “But then it got broken by the internet and replaced by something that corroded the direct relationships and gave all the power to Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg instead.”

As it happens, one of the touchstones in McKenzie’s own writing career is his dust-up with Musk. He worked for a time in communications at Tesla, and Musk, McKenzie writes, threatened to sue to block a book that he wrote about the company after leaving. (Insane Mode was published in 2018. Musk and Tesla didn’t return requests for comment.) Later, McKenzie and Best would turn down acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X.

It was a choice they made, in McKenzie’s telling, to preserve the company’s independence—to prevent the Substack ecosystem from going the same way as those social platforms, which tend to leave their consumers more exhausted and frustrated than enlightened. I proposed to McKenzie that the company’s endurance in the face of its detractors has something to do with the shifting shape of online discourse, and that Substack itself has had a key role in making the tools of mass censure weaker in the age of media fragmentation. “I wonder if a lesson we are all learning,” he suggested, “is that the heavy-handed censorship approach can often backfire.”

“Did it do any good to kick Trump off Twitter and Facebook for two years?” he asked.

In How to Save the Media, McKenzie reflects on an evening he spent at the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles in 2021. He was there to support Bari Weiss, who had struck out on Substack after leaving The New York Times about a year earlier. The schism would go on to shape the future of journalism from the newsletter economy all the way up to the highest echelons of Hollywood and television news after Weiss was appointed editor in chief of CBS News last year. (Of the common criticisms that Weiss has made the network overly Trump-friendly and lacks the requisite TV experience for the role, McKenzie says, “I think for the most part, the media industry is experiencing Bari Weiss as a media gossip story. And I think the more interesting story is the structural story and what it suggests about what’s possible in this emerging media economy. So I’m mostly watching from that perspective and I still think it’s too early to draw grand conclusions about what’s happened so far.”) In her resignation letter from the Times, Weiss wrote that Twitter had become the paper’s “ultimate editor.” On Substack, she built The Free Press, an outlet that has largely defined itself in opposition to what it sees as mainstream media orthodoxies.

That night, the Los Angeles Press Club was honoring Weiss. McKenzie took the accolade, he writes, “as validation of the nascent direct-relationships model”: Despite the ongoing and widespread opposition to her politics, Weiss had identified a journalistic niche that required no traditional media backing. Yet, The Free Press ultimately brought Weiss back to the legacy press—the new Substack class has its eye on some of the old media rewards, to the extent that they remain available.The night served as a sign, McKenzie writes, that “independence can still deliver prestige.”

“I don’t think what we’re going through here,” he told me, “is a moment of change where all the benefits from the old things have to be thrown out.”

Now that the spooky season has officially ended, a certain celebrity family is already decked out in their favorite Christmas attire and bringing in a stylish cheer that’ll last until New Year. The Kardashian-Jenner brood have traded scary movies and creepy costumes for a holiday campaign that brought (nearly) the whole family together. Just two days out from Halloween, the stars are already bringing what they call "SKIMSmas" to the forefront.

This isn’t the first time the famous sisters have come right out of Halloween launching a Christmas-themed campaign for Kim Kardashian’s SKIMS brand. A few years ago, they did a whole photoshoot with a polar bear, and this year fans have been treated to a 1970s inspired vintage photoshoot for the brand's 2026 Holiday Shop that brought Kim together with her sisters, Khloé and Kourtney Kardashian, and half-sisters Kylie and Kendall Jenner. Khloé shared her portion of the campaign on Instagram, and honestly, this is hitting me in my holiday feels:

A post shared by Khloé Kardashian (@khloekardashian)

I’m just loving the nostalgia in the campaign, especially with Khloé’s red and white onesie, paired perfectly with white gloves and boots. There’s a "kid on Christmas" feel to the video due to her sneaking up on Santa and shaking presents under the tree. (Also, don’t think I didn’t catch her being a little Grinch-y by mimicking two of the Dr. Seuss character's iconic moves.)

However, while Kardashian was distracting herself from Halloween, I was almost distracted by Dick Van Dyke's voice. The media personality’s post features a few lines from Mary Poppins. In the 1964 movie, Van Dyke stops his performance of his “One Man Band” to sing that he feels “like somethin’ is brewin’ and ‘bout to begin.” Now, the change in the wind that he feels signals the return of Julie Andrews’ titular nanny, but Kardashian is using the beloved lyrics to signal the return of Christmas. (An act usually done by Mariah Carey’s “All I Want For Christmas Is You.”)

That aside, I’m also not the only one that’s loving this campaign. Fans have called it "cinematic," but what really caught my eye was a sweet comment from Khloé's mom, Kris Jenner:

The cutest Santa’s helper I ever did see 🎅🏽🤶

Kardashian is definitely giving Mrs. Claus vibes and is clearly having fun with the festive fashion. This is only the most recent stage in the Kardashian-Jenner fashion evolution we’ve seen this year. Just a few months ago, the sisters sported some summer-friendly looks and are now trading those in for some autumn-inspired attire. (Just check out Kim wearing a bunch of brown leather to promote the opening of a new SKIMS London store.)

I wasn’t expecting to skip straight to Christmas before the turkey’s even in the oven. However, I also shouldn’t be surprised by all this, as the Kardashians are known to indulge in fun, flirty and stylish seasonal campaigns.

Kylie Jenner actually beat her sisters to the Christmas punch with a winter kissed cosmetic collection she promoted on her Instagram. The limited time collection features “four best-selling formulas, reimagined in the signature winter kissed pink.” Jenner even promoted the collection while wearing blush pink lingerie and a Christmas hat. She’s proving that, once again, she has a full Christmas dance card as she’s continuing to bring in the holiday cheer with products available through her KHY brand. The holiday wear features a black, white, pink, and olive color scheme for a more Kardashian/Jenner-esque aesthetic.

See if you can spot some SKIMS fits or fun holiday looks in Season 8 of The Kardashians, which hit the 2026 TV schedule in early October and will continue into December. New episodes can be watched every Thursday with a Hulu subscription.

#3554. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3553. Crystal Lake Does For Friday The 13th What Marvel Once Did To Spider-Man

Creating a brand new take on a classic character who has literal decades of history to their name is no simple task. No one knows this challenge better than folks who've made writing comic books their career, as so many characters have histories and continuity that are so long and complex they practically make new stories almost prohibitive. To help with this issue, major comic labels such as Marvel and DC Comics introduced the concept of retroactive continuity, which began as a way of allowing writers to subtly shift around previously established lore (or, alternatively, introduce new elements that already took place). Given that characters like Spider-Man and Batman have been around for close to 100 years now, this concept of retconning eventually expanded to include the idea of a fully rebooted or an entirely separate, parallel continuity.

That latter example is what writer Brian Michael Bendis attempted with Spider-Man in the fall of 2000, with the series "Ultimate Spider-Man" (which just ended!). Presented as a way of modernizing the character while reintroducing and remixing his history, supporting cast, and rogues gallery, the series served as both summation of the character up to that point as well as a new beginning. This month's "Crystal Lake" series essentially does the same thing to "Friday the 13th" and Jason Voorhees. Almost as if to prove the similarity, the reaction to "Crystal Lake" has been as passionate and polarizing as the fan reaction to "Ultimate Spider-Man" was. While the two projects share a lot in common creatively, the key difference is that "Ultimate Spider-Man" was always presented as separate from the main "Amazing Spider-Man" continuity, while it remains to be seen where "Crystal Lake" intends to position itself in "Friday the 13th" lore.

While neither "Ultimate Spider-Man" nor "Crystal Lake" would have been worthwhile if the writing had been subpar (or the artwork/performances of the cast had been bad, respectively), by far the most exciting aspect of both projects is the way they took the elements and histories of their respective franchises and examined them anew. In "Ultimate Spider-Man," bringing the character to a then-modern era did a lot of the heavy lifting in making the Spidey mythos feel fresh. Yet on top of that, Brian Michael Bendis added some wrinkles to the mythos which ended up influencing future Spidey adaptations. He came up with the idea of a genetically modified spider as opposed to a radioactive spider that delivers the fateful bite to Peter Parker (which appeared in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man"), and later the development of Peter's Aunt May discovering his secret identity as Spider-Man, as seen in the final moments of Jon Watts' "Spider-Man: Homecoming." Yet even with these new elements, "Ultimate Spider-Man" retained the core tropes and flavor of "Spider-Man."

In a similar fashion, "Crystal Lake" showrunner Brad Caleb Kane has allowed his series to reap the benefits of "Friday the 13th" lore without having to conform to it. Unlike Bendis, Kane did not modernize the Voorhees mythos and instead sets the series in the early 1970s, which is ostensibly the correct time period (more on this in a bit). The legend of Jason (Callum Vinson), his accidental drowning through negligence, his mother Pamela (Linda Cardellini) turning to madness through her grief, and the death curse on Crystal Lake are all present. Yet there are various twists, turns, and expansions on the characters and story which feel fresh, including a new concept for Jason's origin which has already become hotly debated.

A big part of why "Ultimate Spider-Man" and Brian Michael Bendis got to enjoy such creative freedom is due to the comic being part of Marvel's "Ultimate" line, which allowed their various creative teams to essentially make an adaptation of the Marvel Universe. That's because the general idea with the "main" Marvel Universe is that it's on a vague sliding scale of continuity. That's also generally been the idea with the "Friday the 13th" films so far, with even the one remake in the series, 2009's "Friday the 13th," being so close to the core elements of the character that some fans see it as more of a sequel. This is because Jason and his mythos already went to some wacky, improbable places before that film. This dubious veracity was established in the very first few "Friday the 13th" movies, in which Jason is explicitly said to have died in 1957, yet turns out to still be alive somehow.

All this raises the question: Is Brad Caleb Kane's "Crystal Lake" an adaptation of the "Friday" mythos, akin to "Ultimate Spider-Man," or is it intended as a loosely related entry in the main franchise? Though there is much in the "Friday" films which seems to contradict plot points in "Crystal Lake" (like the aforementioned time period change), the show could be establishing a new retconned backstory in a similar fashion to something like what "Freddy's Dead" did for the "A Nightmare on Elm Street" series. Whatever ends up being the case, it's been a treat to see Kane get to play around with Jason, Pamela, and the "Friday" lore, and while it may be upsetting the more literal-minded horror fans, for us longtime comic book nerds, it's all gravy, baby.

#3552. One of the GameCube’s Great Cult Classics Gets the Remaster It Deserves

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee is as clumsy and charming as you remember

When I was a kid, there were some games I only knew through magazines. I never played them, but they were all over the pages of Electronic Gaming Monthly and Nintendo Power, so I knew everything about them anyway. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee was firmly a “magazine game” when it was released for the GameCube in 2002. I even had a free poster of it on my wall as a kid, one I kept hung up even after a wave of middling reviews eventually dropped.

Historically, games like that aren’t prime candidates for remasters. They’re left to become rare collectibles found at retro game conventions while canon classics receive countless double dips on modern platforms. So what a delight it is that Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered now exists, in all of its messy glory. Atari’s surprising revival brings back a quintessential magazine game, rescuing it from its cult-classic destiny with a makeover and online multiplayer in tow.

Does it finally prove 2002’s unimpressed critics wrong? Not exactly. It’s still the same messy and shallow fighting game in some ways. But the purpose of a remaster like this shouldn’t be to engineer a redemption arc; all games, even the ones you never experienced beyond their box art, deserve to be preserved and celebrated.

Developed by Pipeworks in 2002, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee is a 3D brawler where players duke it out with a roster of rubbery kaiju. It’s a mix between arcade classic Rampage and Super Smash Bros., as you brawl your way through destructible cities using directional attacks. Despite receiving a few strong reviews at release from the likes of Nintendo Power and IGN, it largely earned middling scores from critics who took issue with its lack of depth. History has already repeated itself in 2026: the remaster currently has almost exact same Metacritic score as the original game. (73 for the original, 72 for the remaster.) Having spent hours with the Pipeworks’ faithful remaster, the consistent reaction tracks. Despite looking shinier, the new version wears all of its predecessor’s warts like a badge of honor.

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee remains a gleefully silly button masher that’s built for parties. Even now, there’s plenty of immediate pick-up-and-play fun that comes with stepping into Godzilla or Megalon’s rubber boots and smashing up Tokyo. Matches feel as big and exaggerated as professional wrestling bouts, as your monster body slams and tail whips buildings. What can feel a little clunky at first soon comes together as you learn how to block, strategically use your atomic breath to create space between you and your opponent, and duck behind buildings for cover. There’s just enough depth to create a casually satisfying fighting game where punching isn’t your only option.

As someone who never got to spend much time with the original as a kid outside of GameStop demo kiosks, I was smitten with the remaster right away, despite recognizing some obvious flaws. Yes, your grab button is finicky, leaving you struggling to pick up a building or scoop up your opponent. The movement can feel laborious as you trek around open city arenas. Characters can feel wildly imbalanced, with flying monsters like King Ghidorah having some clear advantages over grounded foes. There’s also its disappointingly repetitive arcade mode, which doesn’t bother to give each monster their own distinct story as they go to war against an alien invasion. There’s a good reason that games like Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee were largely enjoyed as weekend Blockbuster rentals in their time; you’re sure to hit the bottom of it in just a few hours.

But however short your fling with the remaster may be, it’s still worth spending some time with a blast from the past that’s so committed to celebrating a goofy piece of GameCube history. I quickly came to admire the brawler for its smart way of adapting old-school kaiju fights into a video game. It really gets across the idea that you’re a guy in a monster suit stomping around a fragile miniature city. The remaster keeps that spirit intact by making the shiny new textures look even more like rubber. I appreciate that the clumsiness of the brawling is preserved too, even if it’s not going to earn any favor with critics; the remaster is at its best when it stands by the original game’s vision.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Conversely, it’s at its worst when it tries to work in arbitrary tweaks. In the original game, you unlocked new monsters and stages by meeting various conditions as you played. The remaster trades that tradition for a long-tailed grind where you gain research points by playing. That approach not only pushes you to replay dull modes over and over again, but it also removes the surprising spirit of unlockables from the experience. Gone is the time-honored joy of getting a new character out of nowhere during a session. It’s one bum choice in a game that otherwise reveres GameCube era design choices.

Despite that flaw, I’m glad Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee has gotten its due on modern consoles — and in a way that isn’t desperate to rewrite history. As a collector of PlayStation 2 and GameCube games, I know that there’s a unique joy in cracking open an old game from an age where developers were still figuring out how 3D games should feel. These days, modern games can feel predictable and uniform, as so many developers have refined what a parry should feel like to a scientific degree. Pipeworks was very much experimenting in 2002 as it tried to crack what a Godzilla game that was faithful to Japanese cinema tradition should feel like. The results may have been messy at times, but it’s always a delight to play an old game that’s filled with deliberate design choices. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like nothing else in 2026, and that’s what makes it a worthy preservation effort, position in video game canon be damned.

Nintendo kicked and screamed against the PlayStation hegemony and its own fans, but it all worked out in the end

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
