#3551. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3550. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Design Leaks Online Thanks To Merchandise

Not even the King of the Monsters is immune to that most terrifying and undefeated of foes: merchandise. "Godzilla Minus Zero" director Takashi Yamazaki has kept his cards close to the vest on the highly-anticipated sequel, even with multiple full-length trailers hyping up the carnage that's to come in post-War Japan (and possibly New York City). But, as we creep closer to the impending release and what looks like a potential box office record in the making, there are always certain aspects bound to escape containment no matter how hard the concerned parties try — like the look of the kaiju-sized villain that Godzilla will be squaring off against this time around. Needless to say, what follows will count as major spoilers for those who wish to go in 100% fresh and unblemished, so don't say we didn't warn you!

For those who're still here and decided to ignore my helpful advice, well, it's hard to blame any of you. In fact, it's kind of hard to consider this a "spoiler" in any real conventional sense, either. "Godzilla" fans who've been following along closely already know that Ghidorah, the famous three-headed dragon from outer space, is set to play a huge role in "Minus Zero." But, despite keeping any actual glimpse of the flying, electricity-spewing monster away from the marketing, the bad guy's final look has leaked out courtesy of a Desktop Monster toy listing that you can see here.

Ghidorah Minus Zero toy design pic.twitter.com/g7slE3UPNr

Yup, sure looks like a three-headed dragon to me! The thing is, the whole look and feel of Ghidorah has been fairly set in stone over the years, and any deviations would have to be considered minor cosmetic tweaks, at best. That's certainly the case here, though diehards will inevitably notice some key details. Let's break them all down below.

Love it, hate it, or something in between, there's no denying the fact that 2019's "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" managed to visualize each and every one of its iconic kaiju — from Big G to Mothra to Rodan — in all their majestic splendor. But everyone's favorite extraterrestrial from outer space, Ghidorah, was a particular highlight. Lifted directly out of the old Toho movies with an updated and modernized spin, the final result raised the bar impossibly high for any other adaptation to come in the future. Needless to say, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has embraced that challenge and come out swinging with its own spin ... and it looks just different enough.

Let's get the obvious disclaimer out of the way: There's only so much you can do with the general look of a giant, golden, three-headed dragon, and "Minus Zero" certainly isn't reinventing the wheel. The snakelike heads, the webbed wings, and club-like tails are all present and accounted for this time around. But a closer look reveals some key differences. There's some gnarly-looking quills/spikes running up and down King Ghidorah's back, reminiscent of the spikey plates Godzilla sports. The wings are more of a wyvern-like design, too, with Ghidorah's "arms" resembling that of a pterosaur (those birdlike beasts that coexisted with dinosaurs, for the uninitiated).

But the most interesting twist is how much this Ghidorah resembles the one featured in Japan's "Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle" — an indoor theme park with a short film directed by Takashi Yamazaki himself, featuring his design for Ghidorah. If it ain't broke, don't fix it! Yamazaki appears to have taken that to heart.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" stomps into theaters November 6, 2026.

I have an annual tradition of watching the best horror movies, and given that Backrooms was so buzzed about earlier this year, I streamed it with my HBO Max subscription. I'd heard some people who saw it found it boring, and while I disagree on that front, I do think it isn't really scary.

The concept of "the backrooms" has existed on the internet for a long time, and I've seen it portrayed across many short films, video games, and horror stories. I wouldn't say I went into this movie with high expectations, but I certainly went in feeling like I'd leave feeling more scared than I was.

The problem, I think, is that I went into Backrooms expecting it to be a horror movie. As mentioned, people generally tackle this premise with a horror bent, typically with weird, deformed monsters and jump scares. This movie has zero jump scares, which bucks the trend of many modern horror movies, but I think it did it no favors.

All this to say, Backrooms is a fascinating thriller, and I really enjoyed the movie. Once I set aside the fact that I expected it to frighten me, I genuinely enjoyed the film and look forward to any future installments. In that way, it reminds me of The Silence Of The Lambs, which is another movie I'd associate with Halloween that isn't really that scary.

A sequel to Backrooms could, and certainly should, be much scarier. Now that the mainstream gets the general idea of how it all works, this is the time for director Kane Parsons to really flesh out how horrifying that concept is and what oddities can come from this space.

I've Been Looking Into Backrooms Theories, And Whoa, There's A Lot More To Unpack Than I Realized

As I mentioned before, we've already seen a lot of other works do this. A lot of what Parsons would need to add to a sequel is sitting there on the internet, and he has the power to make the mythology around it even scarier. It's what made it disappointing that the movie itself was more about being surreal rather than scary.

Without jump scares, Backrooms had me wondering how many people younger than me are genuinely terrified of a generic office layout from the 1990s. Or furniture that's clipped into walls and doors? We saw that all the time in video games growing up! That's not scary to me, that's bad graphics!

The good news is the movie did well and crushed it on streaming, so I think we're going to see the concept further evolve in the coming years. I'm fully on board with showing up for a sequel, but if this next one isn't scary, I don't think I'll stick around for the ride.

#3548. Why Criminal Minds: Evolution Was Canceled At Paramount Plus

"Criminal Minds" has been running since September 2005. But the show is set to come a close with its upcoming 20th Season, marking the end of an incredible run that already included one previous cancellation. The original "Criminal Minds" aired on CBS and ended after its fifteenth season back in 2020, after which the show was reborn as "Criminal Minds: Evolution." This latest incarnation of the procedural crime drama has been available on streaming service Paramount+ since 2022, but it seems the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU) will finally close up shop after Season 20.

Originally created by Jeff Davis, "Criminal Minds" has followed the investigations of the BAU as they've help track down dangerous criminals via their profiling expertise. The show debuted with Mandy Patinkin playing FBI Senior Supervisory Special Agent Jason Gideon, alongside Lola Glaudini as FBI Supervisory Special Agent Elle Greenaway, Thomas Gibson as FBI Supervisory Special Agent and Behavioral Analysis Unit Chief Aaron Hotchner, Matthew Gray Gubler as Spencer Reid, Kirsten Vangsness as Penelope Garcia, and A.J. Cook as Jennifer "JJ" Jareau. But as you might expect given the show's impressive run, "Criminal Minds" has undergone major changes over the years, with Mandy Patinkin's Jason Gideon leaving after just two seasons ahead of several other major departures.

Today, only Cook and Vangsness remain from the original cast, and it seems it's now time for their "Criminal Minds" journey to come to a close. For fans, the show's cancellation will have come as somewhat of a shock, especially since "Evolution" seems to have been faring well on Paramount+. For now, it remains unclear exactly why the series was canceled, but it likely has to do with a combination of cost, the show's broadcast roots, and new leadership at Paramount.

"Criminal Minds: Evolution" Season 19 debuted in May 2026, by which time the show had already been given an early Season 20 renewal in March 2026, with Paramount+ announcing a 2027 debut for Season 20. All of which seemed to bode well for the show. But this was prior to the completion of the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026. Paramount's takeover of the historic studio completed early that month, and by October 30 Deadline reported that "Criminal Minds: Evolution" had been cancelled, making the 20th season its last.

As such, the show became the first victim of the new Paramount+ leadership, but it seems the writing was on the wall even before the merger. Deadline cited sources as having claimed that the previous Paramount+ regime recommended cancelling the series prior to new Co-Chair & Chief Content Officer for Skydance Direct to Consumer, Casey Bloys, taking over. The outlet also noted that "Evolution" was still performing well and could, at the time of writing, be found in the Paramount+ Top 10. As such, it's likely the show's cancellation came down to cost or, as Deadline notes, the fact that "Evolution" retains much of the broadcast sensibility of the original show despite being a streaming series.

Meanwhile, HBO Max, which is now under the same leadership as Paramount+, is following a new "The Pitt"-style approach that, like broadcast, keeps the episode count high each season and follows a yearly release schedule while maintaining the production values of premium streaming series. It seems as though "Criminal Minds: Evolution" might not have fit that approach.

"Criminal Minds" executive producer/showrunner Erica Messer seemed surprised by the news of its cancellation. "It's hard to put into words what 'Criminal Minds' has meant to all of us who have been fortunate enough to be part of this extraordinary journey," she said (via Deadline). "[...] While suddenly navigating the end of this chapter, I'm filled with gratitude for our remarkable cast, writers, directors and crew who have poured their hearts into this show, and for the incredible fans around the world whose unwavering loyalty has kept 'Criminal Minds' going for two decades." The showrunner added that she was looking forward to Season 20, which wrapped filming by the time the cancellation was confirmed, meaning it likely won't provide a definite ending to the story.

Elsewhere, the "Criminal Minds: Evolution" cast reacted to the cancellation via social media. Emily Prentiss actor Paget Brewster kept things simple, posting a photo to Instagram of herself smiling with the words, "Free Agent..." Similarly, A.J. Cook took to Instagram to post a photo of herself in front of a tombstone for her character, alongside the caption "Rest in peace JJ (for now)."

Meanwhile, RJ Hatanaka, who plays Special Agent Tyler Green, posted a photo of the cast alongside the caption, "Just the finest group of people." Finally, Penelope Garcia actor Kirsten Vangsness — who has been part of every season of "Criminal Minds" — posted an Instagram video expressing her gratitude. "My heart fireworks in appreciation for the time at this job," she wrote, while using the video to speculate that the show could still continue elsewhere. For now, nothing has been confirmed, but as Vangsness points out in her video, showrunner Erica Messer has said that there are still stories to tell.

#3547. The Jewelry at the Center of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall’s On-Set Romance

In many photographs from the 1950s, Lauren Bacall appears alongside Humphrey Bogart with a small golden object between her lips. Curiously, it is a small gold whistle hanging from a bracelet. Not exactly the kind of accessory one would expect to find in a Hollywood star’s jewelry box. Yet, for Bacall, that particular piece held a very special meaning. Bogart himself gave it to her, inspired by a line the actor delivered in the film where the two met and fell in love.

In 1944, Bacall was just 19 years old when she made her film debut alongside Bogart in To Have and Have Not, directed by Howard Hawks. Bogart, 44 at the time, was already one of Hollywood’s most famous actors. On set, their relationship developed into something more than professional. They fell in love, and in May 1945, got married.

It was here that the origin story of the unusual bracelet began, with a line from Bacall that became one of old Hollywood’s most memorable: “You do know how to whistle, don’t you Steve? You just put your lips together and blow.” The scene, a candid moment of trust between the two characters, was a standout in the film, and it was this line that inspired the idea for the bracelet.

The result was a 14-karat-gold bracelet with a small pendant whistle, also made of gold and fully functional. The piece has a rather minimalist look, with smooth, polished surfaces and no particular decorations, except for a few personal engravings.

On one side of the tag are the words “Betty Bacall,” a reference to the actor’s original name, Betty Joan Perske, and on the other, “The Whistler.” On the whistle itself, the initials “B&B”—for Bogart and Bacall—are engraved, along with the number “21,” the meaning of which is still a mystery.

Bacall wore the bracelet in her daily life, carrying with her that small memento of the film that marked the beginning of her relationship with Bogart. In 1954, during a television interview with journalist Edward R. Murrow, the actor herself revealed the meaning of the whistle, explaining its connection to the famous line from To Have and Have Not.

Decades later, in September 2023, the bracelet made headlines again, when it was auctioned by Julien’s Auctions. The initial estimate ranged from $100,000 to $200,000, and on September 8, it sold for $158,750—a substantial sum for a small gold whistle. Though, considering who it belonged to—and especially who gave it to her—it’s not all that surprising.

Originally published in Vanity Fair Italy.

#3546. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

Full House might not be hailed as one of the best sitcoms of all time by many, but I have always been a massive fan of the show. I used to watch it every night on Nick at Nite and even own the entire series on DVD. I’ve always adored the Tanners and their extended family and can’t imagine any of them being played by any other actors; but it turns out that Lori Loughlin almost didn’t get to play Aunt Becky.

A majority of the Full House cast reunited at ‘90s Con in Connecticut and appeared on a panel discussing the show. During the panel, John Stamos shared his experience with the show’s creator, Jeff Franklin, when it came to casting Aunt Becky, aka his eventual long-term love interest on the show.

Lori came on at first, and I was like — I think we did some readings together before. I told [series creator] Jeff [Franklin], ‘I don’t know. She’s cute, and she’s adorable. I don’t think she’s tough enough to put Jesse in his place.’

Good casting can make or break a project, especially when it comes to the chemistry between two actors who are playing characters that are romantically linked. At the time, Full House wasn’t considered a hit by any means, so it makes sense that Stamos would want to get the casting right to ensure the show would continue.

While Stamos’ Uncle Jesse and Lori Loughlin’s Aunt Becky eventually became the best couple on the show, their relationship wasn’t always a walk in the park. Jesse was instantly smitten with Becky, as he was with most women on the show, but the same was not true for her character. Thus, it was important that Loughlin be able to play off Stamos’s character in order to build up that will-they, won’t-they tension.

Thankfully, the show’s creator didn’t listen to Stamos and did go on to cast Loughlin in the role. In turn, the When Calls the Heart actress proved Stamos wrong and put him and his character in his place on the first day of set.

Scene one, she came and she put me in my place fast. She had the perfect combination of this adorable, sweet girl. But, when it was time for me to get in trouble, you had no problem [playing] that out.

For those who don’t remember, Jesse meets Becky at the Tanner house and instantly tries to hit on her. Unlike most of the women who swoon at his feet, Becky challenged Jesse’s flirting attempts and even compared him to her baby brother, which gutted him. However, despite Becky’s apprehensions, she did end up falling for Jesse’s charm, and the two got together (for the first time) during the second season’s Christmas episode.

Hiring Loughlin turned out to be one of the best decisions, and the show steadily started to grow its fan base. It’s wild to think that she was initially only hired for six episodes and went on to become a fan favorite character. It turns out Aunt Becky was the missing piece all along.

#3544. Who Is The Longbow Killer In Absolute Green Arrow? DC's Murder Mystery, Explained

This article contains spoilers for "Absolute Green Arrow."

DC Comics' "Absolute" Universe has made major changes to classic heroes like Batman. "Absolute Green Arrow," which recently completed its first arc, "The Longbow Killer," leans more toward mystery. Despite the title, the main character here is Dinah Lance, the Black Canary, and she's investigating who the Green Arrow is.

An "Absolute Green Arrow" series from writer Pornsak Pichetshote and artist Rafael Albuquerque was announced in July 2025. Classic Green Arrow Oliver Queen (aka Ollie) then debuted in the "Absolute" Universe in October one-shot "Absolute Evil," by Al Ewing and Giuseppe Camuncoli. An archery-loving billionaire who wants to be a hero, Oliver is murdered by the evil oligarchs who call themselves "The Justice League."

In "Absolute Green Arrow," the murder mystery isn't who killed Oliver Queen; the audience already knows that. The question is why the "Longbow Killer," dressed like a cross of Robin Hood and the Grim Reaper, is murdering people connected to Oliver's death.

The comic presents lots of suspects, like "Absolute" versions of Oliver's traditional sidekicks Roy Harper and Mia Dearden, as well as his illegitimate son Connor Hawke. All three of them are archer heroes in the main DC Universe, and therefore are prime Longbow Killer candidates. Dinah is reluctantly working security for evil businessman (and Justice League member) Hector Hammond. Her partner is Malcolm Merlyn, aka Green Arrow's classic "Dark Archer" nemesis. Considering the comic features zombie villain Solomon Grundy, some readers (and Dinah) even suspected the killer was a vengeful, undead Oliver.

But "Absolute Green Arrow" #6 pulled back the Longbow Killer's hood, revealing Merlyn and Connor Hawke. Oliver was not in Connor's life when Connor was growing up, so Malcolm raised Connor instead. The Longbow Killer has been targeting people like Hammond because Connor is avenging his father's death and redeeming Ollie's mistakes.

DC promoted "Absolute Green Arrow" like it was a slasher movie, with Green Arrow himself being described as "a Robin Hood who is less Errol Flynn and more Michael Myers." Except this slasher is targeting corrupt billionaires, not dumb teenagers. During "Absolute Green Arrow," the Longbow Killer becomes a social media hero because many people think his targets deserve it. But Connor and Malcolm aren't killing to spark a revolution.

"Absolute Green Arrow" gradually reveals Hector Hammond is performing illegal human experiments into anti-aging via advanced cellular regeneration. Jubal Slade, Ollie's former business partner and a Jeffrey Epstein-esque child trafficker, was supplying Hammond with test subjects.

It turns out "Malcolm" is actually Arthur King, a mercenary hired to investigate the disappearance of one of Jubal's victims. Once Arthur and Connor got close to the truth, Connor brought it to Oliver; his dad had always resisted actually standing up to Slade, and Connor wanted to shock him into action. It worked, but Oliver moving against Slade and Hammond is why he was was silenced. Cue Arthur going undercover as "Malcolm Merlyn" to investigate Hammond and provide inside protection for Connor's crusade.

There's a classic red herring where, after Connor is introduced in "Absolute Green Arrow" #2, the Longbow Killer seemingly murders him. In reality, that was Connor and Arthur redirecting Dinah's suspicion. But Arthur dies genuinely in "Absolute Green Arrow" #5, leaving Connor as the only living Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote initially compared "Absolute Green Arrow" to the 1997 slasher "I Know What You Did Last Summer," which is about a group of people with a dark secret being murdered one by one. But the reveal of the Longbow Killer's identity borrows from a different slasher franchise: "Scream," where there is almost always more than one Ghostface killer.

Oliver Queen's legacy influences Connor's choice of weapons. Ollie made his money with a company called Greenarrows Trading (a reference to the real financial app Robinhood Markets). When we first see the Longbow Killer in "Absolute Green Arrow" #1, he pointedly leaves two green arrows in the eyes of Jubal Slade's corpse. His bow is also made from two swords latched together. It's a similar touch to "Absolute Batman" making Batman's chest symbol into an axe; the hero's symbol is a collapsible weapon.

Jubal Slade is a reinvention of a slumlord villain from Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams' "Green Lantern" #76, the beginning of the famous and bitingly political "Hard-Traveling Heroes" arc starring Green Lantern and Green Arrow. The "Longbow Killer" moniker comes from another "Green Arrow" comic, Mike Grell's 1987 "The Longbow Hunters." After Oliver Queen died in 1995's "Green Arrow" #101, Connor Hawke took his father's place as Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote was also once an executive in DC's TV department, where he helped spearhead TV shows like "Arrow." His previous experience reimagining Green Arrow clearly shaped his latest attempt. In "Arrow" Season 1, Oliver Queen (Stephen Amell) is out to kill or ruin the names of people on a list given to him by his father, Robert Queen (Jamey Sheridan); Robert was once part of this conspiracy and wants his son to enact vengeance. Connor being the Longbow Killer makes "Absolute Green Arrow" into the same story: A son goes out to avenge his father's murder by killing a list of his dad's shady associates. "Absolute Green Arrow" also employs a flashback storyline much like "Arrow" did, and the name "Malcolm Merlyn" comes from "Arrow."

Oliver was presented as a kind of serial killer in "Arrow" Season 1. (Season 2 was even all about him swearing that "I can't be the killer I once was.") "Absolute Green Arrow" embraces that approach, and then some.

#3542. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

Inside the NBA fans were hit with some major news last week, as longtime co-host Ernie Johnson confirmed his plan to leave the show at the end of the professional basketball season. Right now, many are simply taking the time to pay tribute to the man affectionately known as “E.J.” However, there are those who are also questioning what lies ahead for the show in the long run without Johnson. The man himself recently expressed his hope that the show will go on, and there’s also been an update on ESPN’s alleged feelings about that.

To put it mildly, Johnson is one of the mainstays of Inside, given he’s been hosting the show for 37 years now. 70-year-old Johnson announced his intention to exit the show nearly a week ago in a social media video that’s since gone viral. The veteran sports journalist confirmed that he wasn’t retiring from broadcasting entirely, though. He’ll continue to serve as a March Madness analyst and produce content under his 32 Bowties production company. Nevertheless, he’s stepping down from Inside as a way to “slow down a bit.”

Johnson recently caught up with Front Office Sports Tonight to discuss his big decision and plans for the future. When addressing what may lie ahead for his long-running basketball talk show, Johnson expressed optimism:

I don’t want to be blamed for ending Inside the NBA. I’m stepping away from my role on there. I would hope that they could continue the show in some form. And there are plenty of great studio hosts out there who could do what I do.

On paper, it would definitely make sense to keep the TNT-turned-ESPN sports show on the air, considering its popularity. It’s still hard not to wonder, however, how viewership may be affected by Ernie Johnson’s absence next season. Plus, there’s the fact that Charles Barkley has been discussing retirement again as well. With that, sources are now saying that ESPN has been giving the future some thought amid these developments.

Shaq Explains Why Inside The NBA Works, But I’m Just Loving The Ernie Johnson Detail He Revealed

Weeks before Johnson confirmed his intention to leave Inside, Barkley already indicated that his longtime co-star would do just that. The “Round Mound of Rebound” also said at the time that he was planning to exit the show after this current season as well due to him and Johnson being a “package deal.” Considering that Johnson and Barkley have shared the screen for over 25 years, their dual exits would mark a major shift. However, per FOS’ sources, ESPN remains committed to keeping the show going even without the pair.

That would theoretically leave co-hosts Kenny Smith and Shaquille O’Neal alongside two others. Interestingly, since Johnson shared his news, Barkley hasn’t said anything more about whether he’ll ride off into the sunset as well. Johnson was also asked about Barkley’s plans when he appeared on FOS Tonight, and he had this to say about him:

As for what Chuck is going to do, I have learned many many moons ago, you never try to predict what the Chuckster is going to do. But he and I have had a lot of conversations in the past about what we’re going to do, so I will leave that final word to him.

If any other Inside the NBA fans are like me, they’ll be waiting with bated breath for Charles Barkley to deliver a definitive decision. The fact that Ernie Johnson is leaving (for some well-deserved time with his loved ones) is already tough to think about, so Barkley’s exit would also be a lot. At the very least, though, it’s encouraging that ESPN is reportedly still aiming to keep the show on the air for the foreseeable future.

Check out Inside the NBA’s next broadcast, which will hit ESPN on Wednesday, November 4, with NBA Tip Off starting at 6 p.m. ET amid the 2026 TV schedule.

#3540. Jenna Ortega's Klara And The Sun Movie Set An Unwanted Box Office Record

Things have gone from bad to worse for "Klara and the Sun." Fronted by "Wednesday" star Jenna Ortega and hailing from "Thor: Ragnarok" director Taika Waititi, it's been nothing shy of a crushing disappointment for all involved. Now, the movie has etched its way into the box office history books, but in a very unfortunate way.

Hailing from Sony Pictures, "Klara and the Sun" flopped at the box office on its opening weekend, pulling in just $701,000 in its debut against a $20 million budget. That was bad enough, but in its second weekend, the sci-fi flick dropped a staggering 93.6%, taking in just $45,000 on 880 screens. That means it averaged just $51 per screen. This is just about as bad as it gets for a movie from high-profile filmmakers in Hollywood.

With that, Waititi's latest has etched its way into the history books. This represents the biggest second weekend drop of all time for a new release narrative feature film. The only movie to ever have a worse second weekend drop was the concert film "Stray Kids: The Dominate Experience" (94.9%) earlier this year, according to Box Office Mojo. Concert films are generally more niche and front-loaded. A would-be awards season play like "Klara and the Sun" is designed to hopefully pick up steam, not drop like a rock.

The movie is based on the acclaimed 2021 novel by Kazuo Ishiguro. It focuses on Klara (Ortega), an Artificial Friend who meets a girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). Klara's innocent wonder and loyalty begin to heal Josie's family and bring light to her complicated world. Waititi recently slammed critics after "Klara and the Sun" flopped, taking it all very personally.

There's nothing for Taika Waititi to be happy about. His new movie has made less than $2 million worldwide and is pretty much dead in the water at this point, despite the promising source material and a cast that includes Amy Adams, one of the best actors who has never won an Oscar (though she's been nominated several times). Waititi is also an Oscar winner himself, winning Best Original Screenplay for "Jojo Rabbit."

It doesn't matter at the moment that Waititi directed one of Marvel's most beloved hits, "Thor: Ragnarok" ($855 million worldwide). It doesn't matter that "Thor: Love and Thunder" ($761 million) was also a big hit despite not being as well-liked, broadly speaking. In a "what have you done for me lately?" business, Waititi is floundering. It certainly doesn't help that Waititi's "Next Goal Wins" was also a box office bomb in 2023, even though it was a low stakes one with a low budget.

Jenna Ortega evolved from Disney princess to scream queen, becoming one of Hollywood's most in-demand A-list stars. Right or wrong, she's had enough success in recent years that this probably won't ding her reputation too much. She's also not out there publicly decrying critics for not liking the movie. Waititi, through his own doing, is ensuring that he's going to shoulder the blame.

Big box office flops can put creators in director's jail. This is a lower budget movie, but still, Waititi's on a cold streak and it's very possible that he's either headed for director's jail or is already in it.

"Klara and the Sun" is still in theaters now, but probably won't be for much longer.

#3539. How Greg Brockman’s Wife Anna Became a Trump and MAGA Mega-Donor

It was weeks before the election and spirits were low in MAGA’s top ranks. The president’s approval ratings had plunged to historic depths. Polling suggested his endorsement had become an albatross for many of his preferred candidates. And so Donald Trump had retreated to the gilded comfort of Mar-a-Lago to attend to “matters of national importance,” including, on October 17, a candlelit dinner with some of his most loyal supporters.

At the head of the table were just four seats: Google cofounder Sergey Brin, President Trump himself, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and his wife, Anna Brockman.

Anna Brockman, Greg Brockman, President Donald Trump, and Sergey Brin during a MAGA Inc. event at Mar-a-Lago. October 16, 2026.

The Brockmans, worth nearly $30 billion, have used their wealth to become the 16th-biggest political mega-donors this midterms cycle: Last year, the couple donated a combined $25 million to MAGA Inc. and $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. Greg has said that he and his wife are “single-issue donors,” their lone cause being AI, the technology he’s helped build. “It’s not popular,” he recently acknowledged, so “we really want to support politicians who really lean into [it].” And it has been “we” at each of these turns—the Brockmans working in tandem toward a shared vision of the future.

Yet despite Anna Brockman’s frequent presence amid the backdrop of this pivotal scene in history, next to nothing has previously been reported about her. When The Wall Street Journal profiled Greg Brockman in May, they wrote of his elusive wife, “She is intensely private: almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.”

Anna Chang has an unlikely past—one that raises some new questions. How did a onetime registered Democrat and ambitious tech worker who “loves everything that positively changes the world” become the retired wife of one of the wealthiest men on earth, Donald Trump’s frequent guest, and one of the single-largest donors seeking to hasten a future where artificial intelligence is developed with minimal regulatory oversight?

Sources close to the Brockmans and to OpenAI suggested that Anna is no bystander, and is worthy of scrutiny as a significant player herself. “She’s not a silent sidekick to Greg,” says one AI industry insider. “She is a force.”

When Greg and Anna met at a Silicon Valley dinner party in 2018, Greg said they “instantly connected.” She was the daughter of Korean immigrants, and he had a long-standing reverence for Korean culture: He has a black belt in tae kwon do, and even attended Korean summer camp as a teenager, picking up some of the language. They had also both worked at the payments-software start-up Stripe in the 2010s, though their tenures never overlapped. (Both Greg and Anna Brockman declined Vanity Fair’s request for comment for this story.)

In 2015, Greg had left his position as Stripe’s chief technology officer to cofound OpenAI with 10 fellow visionaries out of his San Francisco living room. A gifted and relentless coder, he muscled his way through seemingly impossible projects in the hopes of eventually achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI (the point when the technology can match or exceed human-level capabilities at every possible task). He sometimes clocked 90-hour workweeks. Greg’s colleagues from over the years describe him as fiercely competitive, not just with work projects but also with hobbies like running and weight lifting.

Anna was a quirky and exuberant animal lover from Texas—one source estimates she and her husband live with over 20 animals—who had worked for AmeriCorps mentoring working-class students after graduating from Wesleyan University, well known as an ultraliberal school. (In a total coincidence, I discovered midway through reporting that Anna and I had overlapped there during our college years.) When she became one of the first 100 or so employees at Dropbox, her idealism persisted. In an introduction to her new colleagues, she told them she spent her free time “taking on adventures to help save the world.”

While a source close to Anna said she doesn’t drink alcohol, sources who’ve spent time with her said she has sometimes drawn attention for her juvenile humor and unconventional manner. She “curses like a drunken sailor,” said one. Another described her as “fratty.”

Early in the Brockmans’ relationship, Anna experienced a series of mysterious health mishaps. The couple spent years visiting doctor after doctor, and eventually discovered she had Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS). Greg has also said that she has Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). She believed that with the right AI tools, her arduous investigation might have been made much simpler. “Her whole passion for AI is driven by this medical journey,” said her friend and former colleague Sujay Jaswa.

In her late 30s, Anna was also diagnosed with autism. “Her autism can come at a cost, one of which is requiring a lot of alone time (the fur kids and myself excluded) and downtime to rest and recover,” her husband wrote, referring to their many pets. “A beautiful trait of her autism is her deep connection to animals and attention to understanding their needs,” Greg posted on X.

He, too, required patience from his partner while he focused on his interior life. During their first holiday season together, he decided to teach himself machine learning, scratching out equations in a notebook. “She was there with me no matter how many planned activities it meant skipping,” he wrote on his blog. He described her as “someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed.” Greg said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast that they even put off having children so that he could focus all his energy on AI.

Anna’s early adoption of AI tools helped her practically float up the corporate ladder, but it also opened the door to loftier visions. In a 2018 blog post, she wrote, “I believe in the power of AI to allow us to become more human, today and in the future, by alleviating monotony and opening the space for creativity and intuition.”

Meanwhile, Greg sounded like he was experiencing vertigo from the progress they were making at OpenAI. His journals from this period, portions of which were later made public as part of discovery for the Musk v. Altman trial, ricochet between self-doubt and megalomania. “No person should have control over what we’re creating,” he wrote in August 2017. Then three months later, he appeared to copy and paste a chat with an unknown correspondent into the journal document. “It is better for us to become increasingly kings of this industry,” one of them wrote. “Being the kings of AI is not so bad.”

In Anna, he found the ultimate support system. According to the WSJ, he took the other side of a bet with his then OpenAI colleague (and later Anthropic cofounder) Daniela Amodei, who wagered $100 that Anna was not the one. He won. As Greg put it, they “have been inseparable ever since.”

At the Musk v. Altman trial, Anna was by her husband’s side almost every day. Some observers noted that she held his hand right up to the last second as she walked him to the witness stand. Sources who know the couple described Anna, 38, as “very devoted” and Greg, 38, as “the ultimate wife guy.”

When Anna and Greg got married in 2019, they held a civil ceremony in OpenAI’s office officiated by fellow OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever. The ring bearer was a robotic hand.

As wife to the “wife guy” at the helm of one of the most powerful companies on earth, Anna has enjoyed a front row seat to scenes of such intrigue that they have inspired multiple books, and the highly anticipated upcoming film Artificial. (Cooper Hoffman, the actor who plays Brockman in the film Artificial, recalls director Luca Guadagnino’s guidance on how to approach the role: “Greg is all-American,” Guadagnino told him. “He’s like a cheeseburger.”)

The Brockmans attended the Met Gala in 2025.

While it isn’t uncommon for spouses and partners to turn up in the offices of start-ups, sources who’ve spent time with the Brockmans noted that by the late 2010s Anna was unusually engaged in his work life, having left her own job at the venture capital firm Basis Set Ventures. While, per The Information, Anna has never been formally employed at OpenAI, over the years she has appeared in live product demos; accompanied executives on trips, like one to South Korea to meet with local start-ups; and even been spotted at high-level meetings at the OpenAI office.

When OpenAI’s top executives were appointed drivers and private security, Anna would sometimes be spotted in the car with Greg, taking him to work, according to former colleagues.

As the money piled up, the relationships between the company’s early team—including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Jakub Pachocki, Mira Murati, and Dario and Daniela Amodei—began to fray. While the imaginations of many of their Bay Area peers ran wild with sci-fi visions of uploaded consciousness and unfathomable abundance, and AI doomsayers warned of extinction events, the Brockmans’ hopes for an AI future felt relatively pedestrian.

Greg was firmly in the pro-commercialization camp, according to OpenAI researchers who’ve worked with him, believing that above all, AI can empower individuals to transform their own lives. Anna, meanwhile, is driven by the “idea that AI for all is gonna take all these major social problems, like the extreme cost of health care and education [and] extreme inequality in access…and it’s gonna democratize all of it,” according to Jaswa.

And to do that, the Brockmans understood that AI leaders needed to win over the policymakers that, in their view, could stand in the way of AGI.

Following the release of ChatGPT in 2022, OpenAI’s founding team found themselves on the other side of overnight fame—at least in the insular tech bubble of the Bay Area. While some of the more socially awkward researchers chafed at the attention, Greg—who’d been promoted to president of the company—and Anna have seemed to bask in it.

The Brockmans have dined with Sylvester Stallone at the Kennedy Center, attended black-tie events at the White House, and even walked the blue carpet at the Met Gala, where Anna wore a black-and-white ruffled gown by Korean designer Ashlynn Park.

The power she’d been quietly amassing by Greg’s side played out in a more significant and dramatic way in November 2023, when the board of OpenAI removed Sam Altman from his position as CEO over concerns that he was untrustworthy. Sutskever, who was on the board, also compiled a memo detailing allegations against Greg, and Greg was removed from his position as chairman of the board (but allowed to stay on as president). When the board called Greg to inform him of their decision, the first thing he did was talk to his wife. He told her, “‘We have to leave.’ And she said, ‘Yes, we do,’” he said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast. He warned her they would have to be prepared for his equity to disappear if he quit. “‘Still want to do it?’ And she said yes.”

But when the board began to reconsider its decision, Sutskever became the deciding vote. In an oft-repeated piece of OpenAI lore, Anna allegedly begged Sutskever in a tearful encounter to reconsider. (Sources familiar with the events have suggested that the impact of this encounter has been overstated.) According to the WSJ, when Sutskever decided to reverse his decision, Anna left him a cactus as a gift.

After a long negotiation over his place at the company, Sutskever left to start his own venture, Safe Superintelligence. “There were some deep and bitter things” that went down during this period, according to one high-level employee at the time.

After this dramatic inflection point, which has come to be known as the blip, Greg took a three-month leave of absence. This period allowed him to dedicate himself to a project he was passionate about: developing a biological foundation model for genome modeling and design at the Arc Institute—“a domain that’s very personally meaningful to both me and and to my wife,” he has said.

Meanwhile, the company had replaced nearly all the board members who’d risen up against Altman with what one former senior OpenAI employee called a “more loyal and ‘normie’” board who were supportive of the company’s commercial push.

The center of gravity began to shift in Greg’s direction, solidifying his place as Altman’s second in command, soon to be tasked with an even more fraught assignment: building political goodwill. What wouldn’t the billionaire couple do to help the technology that they consider vital to humanity’s future?

“He thinks big, but he is also very practical, kind of a realist,” Peter Welinder, OpenAI’s vice president and general manager, says of Greg. Others felt that his techno-optimism, and subsequent push into Washington to defend those ideals, is “naivete,” says the former high-level employee. “I don’t think he’s very carefully thinking through the political and power implications.”

When Donald Trump was reelected in late 2024, OpenAI found itself facing down a new threat. Elon Musk, an original cofounder of the company who left in 2018, had grown increasingly antagonistic toward his onetime colleagues while also growing close to the incoming administration. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, OpenAI, and Altman in particular, feared political retribution from Musk, who now had his own competitor company in xAI, if he was allowed to take up all the oxygen in Washington. At the same time, OpenAI’s need for energy and compute had grown so insatiable that the company had no choice but to seek the government’s help. In an administration run on quid pro quo, OpenAI would have to make nice.

Brockman found himself uniquely well-positioned to lead the infrastructure-scaling bonanza, thanks to a preexisting relationship with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who hailed from his home state of North Dakota. Greg was also “the most credible” face of the political donations, said one former OpenAI employee.

And so Greg and Anna Brockman became White House mainstays. They have attended state dinners for foreign leaders like Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Xi Jinping, and joined top tech executives at a White House event about the future of AI. Brockman, rather than Altman, flanked Trump during the signing of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence in September.

When the political pendulum began to swing back this summer, it began to appear as though whoever had made the call on those political donations might have made a severe miscalculation. Following a steady drumbeat of negative headlines about Leading the Future’s work and significant internal dissent among OpenAI employees, the Brockmans rescinded their second planned $25 million donation to the PAC. Greg wrote in a Slack message, obtained by The New York Times, that Leading the Future had become a “distraction” from OpenAI’s work.

When I reached out to OpenAI to discuss the Brockmans’ political giving, it directed me back to the Brockmans’ team. In an interview this October with Vanity Fair’s global editorial director Mark Guiducci, Altman said, “I did not ask him to donate or stop donating. He can make his own personal decisions.” It seems the Brockmans’ donations are a hot potato no one is eager to catch.

Regardless, their $25 million checks have helped provide the funds to enable a torrent of preelection ads, including warnings like, “This is the final battle” to “liberate America from these villains, once and for all.”

Some observers of the company have come to believe that the plan was “to have Greg be the scapegoat if/when the Democrats come back into power, but to allow OpenAI to privately (with the White House) claim credit for the MAGA PAC donations with the Trump administration while privately (with employees) distance itself from them,” according to the former senior employee. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.)

Meanwhile, Greg has returned more of his focus to the product realm, and he and his wife have found a less controversial way to spend their millions. When the couple found out that the Big Bear Valley habitat of two publicly beloved eagles, Jackie and Shadow, was under threat, they donated over $5.5 million to preserve the land this summer. “[Jackie and Shadow] inspire perseverance and a sense of connectedness to something greater,” Anna said of their donation.

“It was clear in talking to her that she loved her husband very much and that she loved the eagles,” says Jenny Voisard, the communications and PR leader for Friends of Big Bear Valley, of her experience working with Anna on the donation. They never talked about politics.

#3538. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Has Some Controversial Thoughts On AI [Exclusive]

There's no question Andy Weir is an absolute wizard at crafting wildly entertaining hard sci-fi adventures. The man wrote "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary," both of which have been adapted into hugely successful blockbusters, with "Project Hail Mary" absolutely dominating the box office. But Weir also has some dodgy opinions, like when the "Project Hail Mary" author took "Black Mirror" to task for being anti-tech. Evidently, the writer also has no time for artificial intelligence doomerism, maintaining that this darkly sinister tech is good, actually.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai spoke with Weir, who characterized AI as a "tool" that can be used for good or evil. "It's the first time that we've had something on Earth that's smarter than us," he said. "So that's a little scary, but we have forklifts that are stronger than us. We have race cars that are faster than us. Okay, so we have computers that are smarter than us." It's not a great start is it, comparing advanced technology to a forklift? Maybe if forklifts consumed exorbitant amounts of electricity and water, were capable of replacing large swathes of the global workforce, and were pumping out the artistic equivalent of effluent via music, images, and videos that essentially represent the most large-scale theft of copyrighted material in human history, it might be a fair comparison.

You'd think a creative like Weir might be a tad hesitant to embrace this still nascent technology, but it seems he's all for it. "It's a tool that we can use and we can unplug when we don't want to use it," he continued. "In the end, if I give you a hammer, you can build a house or you can murder someone. It's not the tool that's the issue, it's the user."

"AI is a tool" is an oft-used defense of the technology that doesn't hold up. Co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology, Tristan Harris, addressed this point during a GZERO World interview:

"Imagine a hammer that can think to itself at a PhD level about hammers, invent better hammers, recursively go off in the world, duplicate itself, do research on what would make better hammers, make money, send crypto around [...] It is not a tool. It's more like an intelligent species that we are birthing that has more capability than us."

It's not an unreasonable point. According to Weir, however, it's one not worth considering. Unfortunately, he had more to say on the topic. The author admitted to having "dorked around with AI" only to find it lacking in the narrative fiction department. For him, however, this is temporary. "I think it's only a matter of time," he said. "Honestly, I think I'm lucky that I ended up being a writer right when I did, because I might be among the last generation of fully human writers." If you keep talking about AI like it's a hammer, you might well be.

Weir also went on to claim that AI usage in entertainment is more widespread than we realize and posed a hypothetical example of a director using AI to see how a line from their lead actor might sound, before asking that actor back for ADR. "If you say, 'Okay, I like that,' call Brad Pitt, have him rerecord the line. So no AI gets into the finished product." Fine. But Weir has claimed to be writing a book that tackles AI and you'd hope for at least some acknowledgement that this is all a slippery slope.

In 2023, Joe Russo set forth his vision of an artificial intelligence garbage future, in which AI creates tailor-made movies for specific viewers. That's a vision Andy Weir evidently shares. The author told /Film he believes entertainment is going to "stop being such a group phenomenon" and that instead of audiences gathering at the multiplex to watch "Avengers: Endgame," they'll be staring at their laptops. "AI will be powerful and portable enough that your own computer will be as good as a modern day AI data center," Weir said, adding:

"It'll know you. It'll know you. It won't even have to tell you about you. It's just by your browser habits, by reading your emails and just by paying attention, it'll get to know you. Then you can say, 'Hey computer, make me a story that I'd like.' It'll make a story that you will like. You'll read it and you'll say, 'This is the most amazing, awesome story ever.'" [...] eventually, the computer will be able to do the video for it as well. You can make a movie that's perfect for you."

It's just sort of hard to believe that this hellish future will actually come to pass given the widespread pushback AI has faced from a public still clearly invested in human expression. In that sense, it's disappointing not to hear a word of support for that sentiment from Weir. Likewise, for a guy who's made his name as a hard sci-fi maestro capable of weaving real science into his narratives in a way that speaks to his knowledge of the current state of technological and scientific progress, it's surprising not to hear him address larger points about about how AI might possibly differ from a forklift.

Star Trek: The Next Generation's Brent Spiner revealed he had a small part to play in Patrick Stewart's famous time hosting Saturday Night Live. A story about the Data actor's attempt to get on the show is making rounds after his co-star's death, and I absolutely love it.

Spiner's story popped up in a special video from Dropping Names With Brent And Jonny, which compiled each time the hosts talked about their former co-star and friend, Stewart. This led to a hilarious story in which Spiner tried to get on SNL, only for them to inquire about Stewart instead:

My now-wife, she was a publicist on [TNG], and when she became a publicist she said, 'Is there anything you would like to do? I'll see if I can get that for you.' I said, 'Yeah, I want to host Saturday Night Live.' She said, 'Ok,' and she called them and she said, 'Well, I called them and they said we'd like to have Patrick Stewart.'

Brent Spiner may be the funniest person in Star Trek, which is evident enough from stories from co-stars and the Generations movie. That was enough to get him on Night Court, but Saturday Night Live is reserved for the leads. As such, their staff wanted Patrick Stewart, and as we know, Stewart is who they got.

As A Star Trek Fan I'm Eternally Grateful For What Patrick Stewart Did For The Franchise

Patrick Stewart only hosted SNL once in the 90s, but the night lives on in the show's history thanks to a story John Mulaney worked into his stand-up comedy. Mulaney stressed that Stewart's delivery when introducing Salt-N-Pepa was interesting because he sounded surprised by the Pepa bit of it, though people debate whether it really was that silly after watching the clip.

As for other stand-out moments of the Saturday Night Live appearance, there are a few skits that stand out. There's a skit I love that combined Star Trek: The Next Generation with The Love Boat, as well as another about him working in an erotic bakery shop. Both had me laughing out loud when I watched, so those who can seek it out certainly should.

It's yet another story about Stewart appearing on another show, which I found just after writing about Jeremy Clarkson having him on the set of Top Gear. I'll always appreciate the wild Star Trek stories about Stewart, but I've heard a good deal of them already. Learning his experience on other shows is great, and further illustrates what kind of man he was behind the scenes.

Both his Star Trek and Marvel co-stars insist that Patrick Stewart was exceptionally kind. He played a Captain on television and a super-powered Professor in the X-Men, and by all accounts, both were a good show of just how heroic he was as a real-life individual. As a fan, it's great to see the man measured up to all I imagined he'd be.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family of Patrick Stewart, and the friends who continue to mourn him. It's been great to see all the stories hitting the internet, and how it's given fans comfort in the wake of a tremendous loss to the Star Trek world.

#3536. This Marvel And Alien Crossover Features The Most Dangerous Xenomorphs Yet

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

This article contains spoilers for "Alien vs. X-Men" #2.

After Disney acquired 20th Century Fox in 2019, "Alien" and Marvel Comics became housed under the same corporate umbrella. While we've yet to see any Xenomorphs pop up in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the two franchises have crossed over in the comics.

The first time was in the surprisingly excellent 2024-2025 miniseries "Alien vs. Avengers" by Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribic. That series features the Marvel Universe's Earth falling prey to a Xenomorph infestation; most of the story takes place decades in a post-apocalyptic future of the few remaining Marvel heroes trying to survive. Mutantkind takes refuge on Mars, where evil scientist Mister Sinister begins experimenting on Xenomorphs to predictably disastrous results.

The mutants are facing off with the Xenomorphs again in the new miniseries "Alien vs. X-Men," co-written by the defining "X-Men" writer Chris Claremont and Kieron Gillen with art by Geraldo Borges. The comic begins in media res: An X-Men team (Cyclops, Beast, Kitty Pryde, Emma Frost, and Wolverine) is in space trying to find a Phoenix Egg, the egg from which the Phoenix Force hatches when it reincarnates. Instead, the ship is filled with Xenomorph eggs.

When the ship returns to Earth and crashes in front of Xavier's School, all the X-Men but Wolverine are dead — and Logan is being kept alive as a repeat incubator. Worse, the Xenomorphs spawned from him have his claws, just as the hive queen has Emma's diamond skin.

In the "Alien" films, Xenomorphs take on qualities of the hosts from which they spawn. For instance, in "Alien 3," a Xenomorph that spawns from a dog walks on four legs. This is the horrifying culmination of that idea: Xenomorphs birthed from mutants have mutant superpowers.

During "Alien vs. X-Men" #1, the mutant Xenomorphs attack the X-Mansion and the remaining X-Men; their acid blood proves strong enough to melt Colossus' steel skin. Worse, they take Jamie Madrox, the Multiple Man, who has the power to clone himself into endless duplicates. The stakes of that are laid out in issue #2; if the Xenomorphs absorb Multiple Man's power, they'll be able to spawn endlessly, without the need for living hosts, and Earth is doomed.

Now, the X-Men often fight parasitic aliens called the Brood that are inspired by "Alien." (Chris Claremont originally created the Brood in 1982 during his titanic "X-Men" run.) Unlike Xenomorphs, the Brood can talk and explicitly share a hive mind. The Brood also reproduce by infesting living hosts with their spawn, though the hosts' bodies are transformed into Brood drones. It's slightly less gruesome than how Xenomorphs spawn in the "Alien" movies via chestbursters. The Brood also absorb mutant powers with infestation, hence why the X-Men are such desirable hosts.

Earlier this year, animated series "X-Men '97" used the Brood to do an extended homage to "Aliens" in the episode "Weapon X, Lies, and DVDs." So what makes "Alien vs. X-Men" different from an "X-Men fight the Brood" story? The Xenomorphs have one weapon the Brood don't: Acid blood. In a flashback in "Alien vs. X-Men" #2, when the X-Men are overrun, Cyclops destroys a chestburster launching at his head with his eyebeam ... but then it explodes into a splash of acid right in his face, killing him.

We'll see if the X-Men can still triumph despite their losses. But either way, Ellen Ripley should count herself lucky she never had to fight Xenomorphs with adamantium claws.

"Alien vs. X-Men" issues #1-2 are now available for purchase.
