#3510. Marshals Season 2 Teases Yellowstone Fans With A Major Character Name-Drop

"Marshals" continues to tease a crossover with "Dutton Ranch," with Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton name-dropping his sister in the latest episode. By this point, however, fans are surely tired of the references and eager to see the "Yellowstone" cast reunited.

With its Season 1 finale, "Dutton Ranch" gave itself the perfect excuse for a "Marshals" crossover. Meanwhile, "Marshals" did the same, ending its debut season by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton kidnapped and taken to Texas, where, it just so happens, Kelly Reilly's Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser's Rip Wheeler now live. Meanwhile, Hauser and Reilly spoke positively about a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, suggesting that's exactly what fans would soon be getting — especially considering Reilly referred to the lack of such a thing as a missed opportunity.

Alas, when "Marshals" Season 2 arrived, not only was there no crossover, but Kayce didn't even have to go to Texas, as it turns out Tate was taken to a Wyoming ranch instead. Now, we have the latest example of "Marshals" referencing Beth, which more than anything else serves only to remind us that we're yet to receive the crossover we've been waiting for.

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" picks up in the aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding a bomb and taking himself out in the process. After the Marshals track down his accomplice, Derek McCoy, Kayce chases Derek's brother, Will McCoy (Keean Johnson), into a barn that collapses, trapping the pair below ground. It's here that Kayce decides to bring up his family and once again tease audiences with a crossover that is yet to materialize.

In "Secret Weapon," after the barn floor collapses, Will McCoy's leg is badly injured. While trying to find a way out of their predicament, Kayce tries to convince Will to give up details about his brother, who evidently treats Will like a "punching bag." Kayce takes the opportunity to talk about his own brother, Jamie Dutton (played by Wes Bentley on "Yellowstone), and his sister, Beth Dutton, who also treated Jamie like a punching bag. Of course, Beth ultimately kills Jamie Dutton in the final season of "Yellowstone," but Kayce stops short of mentioning that still buried crime.

"You remind me of my middle brother," he tells Will. "Never quite fit in, always on the bad end of a beatdown. My sister made his life hell." Will replies with antagonism. "Picked on by his sister? I'm not that pathetic." But as Kayce quite rightfully points out, "She'd eat you for lunch," adding, "Meaner than any of your brothers, guaranteed."

It's true that Beth Dutton is a force of nature, and that only makes it even more frustrating that she hasn't shown up in "Marshals," which could do with a jolt of energy at this point. Beth and Rip are too busy setting up shop in Rio Paloma, Texas, in the far superior "Dutton Ranch." But this brief mention of Kayce's sister and how she'd eat Will for lunch is a reminder of just how good we once had it with "Yellowstone," and how much "Marshals" is struggling to match the excitement of its predecessor. Of course, "Yellowstone" lost its way at one point, but Beth was never anything less than electrifying, and "Marshals" would benefit from having anyone in its cast with half as much charisma.

For now, these brief references in "Marshals" to beloved "Yellowstone" characters aren't doing the CBS procedural any favors. In "Secret Weapon," Kayce Dutton recalls how fighting wasn't in Jamie Dutton's nature. "He had to be smarter, more cunning," he says, "And eventually he broke from the family, forged his own path." Of course, that path ultimately ended in his death, with Beth taking a knife to the middle Dutton brother's stomach and exacting revenge for the controversial death of Kevin Costner's John Dutton earlier in "Yellowstone" Season 5.

The thing is, being reminded of the "Yellowstone" years is bad enough on a show that clearly struggles to match the quality of Taylor Sheridan's original neo-Western. But when you take into account the anticipation for a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, it's just downright frustrating.

The "Marshals" Season 1 finale seemed to set up a perfect crossover with "Dutton Ranch," but in the end we got nothing of the sort. We could still see Beth show up later in the season, but for now all we know is that another "Yellowstone" fan-favorite character will be appearing in "Marshals" when Jefferson White's Jimmy Hurdstrom makes his return to the Montana plains. In the meantime, let's hope the show finds a way to keep the "Yellowstone" connection alive without reminding us of what we're missing out on.

#3509. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3508. 4 Planet Of The Apes Movies Are Now Streaming On HBO Max, Including Sci-Fi Masterpiece Dawn Of The Planet Of The Apes

Showcasing the evolution of Earth as its predominant species shifts from humans to intelligent apes, watching all four films in the modern Planet of the Apes franchise, which first began 15 years ago, is quite the experience. From Rupert Wyatt's Rise of the Planet of the Apes (2011) to Wes Ball's Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes (2024), few franchises have been as consistently impressive in both story and visuals as this one (each movie has a Rotten Tomatoes score above 80%).

Although all four films have earned generally positive reviews, one sequel absolutely stands above with Matt Reeves' Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. Not only does it remain the best of the entire modern franchise, but it also sits as one of the best sci-fi sequels ever made.

The modern series begins with 2011's Rise of the Planet of the Apes, directed by Rupert Wyatt and starring James Franco as scientist Will Rodman, whose experimental Alzheimer's treatment grants a chimpanzee named Ceaser (Andy Serkis) and more of his fellow apes increased intelligence, while conversely serving as a deadly contagion for a massive percentage of the human population. The movie also stars John Lithgow, Freida Pinto, Brian Cox, and Tom Felton.

Then there's 2014's Dawn of the Planet of the Apes from Matt Reeves, following Ceaser's growing community of apes 10 years after the events of Rise and their clashes with a colony of human survivors. Starring Jason Clarke, Gary Oldman, Keri Russell, and Toby Kebbell, Dawn was an exceptional follow-up (but more on that later).

Reeves returned to direct 2017's War for the Planet of the Apes, set only a couple of years after Dawn. Tensions with the remnants of humanity have only become worse, as Caesar faces a ruthless (and desperate) military leader played by Woody Harrelson in the face of new human crises. Beyond Harrelson, notable stars include Steven Zahn and Amiah Miller.

Lastly, the most recent entry in the franchise is also streaming on HBO Max: 2024's Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes. Directed by Wes Ball, Kingdom is set multiple generations after the time of Ceaser, with apes having transitioned from basically a Stone Age era to more of a structured Bronze Age-type society. The movie stars the ape known as Noa (Owen Teague) and his encounters with a human woman named Mae (Freya Allan), as well as Proximus Ceaser (Kevin Durand), a ruling ape who's taken the name of the legendary ape and his teachings to secure power and build an empire.

Overall, the modern Planet of the Apes franchise is well worth revisiting if you've seen it before, and there's no better time for those who haven't seen it to check them out now that they're all streaming in the same place.

While all four modern Planet of the Apes movies are worth watching, the one I would most recommend personally is Matt Reeves' Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. Taking the foundation of the world and status quo established by Wyatt in Rise, Reeves expands the scope of the narrative into something far more complex and compelling, surpassing most expectations in terms of its depth.

Rather than being a straightforward clash between intelligent apes and human survivors, Dawn also features major struggles within both communities and rising tensions, undermining Ceaser attempts to forge peace with Jason Clarke's Malcom. As the movie progresses and violence becomes inevitable, the action sequences are on another level as the apes storm the humans' defenses.

One notable scene in particular sees Ceaser's rival Koba (Toby Kebbell) leading a force of apes against the humans' community in San Francisco and personally hijacking an armored vehicle. This results in an incredible extended single-take sequence centered on the vehicle as its firing turret rotates, showcasing the full scope of the major battle with a continuous, 360-degree shot.

While the motion-capture work is extraordinary in the entire franchise, it's particularly captivating in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. This is largely due to the personal conflict between the peace-seeking Ceaser and Koba, who believes the ape leader should wipe out all the humans. Remarkably, the visuals impressively enhance the performances rather than distract. All things considered, Dawn is easily the best chapter in the modern Planet of the Apes franchise (though it really hasn't yet had a bad entry). With all four now on HBO Max, the timing couldn't be better for a full marathon.

Planet of the Apes is a multimedia sci-fi franchise that began in 1963 with Pierre Boulle's novel, which was later adapted into a film in 1968 starring Charlton Heston. The success of the movie led to four sequels, two TV shows, a remake from Tim Burton, and a reboot trilogy. The Planet of the Apes franchise has also seen success in video games and comic books.

#3507. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3506. World of Warcraft Forever release time in your time zone

22 years later, it's time to start WoW again

The release of World of Warcraft: Forever brings a third — or, depending on how you count them, a sixth or seventh — way to play World of Warcraft to everyone with a WoW subscription. Joining the modern game and the Classic servers, Forever is based on WoW as it was at launch in 2004, but with new content, rebalanced classes, graphical enhancements, and lots of modernization.

You'll be able to delve into WoW as it felt like 22 years ago, but never actually was, this week on Nov. 4 (or Nov. 5, depending on your time zone). Here's when World of Warcraft: Forever releases in your time zone.

World of Warcraft: Forever is released globally on Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 6 p.m. EST. Here's when that is in your time zone:

WoW: Forever is a kind of retro remix of WoW, based on the content and design philosophy of the classic game but with some new stuff, some modernizations, and some changes.

The core of Forever is the original nine character classes and eight playable races, split into two warring factions who can never communicate with each other or group up together: The Horde and Alliance. All the adventuring zones, dungeons, raids, and cities of the original game are present across its two massive continents.

Access to WoW: Forever is included in a World of Warcraft subscription, but the Skyborne (and access to their starting zone) are sold separately.

#3505. As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually

Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing expanding California’s current film and television tax credit program from $750 million to at least $1 billion annually as the state is struggling to attract entertainment industry jobs. The move comes as a report last month by FilmLA found that production levels fell 3.7 percent in the third quarter even as California has continued to enhance its tax credits. Many of the major studios and streamers are headquartered in Los Angeles, which makes the contraction in production jobs more painful.

Last year, Gov. Newsom pushed to increase California’s film and TV incentive from $330 million to $750 million annually, and the state’s film commission saw an initial rise in applications before the number of productions began falling again. California is not only grappling with increased competition from states like New Jersey, New York, and Georgia that offer richer incentives, but they are also facing off against foreign production hubs such as the United Kingdom and Hungary. Related Stories ‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

In a press release, Gov. Newsom said the proposed expansion would include credits for above-the-line talent, as well as rewards for companies that commit to fielding more than one production in California. If enacted, the tax credit will be extended through 2040, which would give companies more certainty about the incentives they can access. The previous incentives were scheduled to last through 2030. It would also increase independent film funding to $100 million annually, up $26 million from the current program.

“California created the modern entertainment industry; we’re the capital of entertainment and we’re going to keep it here,” Newsom said in a statement. “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry. Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year.”

The governor also urged national lawmakers to pass a federal film and television incentive, which could augment states’ efforts to bolster local production.

“States can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table,” Newsom said.

#3504. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3503. Ridley Scott’s 118-Minute Sci-Fi Thriller Officially Crowned #1 Movie on Prime Video

Widely known and celebrated as one of the greatest directors of all time, most fans and critics would agree that Ridley Scott is losing steam in the later stage of his career. Back at the end of 2024, Scott returned to the colosseum for the legacy sequel to Gladiator, but the film was not met with the same glowing reception as its predecessor. The movie struggled at the box office under the weight of its $250 million production budget, but it has gone on to become one of the most-watched movies of the last few years on Paramount Plus. Just one year before the release of Gladiator II, Scott reunited with Gladiator veteran Joaquin Phoenix for Napoleon, which was also a historic bomb at the box office — the film barely earned back its $200 million budget, and is estimated to have been a major loss for the studio.

Coming into the year, Scott was fresh off a few box office bombs, but the Oscar-nominated director sought redemption with the debut of The Dog Stars. Led by Josh Brolin and Jacob Elordi, The Dog Stars was Scott’s first sci-fi movie in almost 10 years — he last directed Alien: Covenant in 2017 — so there was some anticipation for the film. However, mediocre reviews out of the gate left not much desire for fans to make the trek to the theater, leading to The Dog Stars wrapping up its theatrical run after falling just short of $40 million at the global box office. Now that the film has been completely removed from all theaters, it’s only available to watch on VOD, where it’s now the #1 movie in the world on Prime Video.

The Dog Stars is based on the acclaimed sci-fi novel of the same name by Peter Heller, who also produced the film with screenwriter Mark L. Smith and director Ridley Scott. Additional cast members include Margaret Qualley (Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood), Guy Pearce (The Brutalist), and Benedict Wong (Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness). The official synopsis for The Dog Stars, which earned scores of 41% from critics and 69% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, reads as follows:

“Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars is a riveting, epic thriller set in a world where survival is instinct, but humanity is a choice. Scott tells the story of Hig, a young pilot who, together with a military survivalist, Bangley, has carved out an efficient but isolated homestead in a brutal post-apocalyptic world until a mysterious radio transmission spurs Hig to venture into the unknown in search of the hope and humanity he still believes exists.”

Check out The Dog Stars on VOD platforms like Prime Video and Apple TV and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Ridley Scott’s future projects.

#3502. In Just 1 Panel, Superman's New Logo Changes Everything About His Lore With New Release

It's surprisingly fun to ask others what they make of the "S" on Superman's chest, and it usually tells a lot about what corners of the fandom different people are drawn to. For those who assume it stands for Superman, they'd be right in the simplest contexts rooted in his history. But others may recognize it as the symbol for the House of El, especially those who saw the 1978 Superman movie. Other movie fans and readers of Mark Waid's Superman: Birthright, or viewers of Man of Steel, grew to understand that emblem as a symbol of hope for his people. This is all a fair perspective to have, but in his most recent retelling, one version of Superman's logo has a darker origin.

The S featured in Superman: The Stranger understandably represented the superhero in his Golden Age iteration, but one key feature from the upcoming issue teases a significantly harrowing pledge behind taking it on as his symbol. Shown in Superman: The Stranger #3, the S symbol appears to represent the company he once worked at before his powers fully developed, trapped helplessly inside when a blaze broke out, killing everyone inside but him. In this case, the S stands for "Saturn", as if to say he carries the guilt of surviving that day.

Superman: The Stranger has been doing well to keep readers enthralled with every aspect of this retelling, including consistent teases of Clark Kent's traumatic past. Rather than the symbol being tied to alien origins or designed by the Kent family based on how he was found, the "S" logo appears to be the same one used for the Saturn Building which caught fire when Clark, alongside potentially others from his orphanage, were working. When the traumatic disaster breaks out, claiming the lives of everyone around him, Clark is physically unable to open a door that was bolted shut, pry the bars off the window, or break down the wall. Beyond the question of who would allow such a chain of events, this memory has understandably lingered with him ever since.

One of the best current Superman stories shows a strong appreciation for his core traits, including his penchant for protecting all innocent life.

Moments like this have had a precedent in Superman: The Stranger, namely in how issue #2 starts by alluding to this fire. Superman clearly takes this incident with him wherever he goes, appearing to carry the building's logo with him as a reminder of what was lost. This is all that readers have to go with until the release of issue #3 this Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Although more context will almost certainly shed light on this connection, it's already a fascinating development, making the "S" logo far more personal and tragic for this version of Superman. It begins to show just the sort of hero he'll soon become for the people of Metropolis.

It's fairly clear in each of the issues currently available that Superman: The Stranger portrays its Clark Kent as one racked with guilt, whether it's as a survivor of a horrific tragedy, or the notion of stopping criminals for the mere crime "of being hungry." It's clear that Superman in a world currently devoid of aliens or supernatural threats must decide how to productively use his gifts, but it also makes his story a lonelier one.

Clark is seen consistently preoccupied with injustice, interrupting an intimate moment with a woman he just met to answer a nearby disturbance, ruining his evening (on Christmas, no less.) He recognizes that the people potentially seeing him as a means to enforce order for the city are upholding their own hateful views toward the downtrodden or demonized immigrants. But above all else, Clark worries his powers could leave just as suddenly as they appeared, and he feels compelled to use everything he has to make a difference in the city. But as the flames from Superman's turn from orange and yellow to green with voices calling out to him, he'll soon have to sort out how exactly he'll answer them.

#3501. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3499. New Star Wars Book Reveals the Surprising '90s Inspiration for an Iconic New Character

After years on Disney Plus, Din Djarin (Pedro Pascal) and his surrogate Jedi son, Grogu, made their big-screen debut in The Mandalorian and Grogu earlier this year. Now, The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu by Phillip Szostak is set to hit shelves this week, offering a behind-the-scenes look at the film’s production from start to finish.

Ahead of this week’s release of The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu, Polygon got an exclusive first look at one of the art book's two-page spreads. It features stunning concept art of one of the film’s most intense moments and reveals one of the show’s most striking inspirations: Harry Hook’s 1990 film adaptation of William Golding’s Lord of the Flies.

Though The Mandalorian and Grogu drew on plenty of inspiration — from the city of Chicago to The French Connection — nobody could have predicted that Lord of the Flies would also influence the film’s most underrated factions: the Droid Gotra, an independent faction of emancipated droids that serves as a security force for the Hutt Twins.

According to concept artist Brian Matyas, the droids’ aesthetic drew inspiration from Lord of the Flies, the tattered, tribal-esque outfits the boys gradually put together, and junker cars. What would that look like when mixed?

“There is something quite striking when you build off of the recognizable droid aesthetics by introducing tribal and low-tech motifs, layering, mix and match droid parts, and paints,” Matyas shares in The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu. “Lord of the Flies meets junker cars.”

Alongside the reveal of some of the inspiration behind The Mandalorian and Grogu, we get stunning artwork depicting Din’s fight with the gigantic albino Dragonsnake beneath the Hutt Twins’ chamber on Nal Hutta. Director Jon Favreau did a fantastic job showing the creature’s colossal size, but this artwork captures its scale and menace beautifully.

This exclusive sneak peek offered just a taste of what fans can expect when they get their hands on The Art of Star Wars: Mandalorian and Grogu. Szostak’s book also includes concept art and sketches, as well as interviews with the cast, crew, and creatives behind The Mandalorian and Grogu. If you want to uncover the stories and hard work behind the film’s characters, locations, and vehicles, you’ll want to snag this book ASAP.

The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu arrives on Nov. 3, 2026.

#3498. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3497. ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

When I first thought, “Is ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ the funniest show on television?”, I worried saying as much would be damning the uproarious NBC sitcom with faint praise. After all, the modern TV landscape is awash with crime shows, genre mash-ups, and I.P. brand extensions. Bad comedies abound (and tend to be mercifully easy to spot), but great ones? Hmm. At least the most recent Emmy winner for Best Comedy Series is an actual comedy, but the nominees (including a feel-good weeper, a rom-com heavy on the rom, and that cooking drama) were still emblematic of a Hollywood era when laughs aren’t the top priority. Related Stories As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually ‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination

So, returning to the original question, how many funny funny shows actually came out this year?

Turns out, quite a few. “Adults” jumps to mind among recent releases for its successful Season 2 evolution into a hang-worthy Gen-Z hangout sitcom. “Colin From Accounts” capped a three-year run that saw the Aussie romantic-comedy get stronger every season. “Youth” has Sharon Horgan back at the top of her game (let’s not speak of “Bad Sisters” Season 2), and “The Comeback” did the impossible by delivering a worthy successor to one of HBO’s greatest-ever TV seasons. Then there’s trusty comedy staples like “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia” and “Abbott Elementary,” which don’t need another crossover to keep us laughing, as well as the half-comedies that feel full to anyone with the same funny bone, like “The Lowdown” (a noir comedy), “The Audacity” (a black-comic drama), and “Trying” (a family comedy). I didn’t even mention the final season of “Hacks” (which is great) or the first (and hopefully final) season of “The Hawk” (which is not).

Following fallen NFL running back Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan), decades after he’s ousted from the league for gambling, Season 2 picks up amid incremental progress toward his crowning redemption: making the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His documentarian, Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), is still searching for the right angle to support their comeback film (Arthur needs it as much as Reggie wants it), while Reggie’s agent and ex-wife Monica (Erika Alexander) tries to build on the little momentum they gained at the end of last season (when Reggie earned his first votes ever).

The irresistible ensemble doesn’t have a weak link. The staging is vibrant. The writing is as happy to delve into topical subject matter (like documentary subjects paying their documentarians) as it is to revel in carefree absurdity (like a harebrained murder-conspiracy or calamitous Thanksgiving gathering). And every element of it is always focused on being funny. Not only is Robert Carlock and Sam Means’ NBC sitcom designed to squeeze in as many jokes as the human brain can process in 21-minute chunks, it’s also carefully paced and polished to keep those jokes as superb and surprising as possible.

Take a check-your-phone-and-you’ll-miss-it gag from the Season 2 premiere: Monica is struggling to keep up with the media landscape’s sprawling marketing opportunities and admits she booked Reggie on the wrong show: She mixed up Pablo Torres’ sports podcast with Julio Torres’ “something.” Quick cut to Julio (as himself) interviewing Reggie about “the color clear.” There’s a laugh in recognizing Monica’s mistake, another laugh in Julio’s question (“What do you think about the color clear?”), and another laugh in Reggie’s response (“A lot!”).

But rather than one joke stepping on the next, they amplify one another. Monica’s explanation is given the most space to land, since technically it’s setting up the cutaway jokes to come. Those jokes hit one after the next, but in a rhythm that makes them easy to process independently. They’re calibrated to keep you laughing all the way through, but they’re not so rushed that you feel overwhelmed instead of entertained.

That’s the magic (or maybe the math) behind what’s recognized as Tina Fey (an EP on “Dinkins”) and Robert Carlock’s comedy style, as established by their landmark sitcom, “30 Rock” and extended more successfully than not in comedies like “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” (where they picked up Radcliffe), “Great News,” “Mr. Mayor,” and “Girls5Eva.” Carlock continues it here with Means, who worked on all those shows, while relying on their proven bonds with Morgan, Radcliffe, and stealth MVP Bobby Moynihan to maintain the right balance. (Moynihan’s understanding of tone and timing is impeccable, and he’s such a joyful presence it’s hard not to smile whenever Rusty surfaces.)

The Season 2 premiere illustrates the trust the writers’ have in their entire acting company. The story still pivots around Morgan’s lovable doofus, but the emphasis is elsewhere. Arthur is dying for the family to find out about Reggie’s son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall) and his secret relationship with Delilah Basmati (Arica Himmel), daughter of Reggie’s nemesis, Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson). Brina (Precious Way) gets close, while Monica is busy hiring a new assistant “head of publicity” to help her tap into younger markets with a broader reach. Moynihan’s Rusty is everywhere, chipping in enough quips, reaction shots, and physical comedy to convey his supportive yet integral presence in each character’s life.

By the time our original dynamic duo gets a cathartic moment near the episode’s end, it’s hard not to notice that Reggie and Arthur almost feel like an afterthought — and that’s just fine. They take back control in the ensuing episodes, after “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” proves it can thrive no matter who gets to press the most buttons. The joke-delivery machine is operating at peak volume, and it needs every capable hand to keep its performance at the same incredible sweep.

With only four episodes screened for review, there’s plenty of time for Season 2 to break down. The charming vibe could fade, the sharp jokes could soften, the elastic performances could calcify. But not only does Carlock and co.’s lengthy track record suggest the opposite trajectory, so does the excitement shown in creating this specific project. You can feel it in the ideas, big and small, throughout “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” and their cumulative impact makes the series special — not because of a general dearth in great comedies, or even because it harkens back to an era of Must-See TV, when multiple classic sitcoms airing on the same night spoiled viewers with an abundance of laughs. It’s just because laughing this hard, this often, is a gift. And there’s nothing faint about it.

“The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” Season 2 premieres Monday, November 2 at 8:30 p.m. ET on NBC. New episodes will be released weekly and made available on Peacock the next day.

#3496. 8 Near-Perfect Prime Video Thriller Series That Hooked Us in the First 5 Minutes

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

It's a good rule for show-runners to follow in the modern entertainment landscape: try and hook viewers within their first five minutes. That might seem short, but so are attention spans nowadays. It is a harsh rule to follow, but it also tells you a lot about the inner makings of a quality thriller. However, Prime Video has a strong record on that front.

The platform has made its name with large-scale action and the Chris Pratt-led, The Terminal List, returned in October with all eight episodes of Season two at once. Reacher is coming off a season four that pulled 66 million viewers in its first 28 days. Fallout has finished filming season three, though it will sadly not arrive in 2027.

Every series here opens with something specific, an image or a scene or a question that sticks. However, the best entries on this list open with small subtleties like a funeral, a birthday party, or even a slice of pie. The genre stretches from spy comedy to a supernatural mystery, but all still bring a stereotypical thriller's infrastructure of high stakes, tense physical confrontations and an atmosphere of narrative uncertainty.

Jack Ryan creates its opening premise on a rather mundane but clever idea, which is that its hero finds the threat in a money transfer spreadsheet. The series opens in Lebanon in 1983, where two brothers dance around their bedroom until bombs fall on their village. The boys grow into the man John Krasiniski's Ryan will spend the first season chasing. Carlton Cuse and Graham Roland ask the audience to understand the villain first before meeting the hero. That narrative technique alone brings a moral depth and weight rarely seen in Tom Clancy adaptations for the screen.

Krasinski plays Ryan as an analyst first and an action hero second, which makes his reluctant move into the field believable. Ali Suleiman and Dina Shihabi as his wife, Hanin, get nearly as much screen time as the American characters. That lifts the first season out of the standard spy manhunt procedural. Wendell Pierce gives Ryan's boss James Greer a rumpled authority that anchors every scene he is in. The series ran four seasons and in the later ones it chased bigger set pieces at some cost to that earlier character work. Although it might settle into a familiar rhythm, the opening hook still lands.

Donal Glover and Francesca Sloane open Mr. & Mrs. Smith with another John and Jane Smith, played by Alexander Skarsgård and Eiza Gonzalez and then promptly kill them off. The scene, of course, winks at the 2005 movie with Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie while promising a very different take. Donald Glover's John and Maya Erskine's Jane each sit down for an interview with a faceless agency, where a terminal greets them with a cheerful "hihi." Jane's terminal even asks for her nail clippings, a detail that helps to set that dry and strange tone. Hiro Murai directs the pilot with his usual sharp eye for awkward silences and comedic undertones.

Glover and Sloane built each episode structurally around a single idea, much like Atlanta did, which keeps the missions fresh. Erskine and Glover trade awkward banter as each episode turns into a test of their relationship. The first season ran eight episodes and a second season began filming this past April under a new show runner.

Short on time, long on suspense. Five Netflix miniseries you can finish before the weekend ends.

Chris Pratt stars as Navy SEAL Lieutenant Commander James Reece and the show does not waste a second before putting the audience in front of its rather grim circumstances. The Terminal List begins at a funeral, with Reece smashing a SEAL pin into a coffin. This cuts between flashbacks of Reece leading an Alpha Platoon into a tunnel in Syria on a mission that nobody believes in. They go underground searching for a chemical weapons terrorist and walk into an ambush. The explosion that follows kills nearly everyone and Antoine Fuqua's (Training Day) slick direction makes the opening sequence feel like a feature film.

Jack Carr's novel supplies the revenge plot, and Pratt trades his usual charm for a hollow stare that suits a man who loses everything. Riley Keough plays Reece's wife, Lauren, and Taylor Kitsch plays his friend Ben Edwards, and they give the family and friendship at the center of the story a real lived-in warmth. A prequel, The Terminal List: Dark Wolf, followed in 2025. Season 2 just hit Prime on October 21st and takes Reece across the world. A third season has not yet been confirmed. The show operates as a single-minded thriller though its pleasures narrow after the opening hour.

Titus Welliver's first scene as the now iconic Harry Bosch was in an undercover car, watching the weather and muttering under his breath about how the rain will wash the city clean. Within minutes, he is chasing a suspect on foot which ultimately ends with a fatal gunshot. Later on in Bosch, he is sitting in a courtroom defending that shooting against a wrongful death suit, while a dog in Laurel Canyon has dug up a child's bones. The pilot juggles the psyche of Bosch, the trial and a dark cold case without overwhelming you.

Eric Overmeyer developed the series with Michael Connelly, and the pilot's mix of courtroom drama and cold case work set the template for seven seasons. Jamie Hector as partner Jerry Edgar and Mimi Rogers as his fierce opponent in court, Honey Chandler, give the opening hour a sturdy supporting cast. The success of the show led to Bosch: Legacy and opened the door for Bosch: Start of Watch. Start of Watch is the new MGM+ prequel with Cameron Monaghan as a rookie Harry set in 1991 and adds a full reboot of the cast to the franchise. Bosch, much like its lead character, is more patient than explosive and uses that unique approach to its advantage.

Stefano Sollima opens ZeroZeroZero with a shock, showing Gabriel Byrne's Edward Lynwood wounded on the ground under falling glass and gunfire. The camera then rewinds, and a single cocaine shipment becomes the thread that connects a Calabrian crime family, a Mexican cartel, and a New Orleans shipping company. Sollima directed the first two episodes, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2019. Andrea Riseborough and Dane DeHaan play Lynwood's grown children, who inherit the family business and its dangers. Dehaan's Chris carries Huntington’s disease, a diagnosis that colors every decision that he makes.

Harold Torres plays Manuel Contreras, a Mexican special forces sergeant pulled toward the cartel he is supposed to fight. Each storyline has its own unique mood, with Janus Metz and Pablo Trapero directing later episodes, which gives the series this relentless international feel. Robert Saviano's book about the global cocaine trade supplies the foundation. ZeroZeroZero is the entry most demanding of your full close attention here, yet it is also one of the most rewarding for that reason.

Peter Capaldi's convicted killer Gideon shows up in the very first scene of The Devil's Hour questioning a bruised Lucy Chambers about whether her life feels like her own. Gideon has an unsettling calm about him that makes every scene feel like a trap. Jessica Raine plays Lucy, a social worker who wakes every night at exactly 3:33 from the same nightmare. In the dream, a woman presses a shotgun under her chin, and Lucy believes the woman is her mother.

The time-bending mystery includes Nikesh Patel as Detective Inspector Ravi Dhillon, who investigates the murders that overlap with Lucy's life. By the end of the first episode, the detectives find a message scratched on a window that asks where Lucy Chambers is. Tom Moran created the series for Amazon, and the story slides between horror, procedural and family drama fairly seamlessly. Lucy's son, Isaac, speaks of people nobody else can see, which adds an extra eerie element to every domestic sequence. The Devil's Hour returned in 2024 for a second season and the first premiered on October 28, four years ago, which makes it a natural pick for this time of year.

Alan Ritchson's Reacher opens with a man being shot at midnight outside the small Georgia town of Margrave, then beaten and hidden under cardboard. The next morning, Reacher steps off a bus and walks into a diner for a slice of peach pie. He never gets the first bite, since the police burst in and arrest him for the murder. By the time the cuffs go on, a killing and a mystery stranger are already in play.

Ritchson's physical presence sells the premise alone, and the writing gives him just enough dry humor to keep the character from becoming a full brute. However, the detective who questions him upon his arrest (Malcolm Goodwin), quickly realizes that the giant in front of him sees the case more clearly than his own fellow officers. The show works directly off its simple but effective narrative and precise manner of execution. Season four premiered on August 12th and Prime has already renewed the series through season six. A spin-off, Neagley, released its first season in September.

Fallout starts in Los Angeles in 2077 with Walton Goggins in a cowboy hat, performing rope tricks for the kids at a rich family's birthday party. The great late Nat King Cole's "Orange Colored Sky" plays over the sinister radio reports of an impending nuclear war. Adults whisper about the news, a radio crackles, and Goggins' Cooper Howard, a fading movie star, declines to give the thumbs up that made him famous. Then the sky changes when a mushroom cloud rises over the city and families race for their private shelters as the bombs fall.

Jonathan Nolan directed the first episode, and few openings in recent television have set such a distinct tone so quickly. The same episode introduces Ella Purnell's Lucy, a vault dweller whose wedding goes wrong, and the Ghoul, the mutated version of Cooper who gets dug out of a grave. Season two aired from December 2025 into early 2026, and season three has finished filming with Aaron Paul, Manny Jacinto, Emily Mortimer and Thomasin McKenzie joining the cast. Fallout stands out amongst such a talented and crowded field due to an introduction that promises a well-defined and designed universe and the series keeps delivering it.

#3495. Dungeon Crawler Carl Officially Returns November 23

Dungeon Crawler Carl fans are waiting with bated breath for an official announcement on Book 9's release date, though it may take a while considering author Matt Dinniman recently released a few teaser chapters and has a ton of story left to tell. That said, the author has proven he can turn out releases like they're going out of style, with Book 8, A Parade of Horribles, releasing in May 2026, just a year and a half after This Inevitable Ruin debuted in November 2024.

Looking at the larger series, Dinniman has released eight full-length novels since Dungeon Crawler Carl first arrived in 2020, an impressive pace considering the increasingly ambitious scope of each installment. With Book 9 set to kick off a two-volume finale, fans could be in for a lengthy wait before Carl and Donut's story reaches its conclusion, but there's plenty to keep them busy until then.

Fortunately, there's another major Dungeon Crawler Carl release officially arriving on November 23, giving fans something new to look forward to in the meantime.

Renegade Game Studios is preparing a massive new wave of Dungeon Crawler Carl releases for November 23, 2026 alongside the larger launch of the upcoming RPG and Unstoppable deck-building game, including the official Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG: Loot Packs, which are currently available to preorder through retailers like Game Nerdz.

These collectible mystery packs are part of the franchise's larger tabletop RPG expansion, with each containing a seven-piece polyhedral dice set and a collectible temporary tattoo. There are 20 different themed dice sets and 20 possible tattoos, with the dice divided into 12 common, five rare, and three legendary designs. Rare sets have advertised odds of one in six packs, while legendary sets are considerably harder to find at just one in 100.

The three legendary designs reference some of the series' most recognizable characters and catchphrases, including Samantha's infamous "I Will Kill Your Mother," Princess Donut's "Non-Alcoholic Dirty Shirley, Extra Cherries," and a special Princess Donut the Queen Anne Chonk set. Fans can preorder individual Loot Packs or an entire unopened display box containing 20 packs, although the randomized assortment means duplicates are possible. The full contents and details are here:

These collectibles accompany Renegade's highly anticipated Dungeon Crawler Carl Roleplaying Game, which allows players to create their own Crawlers and attempt to survive the World Dungeon. The Starter Set covers the first two tutorial floors, while the 300-plus-page Core Rulebook explores floors three through five (or roughly through Book 4), introducing extensive character customization, quests, monsters, familiar locations, and more.

Meanwhile, November also marks the retail debut of Dungeon Crawler Carl: Unstoppable, a separate deck-building game from designer John D. Clair. This solo or two-player cooperative experience lets fans play as Carl or Princess Donut, battling enemies and upgrading their cards as they progress through the dungeon's first three floors. Two expansions, Crawler Chaos and The Iron Tangle, are also arriving this month, introducing additional playable characters and the fourth floor.

All of these releases follow Renegade's record-breaking crowdfunding campaign, which raised over $13.29 million from approximately 55,000 backers. Fulfillment began in October, and some supporters have already received their games and collectibles. However, the official retail release is scheduled for November 23, meaning Dungeon Crawler Carl fans who missed the original campaign will soon have their chance to join the crawl.

#3494. 20 Years Later, Uncle Iroh's Wisest 'Avatar: The Last Airbender Quote' Is Still Undefeated

Uncle Iroh’s confrontation with Zuko under Lake Laogai still hits home

Avatar: The Last Airbender has more than its fair share of heartfelt moments and poignant lines. Whether it’s Aang reassuring a downtrodden Toph in the vast loneliness of the desert, or Ursa’s parting words to her son Zuko before disappearing in the middle of the night, the series can be surprisingly deep for what some might (incorrectly) consider a mere children’s show. No character embodies that richness and depth more than Uncle Iroh, who begins as Zuko's wise mentor and becomes so much more. Time and again, Iroh sits at the center of The Last Airbender's most moving moments, offering quiet wisdom just when it's needed most.

A great example comes in the 17th episode of Book Two: Earth, called “Lake Laogai.” Zuko and Iroh have traded the weight of their royal titles for the quiet grind of daily life in Ba Sing Se, passing themselves off as Lee and Mushi. For the first time in his life, Zuko is free of his father’s purview and unburdened by the Fire Nation regime, and is presented with a genuine chance to build a normal existence. However, after learning of Appa’s imprisonment somewhere in the walled city, he slips back into his Blue Spirit alter ego, intent on capturing the Avatar’s beloved sky bison himself and reclaiming his family’s honor.

In the midst of the secret water-dripping caverns under the lake, just as Zuko stumbles upon Appa’s cell, his uncle pops up out of nowhere to confront him. Known mostly for his easygoing attitude and love of tea, Iroh doesn’t often show any anger (if ever), but in this small scene, his frustration shines through. He berates Zuko's impulsive nature, likening the moment to when Zuko captured the Avatar at the North Pole only to nearly freeze to death in the process. Turning his back on his uncle, Zuko claims he has no other choice; it’s his destiny, after all. But his uncle doesn’t see it that way.

“I’m begging you, Prince Zuko! It’s time for you to look inward and begin asking yourself the big questions,” Iroh says. “Who are you, and what do you want?”

Up to this point in the story, Zuko has defined his entire existence through external expectations and inherited trauma. His father, Fire Lord Ozai (the ruler of the Fire Nation) scarred his face, stripped him of his title, and banished him with the impossible task of capturing the Avatar or living in exile. Desperate to reclaim his lost birthright, Zuko spends years masquerading as a ruthless prince and a masked vigilante, confusing obedience for honor. But in Ba Sing Se, far from the war and his father's suffocating reach, that illusion is finally starting to crack. Rather than hunting out of logic or strategy, he's acting on pure muscle memory, terrified of letting go of the resentment that has fueled him for so many years.

With a single line, Iroh forces a collision between Zuko's conditioned obligation and his true sense of self. Iroh’s "Who are you?" demands Zuko strip away the masks, titles, and toxic expectations assigned by his father. "What do you want?" challenges Zuko to separate his obsession with revenge from his desires for peace and connection. Iroh is offering a lifeline. He sees the good in Zuko that Ozai tried to burn away, forcing his nephew to realize that true honor isn't something granted by a tyrant or some label — it’s earned.

Moments later, after releasing Appa from his cell, Zuko drops his Blue Spirit mask into the dark waters beneath Lake Laogai on Iroh's advice, surrendering his obsession with the Avatar. In the very next episode, he breaks into a severe fever, his body physically fighting off the lasting remnants of his father’s lingering influence. The fever is the price of his awakening, showing just how deeply Iroh’s words struck at his core. In dropping the mask, Zuko finally stops running from himself and begins the agonizing process of answering the two questions that will eventually save him. Who are you, and what do you want?

The scene is one of Avatar’s most brilliant, packing rich emotion into a simple line. It’s elevated even further by the fact that it was among the last episodes recorded by legendary voice actor Mako Iwamatsu before his untimely passing in July 2006. Iwamatsu was an acclaimed actor of stage and screen, earning an Academy Award nomination for The Sand Pebbles and voicing iconic animated figures like the menacing Demon King Aku in Genndy Tartakovsky's Samurai Jack. Following his death, Greg Baldwin stepped in to carry the torch for Iroh starting in Book 3 and into the Legend of Korra, and the creators of the latter show even named the skilled firebender Mako after the original voice actor. Hearing Iwamatsu deliver the line in "Lake Laogai," shouting with a fierce love for his nephew rather than any genuine anger, remains one of his finest moments across a storied career.

Two decades later, Iroh’s words haven't lost an ounce of their force. Before the Avatar universe imagined sanctuaries like the Seven Havens as refuges from a world at war, Iroh offered a different kind of shelter by reminding us that peace must first come from within. Zuko couldn't find his true destiny until he stopped pretending to be someone he wasn't, a timeless lesson for anyone still searching for purpose and a sense of self.

#3493. IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace is officially an Emmy winner.

Wallace won the Editing for a Daytime Studio Program category at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys for his work on Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables.” He accepted the award during the ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium on Friday, October 30.

IndieWire was also nominated for a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Daytime Studio Non-Fiction Series for IndieWire executive producer Mary Pelloni’s work on the show. The two nominations and one win, in categories that also included broadcast talk shows, reflect IndieWire’s increasing presence in the traditional video spaces in addition to our written coverage. Wallace works on IndieWire’s staff as a video producer, where he also produces and edits video content across brands like Filmmaker Toolkit, Future of Filmmaking, and other editorial and sponsored projects.

Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables” highlighted the below-the-line artisans on many of the biggest films of the season. Hosted by IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill, the season consisted of four episodes, each centered around a different filmmaking department: cinematography, editing, production design, and casting. Each episode aired on PBS SoCal and streamed on the PBS App in addition to editorial coverage on IndieWire.com.

The casting roundtable also featured casting directors Nina Gold (“Jay Kelly”), Margery Simkin (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”), and Jessica Ronane (“After the Hunt”).

“IndieWire Craft Roundtables” returned for Season 2 in June 2026, with six episodes devoted to the biggest TV shows of the year.
