#3491. The Star Trek Franchise Officially Reunites Kirk And Spock On November 13

For 60 years, Star Trek has been home to some of science fiction's most iconic characters, but few have left a greater impression than Captain James T. Kirk and his loyal first officer, Spock. Portrayed by William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, respectively, the two became the heart of Star Trek: The Original Series, developing a friendship that helped define the franchise for generations.

While Kirk was known for his bold leadership and emotionally charged decision-making (not to mention his occasional disregard for protocol) Spock's unwavering commitment to logic provided the perfect counterbalance. Their relationship evolved throughout The Original Series and subsequent films, culminating in some of the franchise's most emotional moments, particularly Spock's sacrifice in The Wrath of Khan.

Both Shatner and Nimoy left an extraordinary legacy that continues to influence Star Trek today, with their characters being reimagined by new actors across various films and television series. Now, as the franchise celebrates its 60th anniversary, Kirk and Spock are officially being reunited once again in a highly anticipated new release arriving November 13.

Captain Kirk and Spock are officially reuniting on November 13, 2026, although their latest adventure won't be taking place on television or the big screen. Instead, the legendary Star Trek duo will return as part of Magic: The Gathering's upcoming Universes Beyond crossover, which features four Commander decks celebrating different corners of the science fiction franchise.

Of particular interest to fans of Star Trek: The Original Series is the new Landing Party Commander deck, which brings Kirk, Spock, and several other familiar faces from the original USS Enterprise crew together in one release.

The 100-card deck is primarily built around Commander Spock, who serves as its featured commander, although players can also choose Captain Kirk, Boldly Going as an alternative. This allows players to have both characters in the same deck, effectively reuniting William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy's iconic characters for another adventure.

Landing Party is an "exploration-focused" deck, with Spock's abilities allowing players to draw additional cards and potentially cast spells for free depending on the number of differently named lands they control. Meanwhile, Kirk's abilities revolve around the Starship Enterprise, offering a different approach to commanding.

Beyond these two legendary characters, Landing Party includes cards featuring several other recognizable members of the original crew, including Lieutenant Nyota Uhura, Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu, Chief Montgomery Scott, Pavel Chekov, and Dr. McCoy. There are also cards depicting Christopher Pike, Christine Chapel, the Shuttlecraft Galileo, and several iconic locations, including Vulcan and Earth.

Of course, Landing Party is only one of four Commander decks arriving as part of the November 13 crossover. The remaining three include Federation Fleet, led by Jean-Luc Picard; Klingon Fury, featuring Worf as its commander; and We Are the Borg, which puts players in control of the Borg Queen.

Each deck includes 100 cards, with 32 new-to-Magic cards, alongside several familiar reprints. Special Collector's Edition versions featuring surge foil treatments will also be available.

The larger Magic: The Gathering x Star Trek crossover officially launches on November 13, 2026, bringing decades of franchise history into the trading card game. For longtime fans of the original series, however, the chance to command Kirk, Spock, and their Enterprise crew together again may be one of its biggest attractions.

#3490. ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 13, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.]

You’re going to see the hits coming with this one. When Anthony Ippolito first utters the title of Peter Farrelly‘s “I Play Rocky” — it’s an admission and an ask, a demand and a plea — the moment is primed for stand-up-and-cheer crowd-pleasing. Such is the case with Farrelly’s entire film, which tracks Sylvester Stallone’s wild, improbable Hollywood success story through the lens of his creation of “Rocky,” often functioning as its own version of that underdog story, presumably because “Rocky” proper isn’t available to be remade and Stallone was not formally involved with the production of this one. Related Stories IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’ ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

Stallone has long mythologized his rise to greatness, and that’s no knock on him; his rise to Hollywood royalty was crazy and filled with eye-popping twists and turns. The guy sold his dog when he didn’t have enough money! But Peter Gamble’s script sands down those hard edges into something much more made-for-the-movies, a distinctly knotty treatment for a movie that is meant to be about how hard it is to get original movies made.

While the lightness of the film — including an awkward dinner in which Frank Stallone, Jr. (Matt Dillon) giddily admits to beating his kid, mostly played for chuckles — can detract from the much darker stuff that really happened to Stallone, it’s hard to deny the power of a feature so genuinely built to delight. You can see the strings being pulled (the ropes being strung?), but that means it works more often than not. With a big crowd — a man behind me at the film’s second public screening at TIFF guffawed and hooted with such abandon throughout the film that I could only embrace his joy — “I Play Rocky” does exactly what it’s trying to do.

Stallone’s life story has been threaded through the period just before he started writing scripts and the opening night of “Rocky,” an essential time in the career of a man so dedicated to acting and his craft that it could have ruined him forever. And there’s some light ruin here, including a short stint sleeping on the street (we see literally one night), bonkers financial decisions, and grievous financial choices. Embodied to an almost disarming degree by actor Anthony Ippolito — most people are probably going to get hung up on his impersonation of Stallone’s signature voice, but I’ve never seen anyone make their cheekbones look like Sly’s unexpectedly sunken ones — what feels most real about the film exists because he’s so fully committed to the bit.

And it’s very much to the breakout star’s credit that it doesn’t feel like a bit. While Gamble’s script doesn’t get much further than “this dude just really loved acting,” Ippolito gets pretty soulful here. His Sly (or, as we first meet him during a run of demeaning auditions, “Mike”) is a striver who would likely never call himself “ambitious.” Self-taught, self-educated, and self-aware to a fault, Sly knows he’s not the ideal Hollywood star, but he’s hellbent on showing the world what he’s got.

When his eventual first wife Sasha (a wonderfully calm AnnaSophia Robb) encourages him to just “write a fricking script” worthy of his talents, he does. The first is not “Rocky.” Neither are the seven that follow, but Sly and Sasha still pull up stakes for Hollywood and to chase his dream. No one is buying what he’s selling, though, and even some promising meetings (including one with Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, both played to the absolute hilt by P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell, respectively) end nowhere. A chance encounter — the film’s script lives and dies by those — with a seminal boxing match gives him fresh inspiration, and after just three days, the kid has “Rocky.”

But is he going to be Rocky? Of course, everyone on Earth who sees this film (and plenty who don’t) knows that answer, but what the film lacks in tension, it makes up for in pure grit. Sly learns all about Hollywood negotiations, blustery studio men (a role Tracy Letts was born to play; no one has more fun yelling “Fuck Paramount!” than this guy), and holding fast to seriously deluded dreams. And while the film can flag as we chug through those paces, once “Rocky” is greenlit with Sly in the lead role (and a mess of stipulations, all of them seemingly designed to trip him up), things really start zipping along.

Part of that is due to smart casting. Jay Duplass is a stellar pick for director John G. Avildsen, though anyone who knows anything about Stallone’s on-set approach will chuckle at how much these two seemed to get along (Stephan James should get his own Carl Weathers film now). But more of it comes from the film’s eventual bent toward the mechanics of moviemaking. Come for the high jinks involving beating back union reps (but also, ew?), stay for a subplot about the genius of the Steadicam that is genuinely moving to observe.

That “Rocky” will be a hit is a given — and a fricking huge one at that! — but “I Play Rocky” is far more invested in getting the audience on board with the road it took to get there. And while Farrelly’s approach to this material, extremely glossy and built to delight a wide array of audience members, doesn’t quite speak to the real pain that went into the making of “Rocky,” there’s still plenty here that will make people stand up and cheer. It would, however, be nice if this Hollywood story didn’t feel quite so, well, Hollywood.

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide later in the month.

#3489. Zelda Ocarina of Time release time in your time zone

And what you can get as a pre-order bonus, too

The Zelda Ocarina of Time remake release time is just around the corner, as Nintendo introduces a new generation to one of its classic games. Unlike the 3DS port from 2011, Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 includes a massive visual overhaul, along with several quality-of-life features that weren't present in the original Nintendo 64 release. Pre-orders are still open at some retailers if you're hoping to snag a special bonus, though US-based folks only get one bonus to choose from.

Below, we break down when Zelda Ocarina of Time releases in your time zone.

Nintendo usually doesn't give exact release times for its first-party games, and Ocarina of Time is no different. However, unless stated otherwise, eShop releases launch at midnight in the easternmost time zone of your region. For example, that'd be 12 a.m. on March 5 in New York City, but 9 p.m. PST in San Francisco.

Here's what that looks like around the world:

That means you can play Ocarina of Time early if your Nintendo Account is linked to another region. If you want to play early and haven't linked your account to another region already, however, we recommend just making a new account for that purpose. The process of un-linking and re-registering an existing Nintendo Account is tedious and potentially problematic, since your save data is tied to your account.

Bear in mind that Ocarina of Time is a Switch 2 exclusive. It won't work on the original Switch.

Certain retailers are running a number of Ocarina of Time pre-order bonuses around the world, but if you're in the U.S., you only get one: the game case with a special foil art cover. It's in high demand and has sold out on Amazon, though it's worth checking places like Walmart, as they've had more in stock.

If you're trying to get the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 console and manage to snag one, don't forget it's just the console. It doesn't come with the game.

#3488. ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on February 13, 2026 at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. IFC Films will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6.]

For the final 20 or so minutes of an early screening of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson‘s Berlin-bound “Mouse” that I recently attended, the woman sitting behind me in one of NYC’s smallest screening rooms sobbed. Like, really sobbed. I could hear her gasps in between her cries. Yes, I thought to myself, one of my people.

While I’m not sure there’s yet a cult assembled around the deeply empathetic and uniquely humane cinema of O’Sullivan and Thompson (partners in both film and life), God willing, there will be after more audiences see the pair’s third effort. I’ve been banging the drum on their wondrous output since 2020’s “Saint Frances” (which Thompson directed and O’Sullivan wrote and starred in) and their deep-feeling follow-up, 2024’s “Ghostlight” (written by O’Sullivan, who also joined Thompson in co-directing duties). Around these parts, any O’Sullivan and Thompson joint is an event. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

“Mouse” is no exception, and their best effort yet.

As is typically the case with the pair’s films, its logline does not quite do it justice. “Saint Frances” was about a disaffected nanny who bonds with her young charge. “Ghostlight” followed a fractured family as they found unexpected healing in live theater. “Mouse” is about a shy high school senior looking for ballast after the sudden end of her lifelong BFF-ship. These are all “small” stories, but they are also crucially about people, and thus contain the wild multitudes of humanity itself.

O’Sullivan and Thompson reunite with their “Ghostlight” star, Katherine Mallen Kupferer (whose own parents starred alongside her in the previous feature), who is cast here as our titular Mouse. Well, sort of. Her name is Minnie, but her shyness leans toward the mousy, though no one would ever say that to her, least of all her beloved and extremely outgoing best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). But when Minnie’s itchy nickname is (wrongly, it turns out) attributed to the flashy Callie, it’s hard for her to shake its deeper meanings.

When the film opens, Minnie and Callie are wrapping their final day as high school juniors in the early summer of 2002 (cue the Michelle Branch soundtrack, perfect). The stage is being set for their senior year — and, quite literally, for the very talented Callie’s next big high school musical moment and her eventual plans to attend Juilliard — and it’s obvious that they’re not about to have the same experience. Callie is popular and vivacious, perpetually surrounded by admirers and various hangers-on (Audrey Grace Marshall’s Cara is hellbent on usurping Minnie’s place in Callie’s life, while her himbo-esque boyfriend Brad is given wonderful dimension through Beck Nolan’s sneaky-good performance).

Minnie? She’s much more reserved, orbiting around Callie and company, not quite ever the star of her own show. But this is not a story about two best friends who break up because of the vagaries of popularity, and Coleman’s Callie is not a villain who breaks Minnie’s delicate heart. Well, not on purpose.

It’s clear that Minnie is out of touch with lots about her life — though not her affection for Callie — including her own sexuality (Iman Vellani as cute local video store clerk Kat happily cracks through that) and her fraught relationship with her overworked mother (Mallen Kupferer’s own mom and “Ghostlight” co-star, Tara Mallen). Callie’s friendship and trust are the best things in her life. Her nice house with a fully stocked kitchen is a bonus, as is Callie’s very-put-together mom Helen (a heartbreaking Sophie Okonedo), who wisely seems to like the steady Minnie a whole heck of a lot more than the rest of Callie’s coterie.

That will prove to be the one saving grace of what comes next. When Minnie and Callie’s friendship comes to a sudden end, it’s only through bonding with Helen that Minnie finds any sort of ballast in her life. But as point-A-to-point-B as that might sound, O’Sullivan and Thompson remain uniquely attuned to the ebbs and flows of real life and how real people respond to it. Mallen Kupferer, so outspoken in “Ghostlight” and so wonderfully goofy in “Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret,” here sinks into the far harder-to-crack Minnie. That’s not to say that Minnie isn’t prone to the emotional wilds of any teenage girl, but the young actress’ finely tuned performance is never broad or silly.

Instead, we get to know Minnie during one of the worst times of her life. So too does Helen, who handles her own feelings about Callie through her own coping mechanisms, some of which work, most of which don’t, and many of which center on building her own friendship with Minnie. The pair of them has a lot in common beyond Callie, including a general sense of wisdom beyond their years that has not always been beneficial to them.

Early in the film, Cara insists that Callie’s group of friends (including both Cara and Minnie) partake in a horrific little parlor game she likens to “Personal Feedback.” Mostly, it’s an excuse for the teenagers to say terrible things about each other under the guise of honesty and friendship. Even our golden girl, Callie, doesn’t escape unharmed, though Minnie almost does, because Cara simply can’t be bothered to remember she exists.

“Mouse” is, at its heart, a wonderful rebuttal to just that sort of cruel thinking — for all the Minnies out there — and a reminder that everyone matters and everyone deserves to be seen. Lofty as that might sound, it’s one of the most basic tenets of humanity, and the kind of thing too often forgotten on the big screen. O’Sullivan and Thompson never forget, however, and their films reflect exactly that. Our only request: more, please, our people need this.

“Mouse” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival.

#3487. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3486. All 66 Episodes Of Hulu's R-Rated Thriller Deliver Psychological Horror At Its Best

While Hulu’s greatest dystopian show is often listed among the best sci-fi series of the last decade, the adaptation rarely gets credit for just how great it is at pulling off psychological horror, too. If Blade Runner’s links to the Alien franchise prove anything, it is that the line between sci-fi and horror is often thinner than it might seem.

One need only look at the Star Trek franchise’s Borg or the earliest, eerily human Cylons from the Battlestar Galactica reboot to see that the uncanny line between man and machine can be mined for horror just as much as wonder or awe. Similarly, from the Xenomorph to its natural enemy, the Predator franchise’s Yautja, there are plenty of extraterrestrials in movies and TV that are a lot less friendly than Steven Spielberg’s awe-inspiring childhood favorite.

On occasion, sci-fi shows can also end up taking their dark dystopian plots so far that they essentially become psychological horror shows in disguise. For many fans of the genre, the term “psychological horror” will likely conjure up straightforward horror shows like Prime Video’s Stephen King adaptation Carrie or The Haunting of Hill House. However, with its oppressively bleak tone and truly terrifying sense of dread, Hulu’s Margaret Atwood adaptation, The Handmaid’s Tale, is just as scary as any of these titles.

Set in the Republic of Gilead, a totalitarian near-future America run by Christian fascists, The Handmaid’s Tale is loosely based on Atwood’s award-winning 1985 novel of the same name. While the book is an epistolary novel told mostly through the diaries of one “Handmaid,” the show’s sprawling narrative takes the perspective of various female characters to explore the horrors of its setting.

In Gilead, women like Elizabeth Moss’s Offred are held captive and have their bodies used as incubators to produce the offspring of the Republic of Gilead’s patriarchal zealots. The regime’s leaders are nightmarishly ruthless and the fate of these women is horrifying, but there is some hope despite the country’s fascist takeover as Offred spends season 1 plotting an escape to the Canadian border.

Suffice it to say that things are not quite that simple for Offred, and the horrors of The Handmaid's Tale’s setting don’t end when she escapes in the season 1 finale. This does, however, mark the moment that the show expands beyond the story of Atwood’s novel, with the remaining five seasons of the series expanding on the slight, sparse original story.

While ambitious sci-fi shows like HBO’s Westworld also depicted believable dystopian settings around the same time, The Handmaid’s Tale was notable for the sheer harshness in the show’s depiction of Gilead. Westworld had plenty of graphic violence, like so many shows that arrived after Game of Thrones and The Walking Dead, but lacked the overwhelming dread that defined every storyline in The Handmaid’s Tale.

That said, this wasn’t an unambiguously positive thing for the series. Later seasons of The Handmaid’s Tale were criticized precisely because the show was accused of relying on downbeat shock value to keep viewers invested, with some commentators claiming that the worst excesses of the series felt exploitative and gratuitous. For fans, The Handmaid’s Tale was an unblinking depiction of fascism’s cruelty.

However, for detractors, the show’s lingering focus on torture and public executions felt too lurid and grotesque to be justifiable. The Handmaid’s Tale seemingly addressed this critique when its final two seasons eased up on the brutality somewhat. This also resulted, inevitably, in the ending of The Handmaid’s Tale feeling less impossibly bleak and hopeless than seasons 2 and 3 of The Handmaid’s Tale might have led viewers to expect.

#3485. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses

Lionsgate‘s “Hunger Games” prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” will be available in 3D when it opens in theaters on November 20. That on its own isn’t strictly news, but the 3D conversion on the film is coming from a new and unlikely place: Facebook parent company Meta.

Meta is partnering with Lionsgate to convert “Sunrise on the Reaping” to 3D, with director Francis Lawrence working to adapt the film for 3D viewing. Meta worked with VFX giant DNEG and their internal 3D conversion branch Stereo. This is the first time Meta has partnered with a Hollywood film studio on such an undertaking, and it also won’t be the last Lionsgate movie that will get the 3D treatment down the road (other titles will be announced at a later date). Related Stories ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

In addition to “Sunrise on the Reaping” being in 3D in theaters, the movie will eventually be available on Meta VR Glasses when those VR devices hit the shelves in spring 2027. IndieWire got to demo those recently, and they’re designed to be lighter and less obtrusive than other VR headsets that can be tougher on the eyes while not sacrificing any of the immersive qualities (they feel and look like slightly larger sunglasses that you might get at the dentist rather than a bulky, wraparound headset that weighs on your face).

The demo we saw included a snippet of the Billie Eilish concert doc co-directed by James Cameron, as well as a clip from “Avengers: Endgame” that added an extra expanded screen effect to fill your line of sight. It’s clear that Meta wants to expand into the entertainment space and compete with the likes of YouTube and Google and other tech giants, and they need premium content like a new “Hunger Games” movie in order to do that.

“From the beginning, we wanted ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to feel visceral and immersive, pulling audiences deep into Haymitch’s experience,” Lawrence said in a statement. “Adapting the film for 3D gave us another creative tool to bring audiences even closer to his perspective. I’m excited for people to see the film on the big screen and ultimately experience it in an entirely new way on Meta’s VR glasses.”

“As we continue to explore new ways for audiences to experience ‘The Hunger Games,’ we’re thrilled to partner with Meta on this first-of-its-kind collaboration,” said Jim Packer, Chief Revenue Officer, Lionsgate. “Francis Lawrence has created an incredible 3D experience for ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ and we’re excited for audiences to experience it in theaters and then on Meta VR Glasses. This is a compelling example of how technology can transform existing formats to create fresh, new experiences.”

“With our upcoming VR Glasses, we’re proud to create premium entertainment the way it’s meant to be felt, and Lionsgate is an ideal partner because of the artistic strength and global appeal of its franchises,” said Sarah Malkin, Head of Entertainment for Meta’s Reality Labs. “’The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ is exactly the kind of cinematic experience that will be phenomenal in theaters, and also showcases what this technology makes possible at home. We’re delighted to work with Lionsgate and Francis Lawrence to bring the film in 3D to audiences around the world.”

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the sixth “Hunger Games” film and the second prequel after “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” from 2023, which brought in $363 million at the worldwide box office. This film stars Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy, who is the District 12 character portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original series of films. The film also stars McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., and Ben Wang.

#3484. 3 Elite Prime Video Series to Binge This Week (Nov 2-6)

November is officially here, and The Terminal List is continuing its run at the top of Prime Video’s TV rankings for another week. Created by David DiGilio and based on the novels by Jack Carr, the action thriller series returned with a second season recently and has been performing quite admirably ever since. However, the Chris Pratt-starrer is hardly the only great show worth checking out on the streaming platform. Here’s a look at three great shows that we think you should binge this week on Prime Video.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

A Canadian police procedural series created by Michael Konyves, Wild Cards follows Cole Ellis, a detective demoted to patrol duty who is assigned to work with a spirited con artist, Max Mitchell, to solve cases. Cole’s by-the-book approach often clashes with Max’s street smarts and charisma, but they must find a way to work together and fight crime. The show stars Giacomo Gianniotti as Cole and Vanessa Morgan as Max, who appear in all seasons, alongside rotating recurring and guest stars like Martin Sheen, Jason Priestley, and Tamara Taylor.

Wild Cards follows the classic police procedural format and features a new case every week with underlying storylines revolving around the protagonists’ romantic dynamic and family secrets. The series has earned acclaim for reprising the trend of lighthearted, breezy crime procedurals of the 2000s, making the best of "opposites attract" and "mismatched detectives" tropes that fans might love to revisit. Since its premiere, the series has proven quite popular, with the first season becoming CBC's highest-rated new series and the show earning a steady 100% on Rotten Tomatoes across three seasons.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

A neo-Western crime drama, Longmire is a series adaptation of Craig Johnson’s mystery novel series featuring Sheriff Walt Longmire. The series focuses on the troubled ex-military law-enforcement officer who solves strange crimes in his community while dealing with the competing jurisdictional authority of the bordering native reservation and various other issues of contemporary Native American life. Robert Taylor stars as the titular character, with Lou Diamond Phillips, Cassidy Freeman, Katee Sackhoff, Bailey Chase, and Adam Bartley in main roles.

Longmire may have become more or less forgotten since it ended, but during its six-season run, the Western drama was a major success with both critics and fans, fascinating its audience season after season with its interesting mysteries and unconventional detective. The series combines the best of two popular television genres, traditional Westerns and modern crime procedurals, creating a narrative that appeals to fans of either. Longmire is praiseworthy for its grounded writing, compelling acting, and atmospheric visuals, and is often ranked among the best revisionist Western shows.

Created, written by, and starring Sharon Horgan and Rob Delaney, Catastrophe is a British sitcom that follows Sharon, an Irish primary school teacher in London who meets Rob, an American advertising executive on a business trip to the city. After a week-long whirlwind romance, Rob returns home to Boston while Sharon discovers that she is pregnant with his child, unleashing utter chaos in their respective lives. Besides Horgan and Delaney as the main characters, the series also stars Ashley Jensen, Mark Bonnar, and Carrie Fisher in her final television role.

Before the success and popularity of Bad Sisters, Catastrophe was Horgan’s most critically acclaimed work in television, earning her a BAFTA nomination for her performance. Raw, witty, and often brutally honest, Catastrophe excels in its sharp satire of the hard-hitting realities of modern parenting and marriage, finding its humor and heart in its flawed characters. Horgan and Delaney also earned BAFTA TV Awards and an Emmy nomination for their writing.

#3483. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 26, 2026 at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Asked to explain the goofy title he gave to his globally successful 2023 kaiju smash “Godzilla Minus One,” writer-director Takashi Yamazaki explained that it was meant to convey two co-equal things: 1.) That the movie took place before Ishirō Honda’s original “Godzilla,” and 2.) That “people rise up from a postwar Japan that is at zero, and then Godzilla arrives, making the situation even worse and more tragic.”

Continuing the story of its Oscar-winning predecessor while also doubling down on everything that made it the most acclaimed film in its franchise since the King of the Monsters first lumbered out of the Pacific Ocean in 1954, Yamazaki’s thunderously loud and frequently spectacular direct sequel has in turn been saddled with an even sillier title: “Godzilla Minus Zero.” To paraphrase the scene from “Sideways” where Paul Giamatti’s character reveals that his novel is called “The Day After Yesterday”: Isn’t that just… “Godzilla?” Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

Yes and no. Sure, the title is absurd on its face, but — in keeping with Yamazaki’s logic — it also rather eloquently speaks to the premise of a film about a fragile people who are struggling to maintain (and build upon) the new equilibrium they’ve fought so hard to achieve in the years since their country became the epicenter of Earth’s nuclear era. Another mid-century melodrama with very occasional monster sightings, the more thematically coherent and emotionally affecting “Godzilla Minus Zero” expands on the naive grassroots nationalism of its predecessor by reframing that movie’s characters from victims to survivors, an emphasis that forces ex-kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and his friends to confront a series of impossible questions. How do you balance grief with growth? Vengeance with peace? Self-sacrifice with self-preservation?

By way of answering those questions (or at least asking them in a variety of increasingly anguished ways), “Godzilla Minus Zero” also forces Shikishima and co. to confront a flying, IMAX-sized, three-headed asshole they come to know as King Ghidorah. Possibly the single most hateable kaiju who’s ever eaten innocent civilians on screen before, King Ghidorah is a real piece of work even before he earns his crown. He first rears his ugly dragon head in Matsumoto circa 1949, which is two years after the events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and maybe two weeks after this scaly destroyer of worlds crash-landed into the mountains of Japan on the back of a meteorite (an arbitrary point of origin that feels like a missed opportunity to freight Ghidora with more human-facing pathos). Seeing as how Godzilla was obliterated and left to rot at the bottom of the sea at the end of the previous film, Ghidora is free to terrorize the countryside whenever he isn’t taking cute little naps in the Nagano hills.

Lucky for Japan, and for all of the other nations that are still living under the delusion that none of this monster business will ever be their problem, at least one of the key heroes who “defeated” Godzilla in 1947 has been preparing his people for the possibility of another kaiju attack. Government higher-ups are still nowhere to be seen, but Einstein-haired Naval engineer Noda (a sweet and eccentrically professorial Hidetaka Yoshioka) has been appointed to the head of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, where he’s joined by newcomer Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a preternaturally gifted meteorologist whose ability to predict the weather proves crucial in the fight against Ghidorah, and also embittered biologist Kanji Murakami (“Twilight Samurai” star Min Tanaka), who survived the bombing of Hiroshima, the attack on Ginza in “Godzilla Minus One,” and the assault on Matsumoto that opens this film — a detail that evokes the terribly remarkable story of Tsutomo Yamaguchi.

Thanks to Noda’s hard-earned wisdom, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is able to skip over the part where everyone has to discover that kaiju like Ghidorah are immune to conventional weapons — if not also strengthened by them. That ignorance is reserved for the occupying Americans, who were entirely absent from the previous movie (which nostalgically privileged the self-reliance of Japan’s civilian population at the expense of a more historical view of the post-war struggle). Here, the U.S. Army is represented by a unit of square-jawed, power-hungry jerks who are only interested in helping Japan so far as it helps themselves. They don’t bear the wounds of nuclear devastation, and so they see kaiju as more of an opportunity than a threat.

The opposite is true for our pal Shikishima, who has absolutely no interest in ever climbing back into the cockpit of a fight plane. Now married to the angelic Noriko — Minami Hamabe, who miraculously escaped “Godzilla Minus One” with a new eyepatch and some big secrets — and embracing his role as adoptive father to the devastatingly cute Akiko (returning champion Sae Nagatani), Shikishima just wants to wear his cool brown leather jacket and messenger bag combo in peace.

If only it were that simple. If only Shikishima were convinced, as he tries to convince himself, that staying out of the fight is the best way to protect the women he loves. If only Noda’s plan of electrocuting Ghidorah to death in the skies above Matsumoto were as successful at killing the kaiju as it is at blowing our hair back.

There are only two sustained monster sequences in “Minus Zero,” which adheres to a similar cadence as its predecessor, but they’re both among the most gripping setpieces of their kind in all of moviedom; they match the grandeur — if not the majesty — of those from Gareth Edwards’ “Godzilla,” and eclipse their violent intensity. The ridiculously thrilling aerial sequence above Matsumoto is lifted by the Wagnerian strings of Naoki Satō’s visceral score, kept aloft by special effects that exponentially improve upon the resourceful but weightless CGI from “Minus One,” and seared into your retinas by IMAX razzledazzle of the highest magnitude. And while the final showdown between Ghidorah and Godzilla is slightly weakened by grayscale atmospherics and a few missing beats (one of them very bizarre), it goes without saying that the climatic brawl is one for the ages, as Yamazaki earns the franchise’s first “R” rating with an elegantly choreographed monster mash that rattles with Darwinian force.

Oh yeah, I suppose it also goes without saying that Godzilla is (eventually) in this Godzilla movie. Somehow, the King of the Monsters has returned — if Palpatine had infinitely regenerative flesh, perhaps his resurrection would have been similarly unsurprising. But fans of Honda’s original film, Yamazaki’s previous one, and/or Edwards’ failed 2014 reboot have come to expect and appreciate that Godzilla is most effective when framed as more of a recurring weather phenomenon than a dramatic engine in his own right, and “Godzilla Minus Zero” doesn’t suffer from its title kaiju’s limited screentime.

On the contrary, his absences are crucial to the construction of a florid tear-jerker about a traumatized country trying to move forward in the atomic shadow of a world that will never feel safe again. While a cursed biologist like Murakami might see vengeance as his only path towards peace, a former kamikaze like Shikishima — the guilt he once felt over not killing himself for Japan now bent towards the responsibility he feels towards living for Noriko and their daughter — is left to wrestle over the best way to protect his family: fighting the monsters, or fleeing from them.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is hardly the most nuanced or effective film to explore its country’s post-war despair (the original “Godzilla” still towers above it in that regard, to say nothing of “Drunken Angel,” “The Human Condition,” “An Inn at Osaka,” or any number of other cornerstones of Japanese cinema), but the anger it assigns to Murakami is provocative on its own terms, and the path that it contrives for Shikishima is considerably more nuanced and well-earned than the one he stumbled through before. While the future is still uncertain by the end of this latest Godzilla movie (which feels very much like the middle chapter of a trilogy), “Minus Zero” makes rewarding sense of why the series’ numbers are starting to add up.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” premiered at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in U.S. theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3482. 26 Episodes Of Netflix's Best Time Travel Show Leave Zero Plot Holes

Most time travel movies and shows collapse under their own flawed logic and rules. They start strong and introduce compelling sci-fi concepts and ideas. However, the more they progress, the more their plot crumbles due to increasing paradoxes and narrative loopholes. A rare sci-fi series on Netflix, however, completely defies the norm and even turns its paradoxes into plot devices.

The show in question, Dark, is still remembered as one of the greatest modern additions to the sci-fi genre. When Dark first landed on Netflix in 2017, it was not driven by a hefty budget or a massive production. As a non-English series, even its reach was meant to be limited as it competed with other mainstream sci-fi shows like Stranger Things.

Yet, through its sheer brilliance alone, the Netflix sci-fi show managed to leave a legacy that remains far stronger and more long-lasting than most others in Netflix's catalog. From its background score to its immersive and atmospheric cinematography, a lot works in the time travel TV show's favor. However, its success can primarily be attributed to how meticulously it approaches time travel.

Time travel is not a flowing river in Netflix's Dark. The show does not merely adopt a one-dimensional cause-and-effect format where actions lead to rippling consequences. Instead, for two whole seasons, it sticks to strict determinism where time is a 4D block. The past, the present, and the future unfold all at once in Dark, with each dissolving into one another.

Owing to this, any attempt to change the past in the series is revealed to be a pre-existing part of history. The overarching timeline just cannot be altered because the mere attempt to intervene was already meant to happen. This is perfectly captured when Dark's main character, Jonas, attempts to save his late father by traveling to the past, but his very presence eventually triggers his father's death.

With this deterministic approach towards time almost throughout its runtime, Dark establishes how objects and information exist without any origins. Most time travel stories reverse-engineer their narratives as they reveal the origin of specific objects or devices. This often creates a paradox because their origins become impossible to establish.

Dark embraces these paradoxes by showing how knowledge perpetually exists in its closed temporal loop.

For instance, a book in the show's universe called A Journey Through Time by H.G. Tannhaus was never actually written by Tannhaus. A younger Tannhaus merely published and transcribed it after the main character's older version gave it to him. The same published copy then ended up going back in time to be handed to him.

Even the show's portrayal of family trees is intentionally loopy. There are no linear lineages. Instead of being pyramids that move from one generation to another, the family trees exist as webs where generations overlap and ancestors become their own descendants.

The Netflix sci-fi show features a compelling opening scene where a narrator makes viewers question their perception of time. "We trust that time is linear, that it proceeds eternally, uniformly, into infinity," he says before revealing how yesterday, today, and tomorrow "are all connected in a never-ending circle." These opening lines in Dark bring a spin on Albert Einstein's most profound quote about time:

"The distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion."

Albert Einstein penned the line in a letter he wrote to the family of his deceased friend, Michele Besso. He did not label time as a "stubbornly persistent illusion" to highlight humanity's lack of free will. Instead, he wanted it to be a reminder that even the dead eternally exist all across time even though we cannot help but grieve them in the present.

A similar sense of hope can be found in Dark's existential portrayal of time travel. The Netflix show's depiction of how the past cannot be altered and how the future is pre-determined can be incredibly harrowing. But there is some strange comfort in knowing that everything is already set in stone and one is exactly where one is meant to be.

By showing how even the most painful choices one makes perfectly tie into the grand scheme of things, Netflix's Dark captures how darkly beautiful time travel in sci-fi can be.

Dark is a German science fiction thriller focusing on four families in a small town impacted by the disappearance of a child. As they search for answers, they uncover a web of interconnected secrets, revealing complex temporal and familial relationships spanning multiple generations.

#3480. The 8 Most Amazing Horror Movies Ever Made, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Horror lists built around the question “Which movie scared you the most?” are almost always bad. Fear is too personal and subjective for that. Sometimes the movie that follows me home is the one that barely raises its voice. Sometimes it is a face, a sound from another room, a character making one decision I desperately wanted them not to make.

That is what these eight have done to me. I have watched them enough times to know exactly where the bodies are buried, and somehow they still have power. The scares remain, obviously, but so do the performances, the moral ugliness, the ideas underneath the violence, and those tiny human reactions that make everything hurt more than a monster ever could. These are hands down, the 8 most amazing horror movies ever made.

Chris Washington (Daniel Kaluuya) spends a weekend meeting the wealthy white family of his girlfriend Rose (Allison Williams), expecting awkward questions and passive-aggressive liberalism. Get Out gradually turns those discomforts into something much worse when Chris notices that the Black people working around the estate behave strangely, Rose’s mother offers him hypnosis, and the family’s fascination with his body begins feeling considerably less innocent.

What destroys me is how long Chris is socially pressured into ignoring instincts that are completely correct. Jordan Peele wrote and directed the film, and he understands that politeness can become its own kind of trap. Chris keeps giving people opportunities to explain themselves because walking out would make him appear unreasonable. Then Logan (LaKeith Stanfield) briefly breaks character at the party and screams at Chris to “get out,” and suddenly every uncomfortable little interaction snaps into place. It is frightening, hilarious, furious, and so controlled that even the jokes sharpen the horror rather than interrupting it.

The Texas Chain Saw Massacre follows Sally Hardesty (Marilyn Burns), her brother Franklin (Paul A. Partain), and their friends through rural Texas, where an innocent detour eventually brings them to a farmhouse occupied by Leatherface (Gunnar Hansen) and his deeply disturbed family. There is barely any elaborate mythology. People enter the wrong house, and the nightmare starts almost immediately.

The first hammer killing is nasty. It happens abruptly with almost no ceremony. A door slides open, Leatherface appears, somebody collapses, and the door closes again. Tobe Hooper directed the film. He apparently made everything feel hot, dirty, exhausted, and horribly plausible even when the situation becomes grotesque. The dinner scene. Sally’s screaming becomes so constant. The entire movie feels physically oppressive. Then morning arrives, she escapes, and Leatherface dances with the chainsaw in the road while she laughs hysterically from the back of a truck. That ending does not feel victorious. It feels like somebody’s nervous system has snapped.

This film follows Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) who steals $40,000 from her employer and flees town, eventually stopping at the isolated Bates Motel. There she meets Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins), a shy young proprietor apparently dominated by his unseen mother. Alfred Hitchcock’s Psycho initially seems to be following Marion’s crime and guilt, then abruptly makes the motel itself far more important than the money she stole.

Perkins is the real weapon, though. Norman can appear fragile, embarrassed, friendly, and faintly wrong inside the same conversation. Watch him talk to Marion about his mother while birds loom around the parlor. Nothing outwardly outrageous is happening, but every sentence makes the room less comfortable. The shower murder became the icon. Norman’s nervous smile is what stays with me.

The Exorcist begins with actress Chris MacNeil (Ellen Burstyn) watching her daughter Regan (Linda Blair) undergo increasingly frightening physical and psychological changes that doctors cannot explain. Eventually, she turns to Father Damien Karras (Jason Miller), a priest and psychiatrist already struggling with his faith, who begins to suspect that Regan may be possessed.

I have never thought the pea soup was the frightening part. The horror is Chris exhausting every rational possibility and realizing none of them can help her child. William Friedkin directed the film with an almost clinical seriousness, which keeps the supernatural material from turning theatrical. Karras matters just as much because the demon attacks the exact wound he carries, especially his guilt surrounding his mother’s death. The final exorcism works because it is spiritual warfare conducted through incredibly human weaknesses. Everybody enters that room already damaged. That is why the possession feels personal rather than decorative.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The crew of the Nostromo is returning to Earth when Alien diverts them toward a mysterious transmission on a hostile planet. Kane (John Hurt) encounters an unknown organism, the crew brings him back aboard, and warrant officer Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) soon discovers that the creature now loose inside their ship is only part of the danger. Ridley Scott directed this like space travel had finally become a blue-collar job. On a lighter note, with all the reptilian aliens chit chatter, it is the perfect time to watch a horror film like this.

In Aliens, people complain about pay. Machinery looks used. Corridors feel practical rather than futuristic. Then the chestburster tears through Kane at dinner, and that normal working environment becomes impossible to trust again. I also love that Ripley survives partly because she was the person insisting on quarantine rules everyone else considered inconvenient. She is not “chosen.” She pays attention.

Stanley Kubrick helmed The Shining with an almost inhuman visual precision, making the Overlook feel too orderly to be safe. Writer Jack Torrance (Jack Nicholson) takes a winter job as caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel, bringing his wife Wendy (Shelley Duvall) and young son Danny (Danny Lloyd) with him. Danny possesses a psychic ability called “the shining,” which exposes him to the hotel’s violent past while isolation begins feeding something terrible inside Jack.

What gets me now is Wendy. People talk endlessly about the twins, Room 237, the elevator of blood, and Jack smashing through the bathroom door, but Shelley Duvall gives the film its bruised human reality. Wendy is the opposite of that control. She panics, cries, swings the bat awkwardly, and keeps moving because Danny needs her. Horror movies often make survival look cool. Wendy survives while looking absolutely terrified, which is far more convincing.

John Carpenter’s The Thing traps an American research team in Antarctica with an extraterrestrial organism capable of perfectly copying other living beings. Once MacReady (Kurt Russell) and the others understand what it can do, the problem becomes horrifyingly simple. The creature may already look exactly like somebody they trust.

I could recommend this movie purely for the blood test. Everyone is tied down. Nobody knows who is human. MacReady heats a wire and touches each blood sample because he believes every piece of the organism will instinctively protect itself. The waiting becomes unbearable. Rob Bottin’s effects are still magnificently disgusting, but the paranoia is why I keep coming back. Even the ending refuses to rescue us from it. MacReady and Childs (Keith David) sit together in the freezing ruins with no reliable way to prove either is human. After everything, distrust has outlived the monster.

FBI trainee Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster) is sent to interview imprisoned psychiatrist and serial killer Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins) because investigators hope his insight can help them catch another murderer, Buffalo Bill (Ted Levine). The Silence of the Lambs becomes a psychological duel between Clarice and Lecter while another woman’s life depends on Clarice understanding what Bill is doing before time runs out.

Jonathan Demme directed the film. The film has those extraordinary direct-to-camera close-ups that make conversation feel invasive. Lecter looks straight into Clarice and seems capable of reading whatever she hoped to conceal. Yet Clarice never becomes intellectually passive around him. Foster lets you see the nerves and the steel at once. Then the final hunt places Clarice inside Bill’s dark basement while he watches her through night-vision goggles, reaching toward her without her knowing how close he is. I still tense up even though I know every movement. That is why this sits at number one. The film gives me brilliant detective work, psychological warfare, genuine terror, and a great heroine without wasting a single minute.

#3479. The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece. Related Stories ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies in Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.

#3478. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3477. The Elder Scrolls: Valenwood Officially Releases This Month

After more than eight years of near silence, The Elder Scrolls 6 is finally beginning to show some serious signs of life. Bethesda first announced the long-awaited successor to Skyrim back in 2018, and while updates have been few and far between, a new report claims the sequel will officially be titled The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Although Bethesda has yet to confirm the name, an official announcement could arrive as early as November, coinciding with Skyrim's 15th anniversary.

Of course, one of The Elder Scrolls franchise's greatest strengths has always been its incredible world-building, with each new installment introducing players to another iconic region of Tamriel. From the snow-covered mountains of Skyrim and the volcanic landscapes of Morrowind to the Imperial heartland of Cyrodiil, these locations have become practically synonymous with Bethesda's legendary RPG series.

However, there are still plenty of fascinating regions deserving of more attention, which is largely why Sentinel rumors had been circulating, looking at the region of Hammerfell. However, ahead of TES6's launch, players can head to Valenwood, the sprawling forest homeland of the Wood Elves, in an exciting new release that will officially bring fans back to this beloved corner of Tamriel.

Fans looking to explore Valenwood before The Elder Scrolls 6 finally arrives have a great opportunity thanks to The Elder Scrolls: Betrayal of the Second Era, the officially licensed tabletop adventure game from Chip Theory Games. Its Valenwood expansion, which originally debuted alongside the base game in 2025, is once again available for preorder through Zatu Games for approximately $43, launching later this month.

For those unfamiliar, Betrayal of the Second Era (or BOTSE) is a cooperative strategy game for one to four players, taking place during Tamriel's tumultuous Second Era. Players create their own adventurers, join guilds, explore different provinces, complete quests, and battle enemies across three connected sessions. Character progression is a major component, with players spending experience points to develop unique abilities and prepare for increasingly difficult encounters.

The Valenwood expansion introduces the homeland of the Bosmer, better known as the Wood Elves, with an entirely new map, quests, encounters, enemies, and equipment. Its storyline explores the disappearance of Falinesti, tensions involving independent Wood Orc tribes, and the growing influence of the mysterious Deslandra.

Players can also access three additional classes, including Arcanist, Burglar, and Ranger, alongside the Illusion, Legerdemain, and Light Armor skill lines. The expansion contains new skill dice, enemy chips, encounter cards, and a detailed regional gazetteer. However, Valenwood isn't the only exciting addition to BOTSE. Chip Theory Games has five major expansions in its latest wave, with fulfillment expected to begin in November 2026.

Two of these introduce additional regions: Summerset, featuring the Mage and Assassin classes alongside unpredictable magical anomalies, and Elsweyr, which explores the Khajiit homeland and introduces Thieves, Berserkers, and a dragon that can pursue adventurers across the map.

Meanwhile, Heroes of Tamriel expands character customization with Warriors, Witchhunters, and new combat skills. Fur and Fang introduces werewolf and vampire abilities, while Shadows of Oblivion brings five Daedric Princes into the adventure, each offering unique blessings and curses.

Additional accessories and character packs are also available for preorder. With so much new content arriving, Betrayal of the Second Era is giving The Elder Scrolls fans plenty of ways to return to Tamriel while Bethesda continues developing its next major RPG.

Free up your iPhone's storage without deleting all your stuff

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Why is it that you seem to run out of iPhone storage at the worst possible moment? The knee-jerk reaction is to start frantically trashing holiday pictures or deleting apps you actually use. But you do not need to butcher your camera roll or pay for more just to claw back a few precious gigabytes.

A couple of clever, built-in settings reclaim space without touching the things you care about. To keep things simple, here are the two best ways to clear that storage warning for good.

High-definition clips and photos are almost always the secret culprits swallowing up your storage. If you shoot video in 4K, just sixty seconds of footage can eat through nearly half a gigabyte of local space.

Instead of manually picking through your photo library to delete memories, you can let your phone handle the heavy lifting automatically. Head over to Settings, Apps, Photos, and make sure iCloud Photos is switched on, and tap Optimize iPhone Storage.

This feature keeps smaller previews on your phone and moves the full-resolution files to iCloud, downloading originals on demand when you view them.

Most of us have a digital graveyard of apps we only open once in a blue moon — think airline boarding passes, occasional parking apps, or mobile games you haven't touched in weeks.

Offloading gives you the perfect middle ground. Navigate to Settings, General, and iPhone Storage, where your device neatly lists your apps from biggest to smallest. Tap on any culprits you don't need and hit Offload App.

This removes the app to free up storage while keeping your personal data, settings, and logins untouched. When you need it again, tap the grey cloud icon on your home screen to instantly reinstall it.
