#3475. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3474. AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them

IndieWire and AT&T spent the month of October demonstrating our shared commitment to championing filmmakers and bringing untold stories to life.

First up was the IndieWire Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, presented by AT&T, which assembled artists, executives, and thought leaders from every corner of the entertainment industry for a day of programming about where Hollywood is heading. Then a week later, we partnered to present the Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest, which celebrated the next generation of filmmakers who are bringing their visions to life.

Held at Ovation Hollywood on Saturday, October 25, the Filmmaker Party brought directors and festival attendees together for an evening of networking and movie discussions. The party even featured a complimentary headshot booth for anyone who wanted to take their career to the next level. One of my favorite streaming traditions is checking out what each platform has added at the start of a new month. The very first day of the month is when the majority of the best streaming services refresh their libraries with major movie drops, and Prime Video is no exception.

In fact, Prime Video typically drops more movies on the first day of a new month than any of its streaming rivals, and on Sunday, November 1, 2026, Prime’s back catalog is getting a major boost with 103 movies arriving.

That’s an overwhelming amount of choice, which is why I’ve combed through the list to pick out the gems you should stream first. Because it’s now November, Prime Video’s latest movie drop is heavy on holidays, and I’ve picked a couple of Christmas classics to get you in the festive mood nice and early. However, I’ve also found some exciting thrillers for those who don’t start celebrating the holidays until December.

So, let’s get into my top picks; these are the five movies just added to Prime Video that should be at the top of your November 2026 watchlist.

Some of my fondest childhood memories of the festive season involve rewatching “Elf” so many times that the DVD was in danger of getting worn out. This 2000s holiday classic has it all: seasonal spirit, charming comedy, lovable characters and a message about the importance of family. Even now as a grown-up on the wrong side of 30, it’s still a holiday movie I watch every single year, and I’ve no plans to stop in 2026.

Will Ferrell plays Buddy, a human raised by Santa’s elves. Due to his human proportions and inability to make toys, he doesn’t quite fit in at the North Pole. So when Santa reveals to him that his father (James Caan), a New York City bigwig, is on the naughty list, Buddy travels to the Big Apple to meet his biological father and find his place in the world. Once in NYC, he discovers that humans are sorely lacking in holiday cheer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The perfect movie doesn’t exist. Absolute perfection is an impossible goal. Even my favorite films of all time have some minor flaws. However, when it comes to a movie nailing exactly what it's trying to achieve, it’s hard to argue that “Mean Girls” doesn’t get pretty darn close to perfection. This movie is the quintessential teen comedy, packed with quotable lines, iconic outfits and legendary scenes. And yes, we’re talking about the original here, not the musical remake. Though for the record, I’m a defender of that movie; I think it’s very underrated.

Cady Heron (Lindsay Lohan) is a 16-year-old whose family has recently returned to the U.S. after spending 12 years in Africa. Now attending North Shore High School, Cady is introduced to a complex web of unspoken teenage rules and a strict social hierarchy. At the top of the food chain are The Plastics, a trio of ultra-cool mean girls led by queen bee, Regina George (Rachel McAdams). When Cady is invited into their inner circle, she hatches a plan to sabotage them from within.

This year will see the release of yet another big-screen spin on Charles Dickens’ enduring classic, “A Christmas Carol,” in the form of Ti West’s “Ebenezer.” But why trek out to your local theater when you can already enjoy the best movie adaptation of the timeless tale on Prime Video? Okay, so “Scrooged” is the best adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” that doesn’t feature The Muppets. It's still a great watch even if it doesn't include Kermit, Miss Piggy, and the gang. Plus, it stars Bill Murray at his sarcastic best.

You probably know the basic setup, but if you’re somehow unfamiliar with Dickens’ fable, it follows a cynical and selfish TV executive (named Frank Cross here rather than Ebenezer Scrooge), who is visited by three ghosts on Christmas Eve in an effort to convince him to change his self-centered ways. There’s a pleasant meta twist in “Scrooged.” Cross lives in a world where the “A Christmas Carol” story also exists, so when he starts living the tale for real, he’s not too happy about it.

Moving away from holiday classics and teenage comedies, another movie that’s just arrived as part of Prime Video’s huge November 1 drop is “The Manchurian Candidate.” This 1962 political thriller is one that fans of classic cinema definitely shouldn’t skip. It stars Frank Sinatra, Laurence Harvey, and Janet Leigh, alongside Angela Lansbury, Henry Silva, and James Gregory. And it is perhaps one of the sharpest American movies of the Cold War era.

Raymond Shaw (Harvey) is a U.S. soldier fighting in the Korean War, captured by the enemy, but then released three days later. Returned home, he receives the Medal of Honor, and on the surface it looks like a feel-good homecoming story. But Shaw is hiding a dark secret, a shocking memory that even he can’t recall. “The Manchurian Candidate” is a thriller that hasn’t lost its edge over the last 60+ years and has even inspired modern media like Showtime's “Homeland.”

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

Staying on the theme of political thrillers, “WarGames” is an ‘80s techno ride that does feel a little outdated when watched in the 21st century. However, at the time of its release, it was a real cautionary tale about the dangers of technology and its potential uses in global conflict. Heavily influenced by the Cold War period in which it was released, it marked one of the first movie roles for Matthew Broderick, Ferris Bueller himself.

David Lightman (Broderick) is a smart but unmotivated high school slacker in Seattle. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers for teenage hijinks. But things get serious when he unknowingly accesses a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. He thinks he’s playing a game, but he might have just started World War III…

#3472. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3471. 9 Dystopian Sci-Fi Shows That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

It seems like dystopian sci-fi shows are one of the fastest-growing sub-genres of late. Dystopian shows have been popular for some time, dating all the way back to the early The Walking Dead days and with shows like Lost.

Sci-fi shows, meanwhile, have also been popular for decades. But combining the two? That's a relatively new thing. Apart from shows like Studio One back in 1953 and its "Nineteen Eighty-Four" episode and, of course, iconic series like The Twilight Zone, sci-fi dystopia is a burgeoning space. A few specific shows from the last decade or so have really done it justice.

What makes Paradise especially brilliant is that it doesn't weave sci-fi into the plot until the second season. In fact, it doesn't even reveal the dystopian reality until the end of the pilot episode. The show also functions as an action-packed political thriller, mashing so many genres into one, yet blending them so well.

The story in one of the best thriller shows released since 2020 takes place in an underground bunker where survivors reside. In Season 2, it flips back and forth between the bunker and Earth above, where things are very different from what the few thousands who were saved are led to believe. The sci-fi angle throws you for the loop, suggesting the upcoming final Season 3 will lean more heavily into this side and reinvent the show for another exceptional season to complete the story.

Cryogenic chambers that keep people alive for centuries. Killer mutated insects called Radroaches. Fighters in heavily teched out robot armor. Undead ghouls roaming the streets. It's all par for the course in Fallout, a post-apocalyptic drama based on the video game series of the same name.

With two seasons under its belt and another on the way, Fallout follows naïve young Lucy (Ella Purnell) as she emerges from her underground bunker for the first time and realizes that life outside is far different from the sheltered one she has lived. She teams up with The Ghoul (Walton Goggins) to achieve a common goal, but the dangers they meet are a combination of fractured human nature and creepy sci-fi. It's so entertaining, even if you know nothing about the video games.

Another show where survivors from an apocalyptic event live underground. This time they're in silos in Silo. The towering floors are separated by endless loops of stairwells and people are divided by class; ironically, one aspect of the world before that hasn't changed. Everyone is led to believe that outside is a dangerous wasteland, proven through a projected image from a camera that reveals the immediate death of anyone who dares ask to leave. When Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson) starts to question things, however, the beginnings of a potential revolution emerge.

Like Paradise, the sci-fi element doesn't arrive in a big way until Season 3, when plenty of big revelations are presented for the story. But it is teased throughout. When the big reveal rears its head in the third season, however, you can't help but sit at the edge of your seat, desperate to find out how the story ends. Silo is based on a series of novels by Hugh Howey, but the show has carved a modified path, which means even fans of the books get surprises.

With a heavy spotlight on tech, Mr. Robot combines the dangers of technology with the challenges of mental health. Elliot Alderson (Rami Malek) is a talented and reclusive hacker who works for a cybersecurity company by day but uses his hacking skills to stop people from doing awful things at night. His main goal, however, is to take down the world's biggest corporation, E Corp (he calls them Evil Corp), believing that a financial reset that wipes out debilitating personal debt is the only way to save humanity.

Mr. Robot dives deep into sci-fi as the story progresses and Elliot discovers things about himself and his group's supposed leader, Mr. Robot (Christian Slater). He encounters cyberterrorist enemies, evil CEOs, and the dark implications of anarchy. The show is one of those series you benefit from watching twice.

Severance is one of the best shows of the last five years, a sci-fi psychological thriller about Mark Scout (Adam Scott), a man who undergoes an experimental procedure to divide his memories. The goal is to get through a mundane job without being consumed by grief over the death of his wife. But Mark's "innie" and "outie" are still technically the same person, even if they know nothing about one another.

The show gets bizarre yet gripping as it further explores the concept of personal agency, and the nefarious plans of Lumon Industries, the biotechnology company that performs these procedures. It's an intense thriller show worth watching over and over, obsessing over every detail in Reddit forums with other fans. Both seasons will have you wide-eyed, Season 2 especially upping the ante. By the end of both seasons to date, you'll be screaming at the TV.

Unequivocally the best sci-fi dystopian show of this generation, Black Mirror tells a unique story in every episode of its anthology format. There are admittedly some weak episodes among the bunch, but even the weakest ones are better than the totality of some other shows of the genre. And the best ones? They will blow your mind.

Black Mirror serves as a cautionary tale, a warning of the dangers of rapid technological innovation and our reliance on it. From AI to social media, the monetization of everything, parental controls, and more, each speculative fiction story is like a piece of art. Often, you don't quite understand the point until towards the end, leaving your jaw on the floor. That's especially so with some of the episodes from early seasons, like Season 2's "Be Right Back," fan favorite Season 3's "San Junipero," and the horrifying Season 3 episode "Shut Up and Dance."

From the mind of Breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan, Pluribus explores the sci-fi and dystopian angle from a completely new lens. The world as we know it has come to an end. But survivors have become part of a hive mind. They aren't out to murder and maim, they want to create a utopian society. Carol Sturka (Rhea Seehorn) is one of only a few survivors who are immune to the virus, and she has no interest in joining. It's a race against time to stop the madness before the hive mind uses its vast knowledge to figure out how to bypass her immunity.

Pluribus is subtle. There aren't flashy scenes. It's mostly dialogue driven with compelling discussions that make you ponder if individuality is more important than literal world peace. Is world peace really achievable anyway, and at what cost? Plus, there's the big question of what caused this virus in the first place. The answer leads to somewhere in the stars and potential other life forms.

Sometimes, the best shows in the eyes of viewers aren't necessarily the ones that continue beyond a few seasons. Such is the case with Raised by Wolves, which debuted to positive reception, was even more revered in Season 2, then was shockingly canceled by HBO Max. Even so, the sci-fi drama is still worth your time.

Set in the future following the destruction of Earth, Father (Abubakar Salim) and Mother (Amanda Collin) are androids raising human children on their home planet. A colony of human survivors is forming on Kepler-22b, but political and social views don't always align. This threatens the entire race and leaves the androids struggling to figure out how to deal with this foreign species. The show is so original, wonderfully exploring not only dystopia and sci-fi, but the implications of religion and integration with a completely different world. It's one of the best shows that's no longer available to stream.

Unlike the others, Upload takes a more comedic sci-fi slant. Though it's not a traditional end of the world scenario, it's a story about what happens when the world ends for specific people. Before you die in this future world, you can decide to have your consciousness uploaded to an afterlife community, like a retirement home for the dearly departed. But the system has become heavily monetized as corporations fight to sell their communities as the best, or most affordable. While there, people in their host bodies are inundated with virtual purchase options, their guilty living relatives compelled to buy more credits to show their love by ensuring their dead relatives are able to "live" in comfort.

At the heart of Upload is the story of life and philosophical questions about its finality. Nathan Brown (Robbie Amell) is uploaded by his wealthy girlfriend before he dies from injuries sustained in a car crash. Now, he's forever tied to her purse strings. Heavy on sci-fi, we see humans communicating with the dead through VR headsets and holograms. The story grows to explore how humanity has been able to make this happen and the societal and greed-fueled implications of those who stand to benefit. Upload is a charming, sweet show. It's one of the best Prime Video shows everyone has been sleeping on.

#3470. Alien Meets Interstellar In Netflix's 8-Part Lovecraftian Sci-Fi Series

While a blend of Alien and Interstellar might sound tough to pull off, one Netflix series managed this mix admirably. The scope and scale of a sci-fi story can often end up defining its tone. Even though both Ridley Scott’s Alien and Blade Runner are technically dystopian thrillers where major characters are revealed to be uncannily human-like robots during the narrative, the two movies could not feel more different.

The sprawling cityscape of Blade Runner makes Scott’s adaptation of the seminal Philip K. Dick novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep feel massive and overwhelming. The movie’s setting is a dark, anonymous, rain-drenched city, one that calls to mind the lonely post-human setting of author William Gibson’s iconic cyberpunk novel Neuromancer. In stark contrast, Alien takes place almost entirely on the Nostromo, and the claustrophobic setting makes the movie feel more like a slasher set in space than an immersive, futuristic saga like Blade Runner.

Blade Runner offers viewers an absorbing city to get lost in, while Alien offers the audience a setting so small that it leaves nowhere to hide. Right in between these two extremes is director Christopher Nolan’s 2014 blockbuster Interstellar. While the stakes of its story are existential, the setting is fairly small, with much of the movie taking place on a lone spaceship. Netflix’s underrated sci-fi series The Silent Sea managed to take the high stakes of Interstellar’s story and reintroduce some of the claustrophobic horror of Alien to the mix.

Released in 2021, The Silent Sea follows a crew of astronauts to the Moon’s Sea of Tranquility. The group is trying to retrieve the samples that were left behind at Balhae Station, an abandoned research facility five years earlier, since a dried up earth needs access to water by any means. Of course, the sister of the lead researcher, Doctor Song Ji-an, was one of the researchers who mysteriously disappeared from Balhae Station, so the mission is more than a little personal.

Across The Silent Sea’s eight episodes, the mystery of what happened at Balhae Station, and why the government covered it up and sent another crew to the abandoned site, comes to light. While the basic setup might remind viewers of shows like Stargate and Firefly, thanks to the tight-knit spaceship crews and their high-risk missions, The Silent Sea instead starts out feeling like Interstellar and gradually grows more similar to Alien.

Initially, viewers and Doctor Song Ji-an alike are worried about the Earth’s desertification, so the biggest concern is ensuring that the crew obtains the all-important samples from the abandoned site. At this stage, The Silent Sea still feels like The Martian, Gravity, or even the real-life storyline of Apollo 13. It is only when the crew learns the truth about Balhae Station that things take a turn into another genre.

Much like The Descent is a survival thriller about a caving mishap until suddenly it isn’t anymore, The Silent Sea has a few big twists that radically change the show’s genre and tone. Fortunately, unlike HBO’s similarly ambitious sci-fi series Westworld, these twists never feel jarring or explained.

Instead, the further the crew explore the eerie empty research facility, the clearer it becomes that viewers are watching a body horror/creature feature, rather than just a space exploration story. This was a great choice on the part of the creators, since there was a deluge of similar space exploration shows arriving around the same era.

The Silent Sea needed to stand out in a crowded marketplace, as Apple TV’s alternate history series For All Mankind and its spinoff show Star City, the Star Wars spinoff Andor, and Netflix’s ambitious sci-fi anthology Love, Death, & Robots all explored similar settings. Luckily, The Silent Sea’s blend of Alien's claustrophobic horror and Interstellar’s stakes makes the show a must-watch.

#3469. ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement

The Kasato Maru ferried 325 Okinawans to Brazil in 1908, making it the first immigrant ship from Japan to do so. That history is highlighted by the opening of the documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” (“saudade” being a Portuguese word for bittersweet longing, typically around a memory or place). The film looks at the results a century later, now that an estimated 200,000 Brazilians of Okinawan descent are living in Brazil today, and director and cinematographer Yoju Matsubayashi finds a specific and emotionally straightforward route into complicated history. The director has covered the subject to some extent before in 2020’s “Okinawa / Santos,” a film which collected testimony on the forced deportation and even internment of Japanese immigrants in Brazil in the 1940s.””Okinawa Saudade”” narrows that focus to the families of two third-generation Okinawan-Brazilians, specifically ones with an interest in — and a longing towards — the island their families came from, something partially explored through the arts. Related Stories AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

A visual motif of waves viewed from above punctuates different segments of the film, typically as its subject reflect on the previous movements of their families. In the first instance of the shot, a dissolve to a young girl practicing a traditional Japanese dance on her family’s farm in Brazil immediately communicates that feeling of “saudade,” a soft and gently expressed shadow hanging over much of the film. That feeling of “saudade” is seen in the incidental details the director chooses to include, like how one subject’s grandfather grew dragonfruit with Okinawan seeds, as well as his capturing of more outwardly emotional moments, like a tearful reaction to photos not seen in a long time.

The teenage girl Yumi practices Ryukyu Buyo, while a man named Everton practices Eisa, an Okinawan folk dance involving drums. By unspooling their enthusiasm for the history of such Okinawan heritage arts and the history of their families, Matsubayashi also orbits a history of displacement. This emerges in an accumulation of lots of small personal stories, like how one characters recounts their family’s war-motivated exile from Santos. Yumi and Everton also learn more of these details for themselves, the film following them on their travels to Okinawa through exchange programs and traineeships. (In some delightful cases, the learning cuts both ways, as Everton reunites with estranged family, and Yumi’s Okinawan relative marvels at the dialect being preserved halfway around the world.)

Capturing their subjects’ respective journeys with occasional and mostly spontaneous interviews, Matsubayashi prioritizes personal histories over the big picture,as the assembly of the footage and the occasional interjection of archival material makes the relationship of this diaspora a bit clearer. Some of these families left Okinawa to avoid the military draft as well as starvation. Others were divided because of land seizures by the US military in the wake of the war (“I’ve learned that this is a sad place,” Yumi reflects, a quote placed over footage of lingering American military bases on the island). Some viewers might be dissatisfied with how Matsubayashi never quite engages with World War II and the full history of Okinawan annexation directly, but the context feels like plenty for the stories which he is telling, choosing instead to focus on the feelings which all children of immigrant backgrounds have felt: an uncertainty about their connection with the homeland of their parents and grandparents, and a yearning to understand it. The glimpses are enough, as “Okinawa Saudade”gradually paints a picture of how the historical struggles of the island have translated to the diaspora.

Everton outright says why he engages in Eisa drumming, saying that “we are Brazilians, but we don’t look like Brazilians, so we are always looking for belonging,” and his engagement with these traditional artforms becomes a part of this. Both learn the different nuances of their respective practices at home compared to in Okinawa, though both are graced with teachers who refuse to be super didactic about what is “authentic” (“We are always adjusting,” Yumi’s teacher says, “there is no such thing as perfection”). It’s also simply moving seeing, through Matsubayashi’s rather unvarnished camerawork, how the connections and feelings embodied in performing arts can have such far reach across time and place, highlighting the community found by the Brazilian Okinawans who preserved a little piece of the island for themselves.

“Okinawa Saudade” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3467. Goodbye 'Ocean's Eleven,' Ben Affleck's Heist Thriller Is Now Officially Streaming

A holiday-themed heist thriller released in 2000 that never found an audience, didn't even make back its budget, and was savaged by both critics and one of its own stars, Reindeer Games has fallen largely into obscurity. Still, the star-powered oddity is due a re-evaluation, and that's for two reasons: It's strange enough that you have to see it to believe it, and it was helmed by legendary director John Frankenheimer. And one thing Frankenheimer has never done is phone it in.

Ben Affleck and Charlize Theron head up the film's cast, with Affleck playing an ex-con named (yes) Rudy impersonating a man named (also, yes) Nick. There's snow, ice and Santa suits aplenty amid the borderline nonsensical twists and gunfire, but the man who once directed The Manchurian Candidate and Seven Days in May plays it straight all the way through. For the curious, the Christmas heist film no one really needed is now streaming on Paramount+, after long being only available as a rental — and it's a lot more fun than you'd expect.

Written by Hollywood veteran Ehren Kruger, whose credits run the gamut from several Transformers films to Top Gun Maverick, the story for Reindeer Games seems almost deliberately hard to follow. To keep things simple: Affleck plays Rudy, an ex-con who, upon his release from prison, impersonates his dead cellmate Nick and shacks up with Ashley (Theron), the dead man's pen pal girlfriend, who has never met him in real life. Ashley's got a brother, though, played by a terrifically villainous Gary Sinise, and he wants "Nick" to help him rob a casino, run by the incomparable Dennis Farina.

A series of double and triple-crosses follow, as well as a shootout on a frozen lake, a sex scene between Affleck and Theron that reportedly had to be cut to get an R-rating, and eventually, for some reason, everyone ends up wearing Santa suits. The film is also packed to the gills with brief appearances by actors like Danny Trejo, Isaac Hayes, and even Ron Jeremy. It's frankly a mess that works best if you let it just wash over you — and likely wash it down with a few cocktails.

Theron herself even admitted in a later interview that the whole thing was a bit of a disaster, saying: "That was a bad, bad, bad movie. But even though the movie might suck, I got to work with John Frankenheimer. I wasn't lying to myself — that's why I did it. I mean, he directed The Manchurian Candidate, which is like the movie of all movies. Fuck regret. Just fuck it."

Affleck's movie sees a mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped.

That's a hard question to answer but, depending on your tolerance for lackadaisical performances and nonsense plotting, it could well be yes. Frankenheimer brought the world The Manchurian Candidate and the action-thriller classic Ronin, which features one of the greatest car chases of all time, and he doesn't slouch behind the camera here, no matter how ridiculous the material. Reindeer Games clearly takes delight in its ludicrous number of plot twists, excessive violence, and groan-worthy Christmas references. And Frankenheimer manages to pack in some booming, bloody, and impactful gunplay that keeps things moving at a crisp pace. He also later admitted that he wanted the film to be even racier and more violent, having been made to cut over 20 minutes by the MPAA.

Notably, Frankenheimer was also unapologetic about the sheer number of twists in the film, later saying that he would have liked the story to have been even thornier. In an interview, he said: “Let’s get a reality check here. Today’s audience may not be confused by how fast a film like Reindeer Games moves, but the intellectual level of the person watching this movie is not nearly what it was for the person watching The Manchurian Candidate.”

Even in its compromised form and with its cringe-worthy holiday nods, Reindeer Games is the kind of nasty, unapologetic Hollywood failure we rarely get anymore.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Wet weather and warm homes are a recipe for mattress mold

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mattress mold is a problem that sneaks up on you. A slightly whiffy bed and small stains can quickly turn to itching, sneezing and watery eyes. And right now is primetime for moldy conditions.

A combination of cold, wet weather outside and warm heating inside increases moisture in the air. Your mattress soaks it up like a sponge and, trapped inside your warm bed, that damp helps mold spores to multiply.

Mattress mold doesn't have to spell the end of your bed, but you need to catch it early. We spoke to Dr Gareth Nye, Biomedical Sciences lecturer at the University of Salford working exclusively with M&S, about how to identify early signs of mold — and get rid of it.

Mold can completely ruin a mattress, but before you rush off to browse our best mattress guide for a replacement bed, look out for these early indicators of mold.

You won't necessarily see early signs of mold in your mattress, but you might be able to smell the problem has taken hold.

Dr. Nye describes the smell of mold as "a persistent musty, damp, or earthy odor" and notes that it can linger "even after the bedding has been washed."

If this new smell is accompanied by an uptick in allergy symptoms when you go to bed (itching, sneezing or watery eyes, for example) mold is the likely culprit. Noticed a sweeter musty smell? It might be bed bugs.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Big, dark stains are often a sign that your mattress is past saving. But before you get to that point, Dr. Nye recommends looking for "tiny, clustered pinpoint stains."

These small marks are the signs of an early mold infestation and they can be treated (we'll explore how below). And don't just look on the top surface of the mattress for stains. The underside of the bed as well as the sides can house mold as well.

Signs of mold aren't always visible on the mattress itself. Look in the surrounding area for indicators your bedroom is growing mold.

Dr. Nye describes "spaces up against a wall or behind units" as 'mold magnets' because they prevent airflow. So if your bed frame is pushed against the wall, move it forward when you clean and check for mold.

He also advices looking in any common sites for condensation, including anything pressed to the "external environment" (like radiators against a window).

"The space under the bed is also a prime spot for mold," says Dr. Nye. And if the mold is under the bed, it might not take long for it to move into the bed.

Mold is more than just an unwanted stain. Left to grow, mold in your mattress can have serious negative repercussions on your health.

"Mold reproduces by releasing microscopic spores and mycotoxins into the air, which are easily inhaled during the 7 to 8 hours you spend asleep," explains Dr. Nye. "This triggers an immune response, leading to allergic rhinitis (sneezing, congestion, runny nose, and itchy eyes) and significantly exacerbating symptoms for those with asthma."

And the longer the problem is allowed to grow, the worse the impact it can have on your health.

"Prolonged exposure can result in chronic illnesses," says Dr. Nye. "Mold spores can also severely worsen conditions like eczema and trigger contact dermatitis."

We previously asked the experts how to get rid of mattress mold. They advised spot treating any stains with ingredients you probably have in your kitchen: white vinegar and baking soda.

Begin by mixing equal parts white vinegar and water. Spray the solution lightly on the stain and leave for 20 minutes. Blot dry, then apply a thin layer of baking soda. Leave to sit for several hours and then vacuum thoroughly.

#3465. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3464. Shrinking season 4 just got exciting release timing update

Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming.

TV’s streaming era has brought a lot of advantages over linear TV, but undoubtedly one drawback is that shows tend to have much longer waits between seasons.

Traditional broadcast television usually schedules shows to premiere in the fall and run through the spring, then return after a short summer break for a new season in the fall.

In streaming, viewers are shocked when a show comes back after only a year.

Apple TV has slowly been getting better at this. Slow Horses is the best example, but another recent one is Your Friends & Neighbors. And we’re seeing signs of other series getting quicker turnarounds between seasons, including Shrinking.

Shrinking aired its season 3 finale this April, and by May we heard that filming on season 4 was about to start.

Now Jessica Williams, the star who plays Gaby, has confirmed that season 4 has officially wrapped production. This means the series will almost certainly return in early 2027.

On a show like Shrinking, post-production is a much quicker process than with series that are heavy on CGI and other special effects. So we could see Shrinking season 4 premiere in late January, exactly one year after season 3 debuted.

More conservatively, the show returning by spring 2027 seems a safe bet.

Recent news urges us all to prepare for sudden power cuts. I assumed I was fine, until an honest look around my house revealed I was woefully unequipped

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time an emergency agency pops up on the news suggesting households keep a 72-hour emergency kit on hand, I do the same thing: nod knowingly, assume they’re talking to someone far less organized than me, and scroll on.

In my head, I’m a reasonably capable adult. The fridge is full, there are batteries rattling around in a drawer somewhere, and I have a phone flashlight. Surely that counts as disaster preparedness.

Curiosity finally won out, so I decided to run an honest, room-by-room audit of what would actually happen if our power lines went dark for three straight days. The verdict was... humbling.

It turns out my master survival plan was heavily reliant on an active Wi-Fi connection, an electric stovetop, and blind optimism. Here's five glaring blind spots I completely overlooked, and what you should do so you don't make the same mistakes.

Opening my junk drawer during the audit revealed two decorative candles, a lighter that took six clicks to spark, and I didn't have a flashlight. My entire plan, it seemed, was an iPhone and an ancient power bank that refused to charge past 12%. Using a phone flashlight burns through battery, leaving you without light, or a lifeline.

Retire your phone as a light source and stash dedicated LED lights or magnetic lanterns where you can grab them in pitch black, like a bedside drawer. Pair them with an inexpensive hand-crank AM/FM emergency radio: it pulls in vital civil broadcasts with zero Wi-Fi, and the built-in dynamo handle doubles as a manual charger as a last resort if your devices die.

I went looking for medical supplies and found a dusty tin with three sports bandages, one pack of ibuprofen, and a pair of blunt tweezers. That was the entirety of my home trauma unit. Navigating in the dark makes minor injuries inevitable, and local clinics won't be running at full capacity during a power cut.

Ditch the half-empty tin and get a proper, sealed multi-day medical kit stocked with sterile dressings, burn gel, antiseptic wash, and heavy-duty elastic wraps. Crucially, audit your prescription medications right now and set a reminder to refill them at least a week before they run dry.

When a storm knocks out power, pharmacies can't access electronic dispensary records, and nobody is handing out prescription pills over a dark counter.

A packed fridge gives you an immediate, unearned hit of confidence. But an unopened fridge only holds safe temperatures for about four hours, and my pantry was full of dry pasta, lentils, and rice — meals that require boiling water and an electric stove. Unless I fancied crunching raw fettuccine in the dark, I had zero edible food past day one.

Do a pantry check for foods that require zero heat and zero added water. Build a reserve of ready-to-eat staples: crackers, canned fish, pull-tab soups, peanut butter, spam, nuts. It won't win culinary awards, but it keeps you fed without burning precious cooking fuel or risking food poisoning on day three.

Municipal water relies on electric booster pumps. If the grid fails, pipe pressure drops fast, or contamination triggers boil-water alerts you can't comply with on a dead stove. My total water reserve was half a fridge filter carafe and a gym bottle on my desk.

Store the emergency baseline: four litres (one gallon) of water per person, per day, split between drinking and basic hygiene. For a 72-hour blackout, keep a minimum of 12 litres per person tucked into a dark cupboard or wardrobe, plus extra if you have pets. It's worth noting that your water heater has around 150-300 liters stored inside it too in case of an emergency.

Digital payments die the instant the power cut hits. Point-of-sale card readers, phone taps, and bank networks go dark, turning plastic and smartwatches into useless props. Checking my own bags, pockets and drawers produced exactly zero physical money.

If you're able, withdraw an emergency cash reserve and stash it. The guidance states between $100 and $500 depending on your family's size, covering essentials if card systems remain offline for several days. If you're like me and withdrawing in one go isn't feasible, simply start tucking away leftover change. Every little helps, and it adds up quickly.

#3461. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 adding two new features soon

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are here, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details.

Siri AI is a major tentpole of watchOS 27, and later this year there’s a powerful Siri addition coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It’s called Siri Recap.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

Live Rewind is another ‘Audio Intelligence’ feature coming to the new Apple Watch models later this year. It provides a more direct way to revisit something that was just said.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Apple is expected to introduce both new Apple Watch features in watchOS 27.3, which should launch in beta very soon.

#3460. The 8 Heaviest Gangster Movies of All Time, Ranked

Lots of gangster movies are heavy-going, obviously, but not all. Pulp Fiction has a couple of intense scenes, for example, but it’s not really a super heavy or depressing movie. And then you’ve got something like Scarface, which is very much a tragedy and has bad things happening to its main character (and most of the other characters, honestly), but the style and bombast there makes it all go down a little easier and honestly feel kind of fun.

As for the actually super downbeat movies about organized crime, that’s what you’ve got below. These are some of the darkest and heaviest gangster movies ever made, all of them going the extra mile to stress that whole notion of crime not paying, at the very least. Some of them go further and get more upsetting still, but usually with good reason. And, for what it’s worth, all of these depressing gangster movies are pretty great quality-wise, too.

Battles Without Honor and Humanity was a movie that kicked off the series of the same name, and it’s a yakuza movie more than it is a strict gangster movie, if you're a stickler for definitions, but the yakuza is a kind of criminal organization, so this movie counts. It’s also the best movie in its series, though all of them are pretty downbeat, chaotic, and unapologetically violent, all the while telling something of an overarching story, though it can be hard to keep up, by design.

Broadly speaking, there’s a complicated gang war being fought throughout this one, and a whole lot of people double-cross each other and end up dead. It’s a series of tense situations and sometimes violent ones, or sometimes a bit of both at the same time. Battles Without Honor and Humanity (1973) is a lot, and maybe even close to too much, but in a good (and admirable) way, for the most part. And it is absolutely downbeat and cynical, too.

Though he gained attention for making some later crime films (namely, Drive and, perhaps more infamously, Only God Forgives), Nicholas Winding Refn’s Pusher came first, and it’s a bit more straightforward. It’s still challenging, though, just in a different way, as while it’s about a criminal in a deadly situation following a deal that goes wrong (so, easy to follow), it’s got some rather intense violence and is undeniably gritty.

The extent to which that main character is in danger also makes things feel hectic and heavy, and if all that’s not enough, it’s the first part of a very heavy-going trilogy, too. Pusher does work wonders with what might sound like a slightly too lean premise and what seems like a pretty slim budget, though you do probably need a decently strong stomach to get through it in one piece.

Seeing the words “an Andrew Dominik film” should tip you off that you're in for a likely feel-bad time, since he was behind both Blonde and The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, and so it’s not too surprising that him tackling the gangster genre with Killing Them Softly made for a pretty downbeat time. It is still an engaging film, and maybe even a slightly darkly funny one at times, but all of that is found alongside some serious nihilism, and also, no one in this film comes anywhere close to feeling morally sound.

It’s all very dark, gritty, and largely compelling, and while it’s entertaining to some extent, you're unlikely to come away from it with your spirits raised.

Narratively, Killing Them Softly is about the aftermath of a card game robbery that was supposed to be protected by the mob, so it being targeted has serious consequences, with Brad Pitt’s character being tasked with cleaning up the whole mess as best as possible. It’s all very dark, gritty, and largely compelling, and while it’s entertaining to some extent, you're unlikely to come away from it with your spirits raised, to say the least.

When breaking down the two fast-paced gangster epics Martin Scorsese directed in the 1990s, it’s safe to call them both – Goodfellas and Casino – quite brutal and relatively unromanticized, at least in some regards. But Goodfellas feels gentle if you're directly comparing it to Casino, since this 1995 film is far more cynical, it contains a good deal more explicit violence and language, and the characters are almost entirely without redeeming qualities. Concerning the last of those, some characters in Goodfellas do feel human and are at least a little endearing.

Well, okay, the characters in Casino are also human, with many based on – or inspired by – actual people, but they are meaner and crueler people than what you'll find in most gangster movies. It also doesn’t pull punches in showing Las Vegas as (at least for a time) a violent and totally corrupt city, all because the mob could run the place through owning so many casinos. Casino is pretty much three hours of betrayals, beatings, murders, arguments, threats, and robberies. It is relentless, but maybe it has to be.

Infernal Affairs is a Hong Kong gangster movie that has a premise you might be more familiar with thanks to The Departed being a remake. And sure, The Departed is plenty intense, and also fairly downbeat, but it does have a slightly neater ending than Infernal Affairs. It’s hard to elaborate without going further, but what can be said is that the story is the same either way: there are two people who’ve gone undercover, with one being a detective who’s undercover in a gang, and the other a gang member who’s gone undercover in the police force.

It’s all cat-and-mouse stuff, and it’s also the kind of story that can’t end well for everyone, though there’s a ton of suspense in anticipating whether it can end well for anyone. And if you know what’s coming, or if you think you know what’s coming (like, if you’ve seen The Departed first), it’s still great... just don't expect anything too uplifting here. To further compare it to The Departed, Infernal Affairs might be more straight to the point and perhaps faster-paced, too, for what that’s worth.

Once Upon a Time in America does what a lot of great epic movies do by feeling sprawling in some ways, but then it also manages to achieve a feeling of being quite personal and intimate in other regards. If you look at things chronologically, it’s about a group of young boys who grow up to be ruthless gangsters, making much of their money during the Prohibition era, and then at least one lives into old age, and he grapples with various memories of his violent past.

That’s simplifying things for sure, because Once Upon a Time in America does not play out chronologically, with the previously alluded-to old man looking back on his life, and these play out in a series of sometimes strange flashbacks… and then things get even more unusual – and even surreal – in the film’s “present.” All the while, Once Upon a Time in America works as a deconstruction of the whole gangster genre, so it’s deeply upsetting, oftentimes violent, and totally unafraid to have its main characters do numerous terrible things throughout.

When The Godfather (1972) ends, it’s definitely not happy, but it still feels lighter in comparison to The Godfather Part II. There was a good deal of murder and tragedy to be found in the first movie, sure, though it’s the sequel that bumps things up a notch in those regards, especially because the family side of the first film is on its way to being broken by that film’s end, and then you see the Corleone family (and crime empire) well and truly break down in The Godfather Part II.

It’s a downfall for Michael Corleone, mostly, and he suffers a sort of death in every regard but physical (since The Godfather Part III exists, so he kind of has to make it to there). The Godfather Part II is about him losing friends, family, and much by way of hope of becoming legitimate. The film also contrasts Michael’s downfall with his father’s rise in the past, so that adds another layer to things in terms of it being a tragedy and all.

While The Irishman isn't as violent as Casino, it is a more harrowing and overall sadder film, and you can use it to help make the argument that age has made Martin Scorsese a better filmmaker, in some ways, alongside being a more brutally honest one. Not that his earlier films were lacking those things either, yet if you look at Silence, The Irishman, and Killers of the Flower Moon… like, come on. They're all pretty despair-filled movies.

As a gangster movie, The Irishman is about as dark as things get, and the whole movie pushes things further than Once Upon a Time in America, looking at a person affiliated with the mob aging and looking back on the most violent and life-changing events from his past, usually with regret. All the characters either die suddenly (and usually gruesomely) or they live overlong ages and deal with losing everyone else. The final act of The Irishman is particularly concerned with such things, and it’s an absolute downer in ways that are hard to put into words.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

There are few things I enjoy more than settling in for a good soapy period drama, preferably one involving extravagant gowns, vicious social maneuvering, forbidden romances and people getting spectacularly worked up over who gets invited to dinner. So of course, I'm a big fan of “The Gilded Age.” Four seasons in, I'm still thoroughly invested. I've been looking forward to this new chapter for months, and I'm happy to report that HBO's lavish historical drama has delivered another delicious helping of everything I love about it.

Verdict: “The Gilded Age” season 4 is another lavish, deliciously soapy treat, with juicy new conflicts and a terrific ensemble that makes even the smallest social squabbles entertaining. A few storylines stumble, but I'm still more than happy to spend another season among New York's most extravagantly dressed troublemakers.

Release schedule: Episode 1 on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 9 p.m. ET

The new season picks up several months after the events of season 3, with the usual assortment of New York's elite navigating romance, family squabbles, and the delicate business of maintaining their social standing. Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) and George (Morgan Spector) are facing serious marital difficulties, while their daughter Gladys (Taissa Farmiga) is preparing for motherhood in England.

Across the street, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is adjusting to a household where she no longer calls all the shots; Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) is balancing her writing ambitions with her relationship with Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica); and Marian (Louisa Jacobson) and Larry Russell (Harry Richardson) remain frustratingly complicated.

There's plenty happening across these interconnected households, and while some storylines are more compelling than others, season 4 finds the show giving its best characters fresh reasons to scheme, spar, and occasionally make me want to yell at the television. I've seen all eight episodes, but I promise not to reveal too much, as this is a show's plot turns are best enjoyed weekly.

Warning: Light spoilers ahead (not much beyond the trailer)

Kelly most recently reviewed "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

One of the things I've always loved about “The Gilded Age” is its ability to make seemingly trivial matters feel enormously consequential. A dinner invitation can become a declaration of war.

Season 4 also introduces some genuinely compelling stakes, particularly for the Russell family. I've always enjoyed watching Bertha and George operate as an unstoppable power couple, with her social ambition and his business acumen making them practically invincible. So, seeing them at odds is painful. At the same time, I have to admit that their relationship was in danger of becoming a little too perfect. Now, with their marriage under strain, both have to reckon with what happens when their greatest ally becomes their biggest obstacle.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Coon remains an absolute force as Bertha, who is accustomed to getting what she wants and isn't particularly good at taking no for an answer. Spector gets some terrific material, too, as George grapples with the consequences of getting shot and mounting professional pressures. Their chemistry remains one of the show's biggest assets, and I desperately want these two crazy kids to work things out. But I'm also enjoying the fact that the show isn't making it easy for them.

Meanwhile, Agnes has her own ambitions to pursue, setting up a delicious clash of wills as she and Bertha vie for the opportunity to host President Grover Cleveland (guest star Jim Gaffigan). Baranski is always a treat, particularly when Agnes has a reason to be indignant and mouth off. Seeing these two formidable women competing for the same prize is exactly the sort of society skirmish I break out the popcorn for.

One of the best facets of “The Gilded Age” is its exploration of the world of upper-class Black Americans, and season 4 blessedly gives us more of that. Peggy's growing success as a writer brings new complications as she navigates her upcoming marriage to William and the expectations of his family, particularly his mother, Elizabeth Kirkland Phylicia Rashad), who would make everyone in the r/JustNoMIL subreddit quake. Rashad is simply divine in the role, and I relish seeing her face off against both Peggy and Peggy's mother, Dorothy (Audra McDonald).

Then there's Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) and Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran), whose unconventional partnership is quickly becoming a favorite storyline. The two make a formidable team, and I love watching them scheme their way toward greater influence in New York society. They're a bona fide power couple in the making; long may their unholy alliance reign.

The show also continues to get plenty of mileage out of the household dynamics between Agnes and Ada (Cynthia Nixon). Baranski and Nixon are such a wonderfully entertaining pairing that I could watch them bicker over curtains for an entire episode. Even the lighter storylines involving the servants and their increasingly complicated lives add to the show's rich ensemble feel. Not every subplot lands with equal force, but there's rarely a dull moment.

My biggest frustration remains Marian and Larry, whose romantic entanglement continues to test my patience. I understand that a TV romance needs obstacles, but at some point, the writers have to give these two a break. Their continued complications seem so contrived. Come on, already!

Still, I have few complaints about "The Gilded Age" season 4. The production design and costumes are a feast for the eyes. This is the kind of show where I want to pause every few minutes just to admire someone's dress or the sheer extravagance of a dinner table. The performances are equally strong, with Coon, Baranski, Benton and Rashad among the standouts.

What I appreciate most is that “The Gilded Age” knows exactly what it is. It can explore serious subjects like race and women's independence while also giving us extravagant parties, romantic scandals and enough high-society backstabbing to fill several lifetimes. Sometimes I want challenging prestige television; other times, I just want to watch Christine Baranski deliver a devastating put-down in a spectacular hat. There's room for both. So, take a glass of champagne and enjoy.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3458. iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

What do you think of the latest Apple Photos changes in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.
