#3455. I tested the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential Mattress and it delivered plenty of cushioning for side sleepers — but here's who should steer clear

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The CopperFlex Essential is Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable adult mattress, with a 10" model regularly priced under $600 for a queen. I found its pressure relief excellent for side sleeping, with no pressure whatsoever mounting in my shoulders and hips. Stomach sleepers will need something firmer for more back support, and hot sleepers should look elsewhere for effective cooling. However, couples will detect minimal motion transfer from a restless co-sleeper, and strong edges mean you'll sleep securely. Sure, there are much cheaper mattresses out there that offer better value for money, but the CopperFlex Essential is still worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a super-comfortable mid-market bed.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

We conduct seven robust tests in our lab to capture objective data on the four areas of a mattress that most affect your sleep comfort: pressure relief, temperature regulation, motion isolation and edge support. We also sleep on a mattress for at least three weeks before subjectively rating it. This data is fed into a scoring system, along with feedback captured by our testing panel, to create an overall score. Read our full mattress methodology.

When Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable mattress, the Dreamfoam Essential, was discontinued, it was swiftly replaced by the CopperFlex Essential Mattress. While both models sport a navy-and-grey appearance, come in multiple height options, and are marketed as entry-level, affordable beds, there is one key difference: the addition of copper-infused gel.

With the addition of copper-infused memory foam, the CopperFlex Essential dovetails into Brooklyn Bedding's CopperFlex collection, a cooling line-up of beds that includes the CopperFlex Pro Hybrid Mattress (which rivals some of the year's best mattresses thanks to its luxurious comfort). The CopperFlex Essential is also a mid-range bed, but at the lower end of the spectrum, usually sold for under $600 in a queen.

But while the CopperFlex Essential, like the Dreamfoam, is billed as a budget-friendly, no-frills alternative to the brand's more premium beds, its price still isn't low enough to fit into the budget tier.

So, when compared with the best cheap mattresses out there, including the Siena Signature Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Mattress, does the CopperFlex Essential offer good value for money? And does its addition of cooling copper gel mean it's the right fit for hot sleepers?

To find out, we vigorously tested a full-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential Mattress in our sleep lab and slept on it at home for three weeks. Here are our honest thoughts...

It's easy to tell when you're getting a good deal at Brooklyn Bedding, as the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales are split into two discounts: a regular 25% discount and a holiday-related 30% off sale. If you see a 25% discount on the CopperFlex Essential, then you're looking at the standard price (it's never sold at MSRP).

If there's a 30% off sale, however, then that means you're getting a fantastic discount. This 30% discount typically coincides with the biggest holidays and sale events, including the Black Friday mattress sales, the Cyber Monday mattress sales, and the Presidents' Day mattress sales. This is brand's biggest price drop, and the only time it's ever been topped was a 32% discount during the Labor Day mattress sales in fall 2025.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So, how much is the CopperFlex Essential when these discounts are applied? The price of the CopperFlex Essential varies depending on the height you choose. For the 10" model (which is the model I tested for this review), a queen size is $699 at MSRP and $524.25 with the regular 25% off deal. During 30% off sale, a queen-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential drops down to $489.30.

We define a "budget" or "cheap" mattress as one that's regularly under $400 in a queen, which means that the CopperFlex Essential isn't in the budget price tier (despite being marketed as a budget-friendly option). Instead, it sits in the lower mid-range price tier, along with mattresses such as the Nectar Classic and Bear Original.

The CopperFlex Essential is also a cheaper alternative to mattresses found at the more expensive end of the mid-range tier, such as the Nectar Premier and the Leesa Original (both typically $999 for a queen).

That said, there are plenty of mattresses out there with a similar, if not better, construction. The top-rated 10" Siena Signature Memory Foam Mattress, now $329 in a queen at Siena Sleep is a prime example, as is the cooling 12" CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress, which is regularly $399.99 in a queen at SweetNight.

However, one department where the CopperFlex Essential stands out is its generous benefits, including a free shipping, a 365-night sleep trial, and a lifetime warranty. The only downside is that returns come with a fee of $99.

Thanks to a regular 25% off sale, a queen 10" CopperFlex Essential is always under $600. However, 30% discounts during the biggest mattress sales of the year take a queen 10" model down to $489.30. Whether you buy it for 25% off or 30%, you always get generous benefits, including a 365-night sleep trial and a lifetime warranty (shame about the returns fee, though).

The design of the CopperFlex Essential varies (but not hugely) depending on the height option you choose, with the shortest height (6") containing only two layers with the thicker models (12" and 14") contain four layers.

While the 6" and 8" models are the cheapest, they are not thick enough for most adult sleepers and should only be used as a temporary bed (such as for guests, RVs, and growing children). That's why I opted to test the 10" model, as mattress thickness should be at least 10" to support most adults and sleep styles.

However, all height options have a fiberglass-free all-foam build that features a "Nano Stain Terminator Protector" cover (which safeguards against stains and spills) and a top layer of memory foam infused with antimicrobial copper.

The 10" model I tested features a 1" comfort layer of copper-infused memory foam on top and a durable 5" base layer for stabilizing support at the bottom. In between the comfort and base layer, a 4" transition layer acts as a buffer between the softer and firmer materials for balanced support.

For full context, I'm a side and back sleeper weighing under 130lbs, so I need a mattress that's supportive but has enough softness to soothe my side-sleeper pressure points (namely, my hips and shoulders).

The CopperFlex Essential is not the first all-foam mattress I've tested, as I've also written full reviews for the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress. Both impressed me with their body-contouring comfort and support, but the former did trap some body heat (which is far from atypical for all-foam beds).

So, on the one hand, I was looking forward to testing a memory foam bed, as I know they can make the best mattresses for side sleepers, but I also didn't want to put up with any heat build-up (the testing period coincided with an unseasonably warm fall).

While the CopperFlex Essential didn't deliver the cooling prowess of the SweetNight CoolNest or the universal support of the EGOHOME Black, it still kept this side sleeper comfortable.

Let's see why I recommend the CopperFlex Essential to side sleepers and how it scored in other areas...

Temperature regulation refers to how well a mattress maintains a comfortable sleep temperature and prevents body heat retention. It's a key testing area, as a mattress that doesn't regulate temperature well can lead to night sweats and 3 a.m. wake ups.

While the best cooling mattresses feature top-of-line cooling tech to regulate temperature, most conventional mattresses today feature some degree of thermal regulation.

The CopperFlex Essential is definitely not a dedicated cooling model (and it isn't marketed as one), and the only form of temperature regulation it has is the addition of heat-dispersing copper. That being said, the Siena Signature features very little cooling materials (just a breathable cover) and it performed incredibly well in our temperature tests.

To test how well the CopperFlex Essential regulates temperature, we used a thermal imaging camera to measure how much of my body heat the mattress absorbs and dissipates. To do this I laid on the CopperFlex mattress for 15 minutes while the temperature of the bed was recorded every minute using a thermal imaging camera.

At its hottest point, we observed a maximum temperature increase (MTI) of 11.1°F — that means it was over 11.1°F warmer than before I laid down on the mattress. We generally rate an MTI over 9°F as "poor" and a 1 out of 5. This result was unsurprising, as the CopperFlex Essential isn't a cooling mattress.

That said, the all-foam Siena Signature had an MTI of 9.8°F, despite possessing no specialist cooling materials. Meanwhile, the mid-range all-foam Nectar Premier had an MTI of 8.1 9°F.

I also know from testing the SweetNight CoolNest (which is a dedicated cooling model) that MTI isn't always the best indicator of cooling ability. Despite being a cooling mattress, the CoolNest actually had a much higher MTI of 15.2°F, but redeemed itself through an ultra-fast cooling rate (CR)

The CR refers to how well a mattress dissipates heat during the first five minutes after the MTI. In the CopperFlex's case, the bed shed my body heat at a rate of 1.32°F per minute, a rapid cooling rate considered to "best in class".

The lower the maximum temperature increase (MTI) and the faster the cooling rate, the cooler you'll sleep.

It wasn't the fastest cooling rate displayed by a memory foam mattress (that distinction goes to the SweetNight CoolNest and the Siena Signature, which had a rapid cooling rate of 1.52°F per minute), but it's still relatively fast when you consider that the Nectar Premier dissipated heat at 0.9°F per minute.

15 minutes after I left the mattress, the CopperFlex Essential still hadn't returned to its baseline temperature. However, I should point out that none of its all-foam rivals did either.

In fact, when comparing the way the CopperFlex regulates heat versus its rivals, I was struck by how similarly it performed to the Leesa Original Mattress (usually between $999 and $1,100 for a queen). Both had an MTI of just over 11°F and had an identical rapid cooling rate 1.32°F per minute, which was surprising as Leesa refers to the Original as a "cooling memory foam mattress".

Based on the thermal imaging camera tests alone, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential an objective temperature control score of 3.8 out of 5.

How effectively the CopperFlex Essential absorbed, managed and dissipated heat compared to its closest rivals

In addition to the objective thermal imaging camera tests, we also conduct subjective tests to see how I (and the wider testing panel) perceive the mattress's sleep temperature.

Our subjective feedback was slightly lower than the objective results, with our testing panel awarding a score of 3 out of 5. This score means the mattress offers generally good thermal comfort, but felt mostly neutral with some heat build-up.

I slept on the CopperFlex Essential for three weeks during an unseasonably warm fall in a bedroom with no AC, and while I wouldn't say I overheated or experienced night sweats, I did feel some patches of heat build-up every now and again. I never experienced this while testing the SweetNight CoolNest during the sweltering summer months.

When you're sleeping on a mattress, certain body parts will come into contact with its surface, creating pressure. These body parts are known as pressure points (for example, pressure points when side sleeping include the hips and shoulders), and the way a mattress cushions and supports these pressure points is known as pressure relief.

While each height option comes with a different feel — mattress thickness as a big impact on firmness — Brooklyn Bedding recommends the 10" version I tested to combination back, side, and stomach sleepers.

During our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I agreed that the CopperFlex suits side sleeping the most, as it cushions the hips and shoulders. We also think it could suit some back sleepers, too, even if it doesn't offer the best lumbar support.

I felt I was the ideal candidate to test the mattress, as I'm a combo side and back sleeper. From the first night, I felt ample cushioning when sleeping on my side, especially in the shoulder region. In fact, I found the CopperFlex to be one of the softest mattresses I've ever tested — and I've tested the ultra-plush Helix Sunset Luxe.

Do I think it's one of the best mattresses for back sleepers? No, but I still felt supported when sleeping on my back, and I didn't wake up with lower back pain. Overall, if you're a side sleeper, or predominantly a side sleeper who also sleeps on your back from time to time, then I recommend the CopperFlex Essential.

The deeper the indentation and faster the response time, the better the ability of a mattress to relieve pressure

A mentioned above, Brooklyn Bedding also recommends the CopperFlex Essential to stomach sleepers. For stomach-sleeping tester Ruth Jones, the CopperFlex Essential did cause some lower back strain when lying on her front, and she warned that back sleepers could feel some lower back pressure.

"When back sleeping, I could feel strain on my core," Jones told me.

However, she agreed that its gentle contouring makes the CopperFlex Essential a top pick for side sleepers.

"Side sleeping was far and away the most comfortable position to lie in," she said. "I wasn’t expecting this as the mattress didn’t initially appear to have much contouring but it was soft at the shoulders and hips which meant no pressure build up."

Thanks to its comfort for side sleepers, we awarded the CopperFlex a subjective pressure relief score of 4 out of 5 ("Very Good").

We also performed objective pressure relief tests using a 25kg weight. We placed the weight at the hip and shoulder areas of the mattress, and then measured how deep the weight sank and how quickly the mattress bounced back when the weight was removed.

The CopperFlex had an average Indentation Depth (ID) of 3.6" and Recovery Time (RT), of 2.25 seconds, achieving an objective pressure relief score of 3.4 out of 5, which is a "Good" objective final rating. The weight test results indicate that the CopperFlex is a responsive bed (I agree, as I found it easy to move around on) but I was surprised that the weights didn't sink further on what I perceive as a cushioning bed.

Even more surprising is that Siena Memory Foam had a higher ID of 3.63", despite being a firm bed that is recommended to anyone but side sleepers. The CopperFlex's RT, on the other hand, was one of the quickest. A quick RT is especially important in a memory foam mattress, as they can be notorious for their "quicksand" sinkage.

Combining subjective and objective feedback, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief a score of 3.76 out of 5, indicating a "Strong Performance".

We rate a mattress's firmness on a standardized scale of one to 10, with 10 being the firmest and 1 being the softest. We don't use any objective tests to measure firmness, as this key area is highly subjective and is dependent on body weight, sleep position, and personal preference.

To get a good idea of the CopperFlex's firmness level, I asked each member of our diverse testing panel to rank the firmness of the CoolNest on a scale of one to 10. I then created a collective rating based on everyone's feedback.

The Brooklyn Bedding calls the firmness of the CopperFlex Essential "medium-firm", which indicates a score of 6-7 out of 10 on the standardized scale. As a team, we mostly agreed with the brand's rating, and awarded the CopperFlex Essential a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

Motion isolation refers to a mattress's ability to prevent a co-sleeper's movements from traveling to your side of the bed and waking you up. Its especially important for couples, co-sleeping families, and anyone who shares a bed with their pets.

Memory foam mattresses tend to be better at absorbing motion than other mattress types, such as innerspring and hybrid mattresses, as they contain dense, slow-moving foams and no springs or coils.

To see how well the CopperFlex Essential isolates motion, we conducted an objective slam ball test and a subjective co-sleeper test.

In our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I evaluated the impact of each other's movements by manually performing motions classed as low, moderate and high force to replicate real-life co-sleeping scenarios.

The faster the decay rate, the better the mattress is at reducing motion transfer (which means you'll be disturbed less by a restless co-sleeper)

During the subjective tests, I felt the high-force movements of my fellow tester, but I would not say the high-force movements were as disruptive as they've been on other mattresses I’ve tested.

My fellow testers were also impressed with the perceived motion isolation, with one panelist saying they could hardly feel the low-force movements. "There was some small motion transfer when the tester moved but I would have slept right through it and it wouldn’t have bothered me as I was falling asleep," they said.

Overall, the CopperFlex Essential earned a subjective score of 3.75 out of 5 for motion isolation.

For for our objective lab-based tests, we dropped a 5kg slam ball on one side of the CopperFlex Essential and measured its impact absorption via an accelerometer on the other. The initial impact average (IIA) was 14.569, which is relatively high when compared to Siena's IIA of 5.527 m/s2 and the Nectar Premier's IIA of 7.961.

However, the CopperFlex Essential redeemed itself with a short decay rate (MDS). So, while the IIA was sizeable, its motion transfer only lasted for 1.72 seconds on average. While not as quick as the Leesa Original's 1.116 second MDS, it still shows that the CopperFlex is adept at deadening the slam ball's motion.

Overall, we rate the CopperFlex's motion isolation as "Strong", with an overall motion isolation score of 3.5. This means that, while you'll feel more moderate and high-force movements, they won't last long enough to cause too much disruption.

Edge support refers to how sturdy the edges of your mattress are, with strong edge support indicating that the sides and foot of the bed will make you feel supported when sitting, sleeping, or getting in and out of bed.

To test the CopperFlex's edge support, we placed a 25kg weight 3" away from the edge of the mattress and measured how far it sank.

After five minutes, the average indentation of the weight was 5.25", which we rate as "strong." The sinkage at the foot of the bed was a little deeper than at the sides of the bed, but we should point out that the edge support at the foot of the bed will only affect sitting rather than sleeping.

To measure the available sleep space, we also performed a roll-off test. For this, our reviewer lies near the edge of the bed and another tester records how close they get to the edge before they feel unstable and are going to roll off. The CopperFlex Essential has a roll-off distance (ROD) of 0.5", a measurement which gets a score of 5 out of 5 as it indicates that most of the mattress can be used for sleeping.

Combing the weight and roll-off test scores, the overall edge support score of the CopperFlex Essential is 4 out of 5, which we rate as "Very Good".

Less compression means better support for sleeping close to the edge or climbing in and out of bed

On the brand's website, the CopperFlex Essential has an overall user score of 4.6 out of 5 from over 800 reviews, which is a pretty glowing score.

Five-star reviews praise how comfortable the mattress is, which many customers buying it for their RVs (it's one of the rare mattress that come in a range of RV sizes). As for negative reviews (which are in the minority) customers criticize the mattress for not being as firm as they expected.

In terms of Brooklyn Bedding's trustworthiness, you can look on review platform TrustPilot website for customer feedback. At the time of writing, the brand has an overall "Excellent" rating of 4.6 out of 5 stars from a total of 210 reviews.

Let me start by saying that there are cheaper memory foam mattress out there that offer better value for money than the CopperFlex Essential. That being said, I would definitely recommend this body-contouring mattress to a certain group: side sleepers.

The CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief, is a standout feature that makes this all-foam bed a top pick for anyone who sleeps on their side.

I tend to perceive mattresses as being firmer than my fellow testers do, and I often require good mattress break-in period to feel comfortable. However, I felt well-cushioned from night one on the CopperFlex Essential, and felt zero pressure build up in my shoulders.

Edge support is good, too, and I always felt secure even when sleeping close to the edge. For couples, motion transfer from a restless partner shouldn't be an issue, and the sleep temperature should remain neutral enough for the average person.

That said, hot sleepers will need to look at a model with more cooling ability, such as the SweetNight CoolNest or the Siena Siena Signature, which are both cheaper than the lower mid-range CopperFlex Essential. I wouldn't recommend this soft mattress to stomach sleepers wither, as the lack of firmness won't keep their hips and lower back supported.

However, I do think this is a mid-range mattress worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a mid-market bed for your home, guest room, or even your RV.

Like the CopperFlex Essential, the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress is a conventional all-foam bed designed for medium-firm comfort. However, I found it to be much more supportive than the CopperFlex Essential, and I slept comfortably on it in all sleep positions. Plus, it's always under $400 for a queen.

If you're looking for an affordable memory foam bed, but the CoolNest seems a little too soft for your sleep position, check out the Siena Memory Foam Mattress as a firmer (and cheaper) alternative. It also regulates temperature surprisingly well, but side sleepers will find it way too hard.

If you want something that sleeps cooler than the CopperFlex, check out this cooling model from SweetNight. The SweetNight CoolNest is one of those rare budget mattresses (always under $400 for a queen) equipped with specialist cooling tech.

Frances Daniels is a PPA-accredited journalist and Sleep Staff Writer at Tom's Guide with an MA in Magazine Journalism from Cardiff University. Her role includes covering mattress and sleep news and writing sleep product reviews and buyer's guides, including our Best Hybrid Mattress 2025 guide. She is interested in the relationship between sleep and health, interviewing an array of experts to create in-depth articles about topics such as nutrition, sleep disorders, sleep hygiene, and mattress care. She is also our specialist on mattress toppers — producing bed topper reviews and taking care of our Best Mattress Toppers 2025 guide — and leads content relating to fiberglass-free beds for a non-toxic sleep. Outside of Tom's Guide, she has written for Ideal Home and Marie Claire.

#3454. Ariana Grande Gives NYC Marathon Runner Surprise of a Lifetime

Ariana Grande is spreading a little extra love in the Big Apple ... teaming up with boyfriend Ricky Alvarez to give one New York City Marathon runner the surprise of a lifetime.

The couple was spotted cheering on runners from the sidelines Sunday when an influencer named Ella Schweiger approached them with an unusual request ... write a message of encouragement for a complete stranger who had just tackled the grueling 26.2-mile race.

Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.

Ariana was more than happy to oblige ... grabbing a pen and writing "You did it!" alongside some hearts. She signed the sweet note, "Ari + Ricky."

Ella shared video of the encounter on Instagram ... showing the moment she approached the couple before delivering the message to a runner named Ellie, who was absolutely floored to learn who had written it.

And get this ... Ellie revealed she'd actually been listening to Ariana's music during the race, saying one of her songs helped push her through a particularly brutal stretch around mile 24.

The whole thing was part of Ella's project, "Ella's Envelope," which collects uplifting messages from strangers and delivers them to runners ... proving a few kind words can go a long way.

As for Ariana and Ricky ... the two rekindled their romance earlier this year, nearly a decade after their first breakup, and made things Instagram official in August.

The race may have been 26.2 miles ... but Ari's kindness went even further.

#3453. This Sci-Fi Kids' Series Captures the Horrors of War Better Than Most Adult Books

Scholastic has come a long way since its founding in 1920. Its content ranges from fun, educational adventures like The Magic School Bus to light horror stories like Goosebumps. Then you have more unique and out-there works, like Animorphs, which ran from 1996 to 2001. Written by Katherine Applegate and her husband Michael Grant with the aid of a team of ghostwriters, this was a science fiction series about alien parasites called the Yeerks invading Earth in the hopes of enslaving humans to use in their galactic war against the Andelites, an advanced race of space-centaurs. Earth's only hope comes in the form of five teenagers who use Andelite technology to transform into animals, and a young Andelite cadet who is the sole survivor of a deadly space battle.

What set Animorphs apart from Scholastic's other series wasn't just its creative sci-fi setting, but the level of detail and maturity put into it — namely, its approach to war. The fact that the books were written for kids did not stop the husband-wife duo from writing about gory battles, genocide, paranoia, and propaganda, among other horrors of war. This honesty gave Animorphs a unique identity in the world of children's literature, and even thirty years after the first book was published, it has aged like fine wine for its nuanced handling of such heavy topics.

Most children's media try to keep their depictions of war simple. You'll generally have one side portrayed as the aggressor with aspirations of conquest, and another as the victim or underdog trying to fight against them. At first, Animorphs follows this trend. The six protagonists are underdogs forced to use their morphing powers to keep their identities safe from the Yeerks, a ruthless galactic empire that has already subjugated other species. The kids are forced to use guerrilla tactics to avoid open warfare until the Andelites arrive with reinforcements.

However, the series is very quick to throw a wrench in this perception. The noble and heroic Andelites are soon revealed to be vain, arrogant, and paranoid, as it was one of their scientists who gave the Yeerks the technology to take to space. We even see them use propaganda to cover their tracks. In Book 8, The Alien, the Andelites are furious when they learn their morphing technology is known by the humans and force a young cadet to take the fall for the leak of information. It's just the first of many instances where Applegate and Grant delve into how governments try to control the narrative in wars, showing that often, your allies in a war are only so because they hate your enemy as much as you.

Likewise, the Yeerks are full of nuances. Yes, they are parasites who take away the autonomy of their hosts, but to not do so is to live a blind, deaf life eternally swimming in the pool of your birth, all while possessing a mind as complex as any human's. Their expansionist war occurred partially because they were overwhelmed by this impossible reality they had been exposed to, and partially because the Andelites were trying to contain them on their home world. Several Yeerk characters are complex individuals, with wants, goals, aspirations, and even loved ones. Many of them even sympathize with the plight of their hosts and would gladly try to find a way to peacefully coexist, but they are bullied into silence by the military and the ruling Council of Thirteen. More than an evil alien species out to conquer humanity, the Yeerks are a young empire hated by an established power and internally divided, hampered by their biology and inexperience.

Perhaps the best example of this complexity can be seen within the protagonists themselves. While everything they do is to save humanity from enslavement, they often have to step into morally dubious territory. One example happens early in the series in Book 7, The Stranger, when the Animorphs destroyed a device that allowed Yeerks to feed when outside their hosts every three days. While a major victory that slowed down the Yeerks' plans, it also caused hundreds of Yeerks to die an agonizing death by starvation, to say nothing of all the human hosts who were also quietly killed off. The protagonists would also use torture as needed and had a horrible track record when it came to recruiting members. This makes sense in a lot of ways; what teenager is going to fight a secret war for years and not go a little crazy? It all shows the reader that wars are almost never simple good vs. evil, and that everyone has the chance to be a hero or a villain.

Applegate and Grant vividly detail the atrocities of the conflict. The battles between the Animorphs and Yeerk controllers leave very little to the imagination when it comes to body horror. The Yeerks might have access to advanced technologies and strong alien hosts, but a blow from the paw of an adult grizzly bear or the bite force of a Siberian tiger is enough to cause major damage. These clashes are bloody and hectic, with plenty of severed limbs, torn-out eyes, broken bones, and worse. The morphing technology protects their bodies, but the psychological effect weighs heavily on the kids.

Many times, the kids are reduced to tears when they change back to human form due to close calls with death. They can also get stuck in animal form if they don't change back within two hours. Some, like the athletic fashionista Rachel, end up embracing the violence and become hardened killers. Others, like the animal-loving Cassie, are repulsed by it, leading them to make drastic choices in the name of finding a resolution to the conflict. The longer the conflict goes on, the greater the mental strain becomes, leading to tragic consequences for the characters and their loved ones.

In Book 1, The Invasion, de facto leader Jake learns that his older brother, Tom, is a controller, and he is unable to rescue him. Thus, he is forced to be on his guard constantly. His best friend, Marco, later learns that his mother, who was presumed to have died in a boating accident, is actually Visser One, the highest-ranked member of the Yeerk military. And while the other Animorphs don't have controller family members, it highlights how terrifying the Yeerks are: they can literally be anyone, and you won't know until it's too late. This reinforces a deep sense of isolation and paranoia. When enemies could be anywhere, how do you go about making allies?

In the end, all these qualities make Animorphs such a mature and nuanced series. Sure, it still has plenty of silly adventures and the infamous covers are decidedly goofy, but at its core, the books introduced kids to war by highlighting the human cost, not just in the lives lost, but in how the psychology of those living through such horrors is slowly eroded. Here, good people are forced to do terrible things in order to survive, and atrocities can come from anywhere and anyone. In doing so, Animorphs created one of the best children's sci-fi series that is still remembered and celebrated to this day.

#3452. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3451. Ellen DeGeneres Donates $5K to Producer Matthew Wright's Family After Death at 52

Ellen DeGeneres and Allison Holker Boss are among the famous names appearing on a GoFundMe supporting the family of former "Ellen DeGeneres Show" executive producer Matthew Wright, who died suddenly.

The fundraiser's public donor list shows a $5K contribution under Ellen's name, while Allison, the widow of Ellen's former DJ Stephen "tWitch" Boss, is listed as donating $500.

Ellen's longtime executive producer Andy Lassner is also listed as contributing $1K, along with "Dancing with the Stars" executive producer Conrad Green, who gave the same amount.

The outpouring of financial support comes after Wright died Friday, October 30, while working remotely in Los Angeles, according to the fundraiser. His family described his death as an "unfathomable tragedy."

The GoFundMe explains Wright and his husband, Justin, were both laid off this summer, leaving the family struggling to cover the unexpected costs of bringing his body home to New York, funeral arrangements and a memorial in Los Angeles.

Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.

Ellen paid tribute to Wright Monday in an emotional Instagram video, remembering him as a funny, smart and kind man who was loved by everyone on the show.

She also revealed they had been planning to work on a new project together before his sudden death.

Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.

Lassner shared his own heartbreaking tribute, revealing Wright had visited the set of "The Jennifer Hudson Show" just hours before his death.

The fundraiser says any money remaining after expenses will go into a trust for Wright's niece, Sami.

#3449. Brad Pitt's Daughter Vivienne Officially Drops His Last Name

Brad Pitt has officially been dropped from another one of his kids' names ... his 18-year-old daughter Vivienne has legally ditched her famous father's surname ... TMZ has confirmed.

A Los Angeles judge approved Vivienne's petition Monday, changing her legal name from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie.

The judge signed off on the request after no objections were filed.

As we reported ... Vivienne filed paperwork in July, shortly after turning 18, citing "personal" reasons for wanting to remove "Pitt" from her name.

She had already been using her mom Angelina Jolie's last name professionally, receiving credit as "Vivienne Jolie" in the Playbill for the Broadway production of "The Outsiders," which she worked on alongside Angelina.

Vivienne is now the fourth of Brad and Angelina's six children to legally drop their dad's surname.

Her older sister Shiloh officially changed her name in 2024, while siblings Maddox and Zahara received court approval for their own name changes earlier this year.

Vivienne's twin brother Knox also left "Pitt" off his high school diploma, though he has not legally changed his name.

As TMZ previously reported ... sources close to Brad have claimed Angelina is responsible for the growing rift between the actor and his children, describing the name changes as part of an ongoing effort to alienate them from their father.

Brad and Angelina finalized their divorce in December 2024, but remain locked in a separate legal battle over their French winery, Château Miraval.

#3448. Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac

Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.

Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…

The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.

It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.

John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:

We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL

Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro.

Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.

Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here. The new machines are also available on Amazon.

Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini, M6 iMac, and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration.

The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos. We’re so back. pic.twitter.com/Ce6G8EIVQF

The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.

Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.

The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.

Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

I honestly think this is a downgrade. Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar? It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it. Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook. What’s the actual point?

If it supported the Apple Pencil, I could understand the appeal, especially for designers. But without it, I honestly don’t see much use for it. Maybe I’m wrong, but I’ve used touchscreen Windows laptops before, and I never really found it useful.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction. Apple needs a better marketing team that understands what people actually want, rather than adding a touchscreen that, in my opinion, offers very little practical use.

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.

Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.

You can find Apple’s press release for the new machines here. All configurations are available to order from Amazon.

#3447. Disney Star Erik von Detten: Company From Elder Abuse Lawsuit Owes Over $60 Million

The company Disney star Erik von Detten worked for when he allegedly played an "instrumental" role in finding customers to buy gold says it owes over $60 million to creditors ... TMZ learned.

According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Rosland Capital, where Erik worked for years, revealed the massive figure as part of its ongoing bankruptcy.

Rosland Capital listed debts of $63,695,061. The company's business involved selling precious metals to retail customers.

As we previously reported, Rosland filed for bankruptcy months after the company and Erik were sued for elder abuse by a couple, Sheila Greenberg and Norman Greenberg. The couple claimed Erik worked for Rosland, where he sold them gold.

The couple said they bought the gold for over $2 million, but later learned it was only worth $1.3 million. The lawsuit claimed Erik of took advantage of the couple due to their age.

Erik did not respond to the suit before the company filed for bankruptcy.

As TMZ first reported, the creditors in the bankruptcy claim Erik has been a "roadblock" in obtaining information about Rosland. The case is ongoing.

#3445. Every Jane Austen Love Interest, Ranked

Jane Austen fans have enjoyed a plethora of characters to dissect over the years, especially romantic ones. This is quite fortunate because in Austen's books there are a lot of them. Every main character has at least two romantic interests: one that they secretly love and one that is recommended to them by others.

Diving into this rich and varied territory, there is a kaleidoscope of personality traits to admonish and admire. Austen does a fantastic job of making her characters feel real and paints them so vividly in readers' minds that familiarity with them feels like second nature. Out of the bouquet of leading men who won the hearts of Austen's main characters, here is how they stack up against one another.

Edmund Bertram is the beige of Jane Austen romantic interests. He is neither hot nor cold, but lukewarm in many respects. He is a kind person and takes care of his younger cousin Fanny when she arrives to live with him and his family in Mansfield Park. Even though Fanny develops romantic feelings for Edmund, he spends the majority of the story pining for Mary Crawford.

Edmund's admiration for Fanny feels like an afterthought. He only decides he likes Fanny when he has a falling out with Mary and is determined not to love her anymore. Edmund's last-minute pivot to Fanny feels more like a rebound than a realization. Even though Edmund is more virtuous than the lustful Henry Crawford, he is consistently infatuated with Mary. Though Fanny gets her happily ever after, and they end up together, readers are left to wonder how true his affections for her really are.

Henry Tilney is a great match for Catherine in Northanger Abbey. They share similar interests and love to read, especially Gothic novels. They have different manners, and the sarcastic and charismatic Henry comes to admire the candid and genuine, straightforward nature of Catherine.

Henry was close to his late mother and has a good relationship with his sister. This gives him a keen insight into female feelings, and he expresses knowledge of topics that men of the era had little interest in, like fabric choices for dresses. He empathizes with his mother and sister's plights and recognizes how his father's treatment of them was cruel. Unlike other characters in Austen's novels (Willoughby, Frank Churchill, cough, cough), Henry stands up to his father and proposes to Catherine, despite his objections based on her lack of fortune.

An influence over a person can be a powerful thing, and that subject is brought to bear in Persuasion. Although Captain Frederick Wentworth and Anne Elliot are in love, Anne is persuaded by her father and her mentor not to marry him. Captain Wentworth is snubbed by her family as being poor and beneath them socially, and they want Anne to wait and marry a wealthy gentleman instead. After a successful career in the navy, Captain Wentworth comes back into Anne's life, and they both eventually confess that they have never stopped loving each other.

When Wentworth returns, he is wealthy, successful, and a respected naval officer. His social status has changed, and he is looking for a wife. Although he secretly still loves Anne, he takes the opportunity to get back at her by treating her with indifference and flirting with Louisa Musgrove. Wentworth doesn't seem to realize that his actions could be misinterpreted by Louisa and her family. Luckily, her feelings for him cease, and he eventually proposes to and marries Anne.

It is hard to blame Wentworth for being a little spiteful around the woman who broke his heart, but doing it at the expense of the young and naive Louisa was careless. Luckily, it ended up in everyone's favor, and all's well that ends well. Despite his moody overreaction upon his return, Wentworth is one of Austen's most endearing heroes because of his fidelity to Anne. Persuasion examines long-lost love from both a male and female perspective, and Wentworth is a figure many can identify with.

When readers first meet Edward Ferrars, they wonder if he will be as petty and materialistic as his sister Fanny, but he turns out to be quite the opposite in Sense and Sensibility. Unlike his other two siblings, Edward is humble, kind, and a genuinely nice person. He forms an attachment to Elinor as they spend time together before she and her mother and sisters move out of Norland Park. However, things seem hopeless and complicated for Elinor when she finds out that he has secretly been engaged to Lucy Steele for several years.

For much of the rest of the novel, it appears as though Elinor and Edward will never be together, until a shocking plot twist towards the very end! Austen knew how to keep her readers on the edge of their seats, and Elinor and Edward's delayed gratification is one of the best. Although Edward did not purposefully mislead anyone, it was harsh for Elinor to hear about his engagement from Lucy instead of him. When eventually confronted by his strict and resentful mother about the engagement, Edward was willing to marry Lucy or set her free since he was disinherited, and he would not go back on his word, which is admirable. Fans rejoice along with Elinor when she and Edward get to be together at last in a surprising twist near the end of the book. Edward is as happy as Elinor to be free to marry her, and their bond based on friendship makes a solid foundation for a happy marriage.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

To quote the 1995 film version of Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon is "[…] the kindest and best of men." Suffering numerous heartbreaks, Colonel Brandon perseveres and continues to display love, loyalty, and honor. Brandon is betrayed and conspired against by his father and brother. They force his sweetheart Eliza to marry Brandon's brother and send him into the army. When he returns, Eliza's life has taken a tragic turn, and before she dies, he promises to care for her illegitimate daughter, also named Eliza. Brandon again has to pick up the pieces when the younger Eliza is left pregnant and abandoned by Willoughby.

In spite of all of his setbacks, betrayals, and wounds from others, Brandon does not become harsh or cruel. He develops a strong admiration for Marianne Dashwood and wants to marry her. Marianne is not attracted to Brandon at first because he has a more reserved and quiet nature. As she spends time with him, she starts to realize that there is more under the surface, and he does care deeply about passions and pursuits, like music.

It is completely understandable why Brandon keeps his feelings close to the chest. The last time he openly loved someone, everything went wrong, and he was stabbed in the back by those closest to him. Towards the final chapters of the book, Marianne comes to see all the admirable character traits Brandon possesses, and they marry. It will likely take some time for Brandon to be able to let his guard down fully, but a feeling and open person like Marianne is the perfect partner to help him. He is also unfailingly kind to their family and gets along well with Elinor.

If there is a man who can take notes, it's Fitzwilliam Darcy in Pride and Prejudice. An aristocrat since birth, Darcy has been largely influenced by the affluent crowd around him and has strict opinions on wealth, social standing, and rank. However, all of these long-held ideals get challenged when he falls in love with the socially less endowed Elizabeth Bennet. In perhaps one of the worst marriage proposals ever, Darcy, who has already persuaded his friend not to propose to Elizabeth's sister, makes notable mention of her inferior status as he asks for her hand. After being verbally scorned and put in his proper place by Elizabeth, Darcy leaves, but does not retire to sulk in idleness.

As the novel goes on, Darcy takes several significant steps to change. He becomes more civil towards Elizabeth and her family and comes to the rescue of two of her sisters, including poor Jane, who finally gets to marry Mr. Bingley. Darcy starts out as a very prideful and stubborn character but becomes much more open and humble by the end. He allows Elizabeth's thoughts and observations to influence him, and he doesn't just talk the talk; he sets about making things right time and again. Darcy and Elizabeth are one of the best enemies-to-lovers in literature and a favorite for movie and TV adaptations.

If anyone deserves the blue ribbon for being the best role model for a Jane Austen romantic interest, it is George Knightley in Emma. Knightley proves over and over again in the book how he is sensible, kind, and selfless. He calls Emma out when she behaves rudely toward an older friend and persuades Harriet to reject Robert Martin's proposal. At every opportunity when Emma makes a blunder, Knightley is there having warned her before, during, or after. Despite his frustrations, he is always respectful and honest with Emma.

Knightley continually puts Emma's needs ahead of his own. Even though he disliked Frank Churchill, he did not say anything because he thought Emma cared for him. At the end of the book, Knightley agrees to leave his home and move in with Emma and her father after they are married because she does not want to leave him alone. Knightley only ever loved Emma for exactly who she was, first as a friend and then as a romantic partner.
